9608.q: What is the octopus’s ability to blend in perfectly with its surroundings called?
9608.e: Camouflage is when an animal changes so that it can hardly be seen. The octopus is a master of camouflage.

9609.q: Which animal builds dams and lodges in rivers with branches?
9609.e: The beaver dams a river with branches and twigs to create a calm pond. In it, it builds its beaver lodge.
9609.m: The beaver is a skilful builder.

9610.q: Which animal is a beetle, like the ladybird?
9610.e: Ladybirds and cockchafers both belong to the beetles. Beetles have hard wing cases that protect their delicate flying wings.

9611.q: Roughly how many fins does a trout have on its whole body?
a: Several, for example on the back, belly and tail
Only two fins on the head
9611.e: A trout has several different fins spread over its whole body. These include, for example, the dorsal fin, the pelvic fins and the tail fin.
9611.m: Trout have several fins on their body.

9612.q: What does the word “rhinoceros” actually mean?
9612.e: The name comes from Greek and means “nose horn”, because the rhinoceros has a horn on its nose. That is how the animal got its name.

9613.q: What does a horse absolutely need in its stable?
a: Lots of space and access to the outdoors
A tiny cage with no window
9613.e: Horses need lots of space to move and should be able to go outside as often as possible. A stable that is too cramped makes them unhappy.
9613.m: Horses need lots of space and time outdoors.

9614.q: At what time of year are sand lizards most active in Switzerland?
a: From spring to autumn, in warm weather
Only in the depths of winter
All year round in sub-zero temperatures
9614.e: As soon as it gets warmer in spring, the animals leave their winter quarters. In autumn, as temperatures fall, they withdraw again.
9614.m: Active from spring to autumn when it is warm.

9615.q: What does an Alpine ibex like to eat most in summer?
9615.e: In summer, ibex feed mainly on juicy Alpine herbs, grasses and flowers on the mountain meadows. They eat only plants.
9615.m: Ibex eat Alpine herbs and grasses.

9616.q: What is special about the tiger among the cats?
a: It is the largest cat species in the world
It is the smallest cat species in the world
It is the only cat that lays eggs
It is the only cat without claws
9616.e: The tiger is the largest living cat species. The Siberian tiger in particular can weigh over 250 kilograms.
9616.m: The tiger is the largest cat.

9617.q: What does a sparrow like to eat most of all?
9617.e: Sparrows like to peck small seeds and grains from the ground. In summer they also like to eat insects.

9618.q: In the picture a trout is hiding. Where does it like to stay?
a: Under stones, roots and overhanging banks
On dry land on the bank
In the middle of a bare concrete slab
9618.e: Such hiding places protect it from enemies and from the strong current. It also lies in wait for prey from there.
9618.m: It hides under stones and roots.

9619.q: Roughly how many years can a Bactrian camel live?
9619.e: In human care they can reach an age of about 40 to 50 years. That is long for mammals of this size.

9620.q: What happens when chimpanzees tickle and play with each other?
a: They make a panting laugh sound
9620.e: When chimpanzees play and are tickled, they make a sound that is a bit like laughing. This shows that they are having fun.
9620.m: Chimpanzees can laugh when they play.

9621.q: How does a goat usually carry its tail compared with a sheep?
a: Always dragging flat on the ground
It has no tail at all
9621.e: Goats usually hold their short tail up, while sheep often let it hang down. This is a small difference between the two species.

9622.q: What does the red kite use to steer its flight especially skilfully?
9622.e: The deeply forked tail can be turned and shifted like a rudder. This lets the red kite fly very elegantly and nimbly.
9622.m: The tail steers the red kite’s flight.

9623.q: What does a magnifying glass do to the sun's rays?
a: It focuses them on one point
It turns them into heat without light
9623.e: A magnifying glass is curved and bends the light rays so that they meet at one point. It can get so hot there that paper starts to burn.
9623.m: A magnifying glass focuses light on one point.

9624.q: What does “cold-blooded” mean for an animal like the lizard?
a: Its body temperature adjusts to its surroundings
9624.e: Cold-blooded animals such as reptiles cannot control their body temperature themselves. That is why they often sunbathe to warm up.

9625.q: What colour is a polar bear’s fur usually?
9625.e: The polar bear’s fur is white to slightly yellowish. That way it is well camouflaged in the snow.
9625.m: The fur is white to yellowish.

9626.q: What do wasps often hunt as food for their larvae?
9626.e: Wasps catch small insects such as flies or caterpillars. They feed these to their hungry larvae.
9626.m: Wasps hunt flies for their larvae.

9627.q: In which regions do moose mainly live?
9627.e: Moose need cool forests with lakes and swamps. They are found in Scandinavia, Russia and North America.
9627.m: Moose live in cool northern forests.

9628.q: What does a carrion crow mainly eat?
a: almost anything, for example insects, carrion, seeds and eggs
9628.e: Carrion crows eat almost anything and feed on insects, carrion, grains, fruit and sometimes also eggs or chicks of other species. This variety helps them survive.

9629.q: What do rhinos do during the day when it is very hot?
a: They rest in the shade or in mud
They dig themselves into the ground
9629.e: In great heat, rhinos look for a shady spot or lie down in a cool mud puddle. That way they protect themselves from the sun.
9629.m: In the heat, rhinos rest in the shade.

9630.q: What do male hippos use to defend themselves against rivals?
9630.e: Male hippos have very long, sharp canine teeth. They use them to fight each other for their territory.

9631.q: How do its fins help the goldfish?
9631.e: With its fins the goldfish can swim forwards, brake and change direction. Different breeds have fins of different lengths.
9631.m: Fins help with swimming and steering.

9632.q: How big is the mute swan compared with a duck?
9632.e: The mute swan is one of the largest waterbirds and is clearly bigger than an ordinary duck. You can recognise it from far away.
9632.m: Mute swans are much bigger than ducks.

9633.q: In many falcon species, including the kestrel, what is typical of the size of males and females?
a: The female is usually a little bigger than the male
The male is always much bigger
Both are always exactly the same size
9633.e: In many birds of prey, including the kestrel, the females are a little bigger and heavier than the males. This is called reversed size difference.
9633.m: Females are usually bigger than males.

9634.q: What are the little lumps of pollen on a bumblebee’s legs called?
9634.e: These lumps on the hind legs are called pollen loads. You can see them well when the bumblebee flies from flower to flower.
9634.m: Pollen lumps are called pollen loads.

9635.q: How long can a dromedary manage without water in the desert?
a: Several days, even longer in cool weather
Not at all, it must drink every day
9635.e: Dromedaries can cope with a large loss of water and then drink a great deal at once. How long it works depends on heat and food.

9636.q: How can you vote without going to the ballot box in person?
a: With a show of hands in the classroom
9636.e: Many people in Switzerland vote by post. They send in their ballot paper by mail.

9637.q: How do leafcutter ants carry their pieces of leaf?
a: In their mouths like a sponge
On their backs like a hump
9637.e: The ants hold the piece of leaf high above their heads with their jaws. Long lines of them look like little green flags.
9637.m: Pieces of leaf are carried above the head.

9638.q: What do adult whitefish mainly feed on?
9638.e: Whitefish mainly eat zooplankton, that is small animals floating in the water. These include, for example, water fleas.

9639.q: Roughly how long does it take for a lamb to be born (pregnancy)?
9639.e: A mother sheep carries her lamb in her belly for about five months before it is born. After that the lamb can soon walk by itself.
9639.m: A lamb grows for about five months.

9640.q: What colour is the red panda’s fur mainly?
a: Black and white like the giant panda
9640.e: The red panda looks different from its big namesake. Its fur is mainly reddish brown.
9640.m: The red panda is reddish brown.

9641.q: Which animal is a close relative of the Alpine newt?
9641.e: The Alpine newt and the fire salamander belong to the same family, the true salamanders. Frogs and toads are more distant relatives, and the slow worm is a lizard.
9641.m: The Alpine newt and the fire salamander are closely related.

9642.q: How does a barn swallow usually fly when hunting insects?
a: Low over meadows, water or fields
Always extremely high above the clouds
Not at all, it hunts on the ground
9642.e: When hunting, the barn swallow usually flies low over meadows, water or fields, where lots of insects are about. There it catches the insects in fast flight.
9642.m: It flies low over meadows when hunting.

9643.q: Which kind of baboon also lives in Asia?
a: The hamadryas baboon, on the Arabian Peninsula
9643.e: The hamadryas baboon lives in north-east Africa and in the south-west of the Arabian Peninsula. There it is found, for example, in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
9643.m: Hamadryas baboons also live in Arabia.

9644.q: Apart from roe deer, which prey does the lynx sometimes eat?
9644.e: Besides roe deer, the lynx also hunts smaller animals such as hares or birds. Sometimes it also catches young foxes.
9644.m: The lynx eats a varied diet of meat.

9645.q: What does a grasshopper most often do first when in danger?
a: It jumps away in a flash
It stands completely still and falls asleep
It immediately digs a deep hole
9645.e: Thanks to its strong hind legs, it can make a big escape jump at once. That way it escapes many enemies.
9645.m: In a flash, it is gone.

9646.q: Which measure helps to protect bonobos?
a: Catching them for the animal trade
9646.e: Protected areas preserve the habitat, and hunting bans help the animals directly. Educating local people is also important.

9647.q: What do hamsters like to do with branches and wood?
9647.e: Hamsters like gnawing on branches. This helps them keep their ever-growing teeth short.

9648.q: What is typical of the slow worm’s head?
a: It joins the body with almost no neck
It is broad like a viper’s
9648.e: Head and body form almost one line. This helps it wriggle through thick grass.
9648.m: The head joins the body without a neck.

9649.q: Why do common swifts often run into trouble when buildings are renovated?
a: their nesting sites in wall cracks are often sealed up
the houses are painted too brightly for them
it gets too noisy for them in town
the new roofs are too heavy for them
9649.e: During renovations, cracks and niches in house walls are often sealed. As a result, swifts lose their traditional nesting sites.
9649.m: Renovations often destroy swift nesting sites.

9651.q: What does a dog often do before lying down to sleep?
a: It turns round in a circle several times
It washes itself with its tongue
It digs a deep hole in the house
9651.e: Many dogs turn round in a circle several times before they lie down. This behaviour probably comes from their wild ancestors, who made themselves a comfortable bed this way.
9651.m: Before sleeping, a dog often turns round.

9652.q: Roughly how much does a least weasel weigh?
9652.e: The weight depends greatly on sex and season. Males are clearly heavier than females.

9653.q: Why were geese especially important in a famous old story from Rome?
a: Their loud honking warned people of enemies at night
They guarded a treasure in the forest
9653.e: According to legend, geese raised the alarm with their loud honking at night when enemies were secretly approaching. In this way they are said to have saved the city of Rome.
9653.m: Geese warned of enemies with their honking.

9654.q: Why are sheep important for farming families in the Swiss mountains?
a: They provide wool, meat and sometimes milk
They guard the house like a dog
9654.e: Sheep are important for mountain farming families because they provide wool, meat and sometimes milk. They also look after the steep Alpine pastures by grazing them.
9654.m: Sheep provide wool, meat and milk.

9655.q: What colour is the flesh of wild salmon usually?
9655.e: The flesh gets its colour from pigments in the food, for example from tiny crustaceans. That is why it is pink to orange.
9655.m: Salmon flesh is pink because of its food.

9656.q: What is special about the stag beetle in Europe?
a: It is one of the largest beetles
It is the only beetle that swims
It is the only poisonous beetle
9656.e: Large males, including their antlers, grow up to about 8 centimetres long. This makes the stag beetle one of the largest beetles in Europe.
9656.m: The stag beetle is one of Europe’s largest beetles.

9657.q: Which radioactive element did Marie and Pierre Curie discover?
9657.e: In 1898 Marie and Pierre Curie discovered the element radium and studied radioactivity. They received several Nobel Prizes for their work.

9658.q: Trout have a small extra fin without bony rays on their back, just before the tail fin. What is it called?
9658.e: Fish of the salmon family such as the brown trout have a small adipose fin in addition to the dorsal fin. It has no bony rays.
9658.m: Salmon-family fish have a small adipose fin.

9659.q: How can you recognise an orca in the water from far away?
a: By a horn on its nose
9659.e: The tall dorsal fin sticks far out of the water. That is how you recognise the orca at once.
9659.m: Orcas have a tall dorsal fin.

9660.q: What do two little giraffe calves sometimes do to play?
a: They run and play with each other in the group
They swim together in the sea
9660.e: Young giraffes like to play with each other and already practise fighting with their necks. This way they learn important skills for later.
9660.m: Young giraffes play and practise together.

9661.q: What appears first when a tadpole hatches from a frog’s egg?
a: A small body with a tail and outer gills
9661.e: The newly hatched tadpole has a tail for swimming and outer gills for breathing. Only later do legs and lungs develop.
9661.m: The tadpole first has a tail and gills, then it grows legs.

9663.q: Why is the wels catfish an introduced species in some regions?
a: People released it into new waters
9663.e: In some countries people put wels catfish into lakes and rivers. There it can affect the native fish.
9663.m: People have spread wels catfish widely.

9664.q: What role did Switzerland play in the international negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme?
a: It repeatedly provided Geneva and Lausanne as neutral venues for talks
It mediated as an official member of Iran’s negotiating delegation
It provided weapons for the negotiating partners
It was solely responsible for drafting the nuclear agreement
9664.e: Thanks to its neutrality and long diplomatic tradition, Switzerland is often chosen as a venue for sensitive international negotiations. Geneva and Lausanne were the scene of such talks several times.
9664.m: Switzerland often provides neutral ground for negotiations.

9665.q: Where does a wild rabbit like to live best?
9665.e: Wild rabbits dig underground holes and tunnels where they hide and sleep. There they are protected from enemies.

9666.q: Roughly how soon can a newborn reindeer calf walk?
a: After just a few hours, with the herd
Not at all, it is carried
9666.e: Reindeer calves are well developed at birth and stand up quickly. After a short time they can follow the herd.

a: Yes, it flies fast and for a long time
No, it cannot fly at all
It can only hop a few centimetres high
9667.e: Although it swims on the water, the mallard can also fly very well. It covers long distances when doing so.

9668.q: Which animal group does the starfish belong to?
9668.e: Starfish belong to the group of echinoderms, which means “spiny skins”. These animals all have a spiny body.

9669.q: How does the sand lizard have its young?
a: It gives birth to live young
It feeds its young with milk
9669.e: The sand lizard lays its eggs in warm, loose soil. There the sun warms them until the young hatch.

9670.q: Which family does the llama belong to?
9670.e: Llamas belong to the camel family. But they are at home in South America and have no hump.
9670.m: Llamas are camels without a hump.

9671.q: Apart from crawling, what can starfish do with their little feet?
a: Swim fast as if with fins
9671.e: The little feet do not only help the starfish crawl. It can also hold on with them and pull mussels open.
9671.m: Little feet also help it hold on.

9672.q: Why do wild boar often have mud on their bodies?
a: Because they like wallowing in mud
Because they live in the river
Because they want to hide in it
9672.e: Wild boar regularly bathe in the mud of their wallow. This is good for their skin and cools them down.
9672.m: Mud on the body comes from the wallow.

9673.q: What were water frogs such as the edible frog also used for in some regions in the past?
a: As food, their hind legs were eaten
As guards in front of houses
9673.e: In some regions of Europe, the hind legs of water frogs were eaten as a delicacy, known as frogs’ legs. This is probably also where the species name esculentus, meaning edible, comes from.
9673.m: Frogs’ legs used to be eaten.

9674.q: Roughly how fast can a penguin swim in the water?
9674.e: Penguins are very fast swimmers. Some species reach speeds of up to 25 kilometres per hour in the water.

9675.q: Why is it important for guinea pigs to get things to gnaw such as branches?
a: So that their teeth do not get too long
So that they can build trees
So that they learn to swim
So that they can smell better
9675.e: As well as hay, branches and twigs help wear down their ever-growing teeth. That way the teeth stay a healthy length.

9676.q: How can you tell that a goose feels comfortable?
9676.e: A relaxed goose takes time to arrange its feathers carefully with its beak. This shows that it feels safe and well.

9677.q: Why are brown bears protected in many European countries?
a: Because their numbers fell sharply in the past and they need protection
Because they are meant to be kept as pets
Because otherwise there would quickly be too many
9677.e: In the past, brown bears were hunted heavily in many parts of Europe, so their numbers fell sharply. That is why they are protected in many countries today, so that their population can recover.
9677.m: Brown bears are strictly protected today.

9678.q: Why are leaves left lying in the garden good for hedgehogs?
9678.e: Under piles of leaves, hedgehogs find insects to eat and a good place to hide. That is why you should not clear away all the leaves in autumn.
9678.m: Leaf piles give hedgehogs shelter and food.

9679.q: What is the minimum age to be elected to the National Council?
9679.e: In Switzerland, anyone who is allowed to vote may also stand for election to the National Council. So the minimum age is 18.
9679.m: From 18 you can stand as a candidate.

9680.q: What is the kingfisher’s short, strong tail for?
a: it helps it steer during fast flying manoeuvres
it is used for climbing trees
it is fanned out like a wheel when courting
it protects against predators like a spine
9680.e: The short, firm tail helps the kingfisher steer during fast flight and tight turns. Without it, it would be less agile.
9680.m: A short tail steers fast flying manoeuvres.

9681.q: The red kite’s scientific name is “Milvus milvus”. What is striking about this name?
9681.e: Every animal species has a scientific name made of two words. For the red kite, both words are the same: Milvus milvus.
9681.m: The red kite’s scientific name is Milvus milvus.

9682.q: Roughly how heavy is an edible dormouse outside its hibernation period?
9682.e: A normal edible dormouse usually weighs between 120 and 180 grams. Before hibernation this weight can rise considerably.
9682.m: The weight is usually 120 to 180 grams.

9683.q: Roughly how big is an adult grey heron from head to tail?
9683.e: With a body length of almost a metre, the grey heron is one of the largest birds in our part of the world. On top of that, its long neck makes it look even bigger.
9683.m: Grey herons are almost a metre long.

9684.q: How do newborn red deer calves hide from danger?
a: They lie still and hidden in tall grass
They follow the whole herd at once
9684.e: Newborn calves lie still and hidden for the first few days. Their spotted coat helps them avoid being discovered.
9684.m: Calves hide quietly in the grass.

9685.q: What is the basic legal status of the wolf in Switzerland?
a: It may be hunted all year without rules
It is officially classed as a pet
It is treated like a pest
9685.e: The wolf is basically protected in Switzerland because it once almost died out. Under certain conditions, however, the law can allow its numbers to be controlled.
9685.m: The wolf is basically a protected species.

9686.q: What does a large, bright red comb on a cockerel usually show?
9686.e: A strong red comb is often a sign that a cockerel is healthy and has good blood flow. A pale comb can point to illness.
9686.m: A red comb shows good health.

9687.q: How does the Roman snail seal its shell in winter?
a: With a chalky lid made from slime
9687.e: In winter the snail forms a thin chalky lid called the epiphragm. It closes the opening of the shell.
9687.m: A chalky lid protects it in winter.

9688.q: What is the building where chickens live called?
9688.e: The henhouse protects the chickens from the weather and enemies. They also sleep there at night.

9689.q: What is the highland where many alpacas live called?
9689.e: The Altiplano is a high plateau in the Andes. There the air is thin and the nights are cold.
9689.m: The Altiplano is the highland of the Andes.

9690.q: What is the legal status of the stoat in Switzerland?
a: It may be hunted at any time
It may be kept like a hamster
9690.e: In Switzerland the stoat is a protected wild animal. So it must not simply be hunted or caught.
9690.m: The stoat is protected in Switzerland.

9691.q: From which animal is the domestic pig originally descended?
9691.e: Thousands of years ago, people tamed wild boar. Over many generations, today’s domestic pig developed from them.
9691.m: The domestic pig is descended from the wild boar.

9692.q: What do you get when a cloud reaches right down to the ground?
9692.e: Fog is made of tiny water droplets floating in the air. It is really a cloud lying on the ground.
9692.m: Fog is a cloud on the ground.

9693.q: How can you often recognise a grey heron in flight from far away?
a: By slow, deep wingbeats and a tucked-in neck
By fast, fluttering wingbeats like a hummingbird
By its neck stretched out straight
9693.e: The grey heron’s flight is marked by slow and deep wingbeats. Together with the tucked-in neck, its shape in flight is very typical.
9693.m: Slow wingbeats give the grey heron away.

9694.q: What are the okapi’s broad back teeth made for?
9694.e: The okapi is a plant eater. With its broad back teeth it grinds leaves and shoots.
9694.m: Okapi teeth are made for plants.

9695.q: How does the adder catch its prey?
a: It bites and waits for the venom to work
9695.e: The bitten animal often still runs off a little way. The snake follows the scent trail and finds it.
9695.m: First bite, then follow the trail.

9696.q: How is a pond skater’s body divided into parts?
9696.e: This is true of all insects. The six legs are attached to the thorax.
9696.m: An insect’s body has a head, thorax and abdomen.

9698.q: Roughly how much can an adult common raven weigh?
9698.e: Weighing around one kilogram, the common raven is one of the heaviest songbirds of all. Its strong build supports this weight.

9699.q: Why does an earthworm also swallow tiny stones when it eats?
a: They help grind up the food in its stomach
It builds its tunnels with them
It collects them as a store
9699.e: Tiny stones get into the stomach together with the soil. There they help grind up the food as in a mill.

9700.q: What does a budgie cage absolutely need?
a: Enough space to fly and several perches
Just a small box with no perches
9700.e: Budgies need lots of space to fly and move about. Different perches help them stay active.

9870.q: Which animal found in Switzerland is the Arctic fox most closely related to?
9870.e: The Arctic fox is now scientifically called Vulpes lagopus and so, like the red fox (Vulpes vulpes), belongs to the genus of true foxes. The wolf, golden jackal and raccoon dog are more distant relatives from the dog family.
9870.m: The Arctic fox and the red fox belong to the same genus.

9871.q: Why is the Arctic fox no longer placed in its own genus, Alopex?
a: Genetic analyses showed its close relationship with the true foxes
It was merged with the red fox into a single species
The genus Alopex is considered extinct
It was moved to the martens
9871.e: For a long time the Arctic fox was placed in its own genus as Alopex lagopus. Genetic studies showed, however, that it belongs to the true foxes (Vulpes).
9871.m: The old genus name of the Arctic fox is Alopex.

9872.q: What does the Arctic fox's species name “lagopus” literally mean?
9872.e: “Lagopus” comes from Greek: “lagos” means hare and “pous” foot. It refers to the thickly furred paws, like those of snow hares.
9872.m: The name lagopus recalls the Arctic fox's furry, hare-like paws.

9873.q: Which mammal family does the Arctic fox belong to?
9873.e: The Arctic fox is a fox and therefore a member of the dog family. This family also includes the wolf, red fox and jackals.
9873.m: Like the wolf, the Arctic fox belongs to the dog family.

9875.q: What is the Arctic fox's conservation status worldwide on the IUCN Red List?
9875.e: Worldwide, the Arctic fox has been rated Least Concern since 2004 because it is widespread in the Arctic. Some regional populations, however, are seriously threatened.
9875.m: Worldwide the Arctic fox is not threatened, but regionally it is.

9876.q: In which region is the Arctic fox especially rare and seriously threatened, despite decades of hunting bans?
9876.e: In Norway, Sweden and Finland the population collapsed because of intensive hunting for fur. In 2012 fewer than 200 adult animals lived there; thanks to conservation projects there are now about 400 to 500.
9876.m: In Scandinavia the Arctic fox needs special protection.

9877.q: What does the example of Finland show about protecting the Arctic fox?
a: Despite a hunting ban since 1940, the population has not recovered
After the hunting ban the population quickly doubled
Finland has never protected the Arctic fox
The Arctic fox was reintroduced there and is common today
9877.e: Finland protected the Arctic fox from hunting from 1940. Even so, the Finnish population has not recovered and is regarded there as threatened with extinction.
9877.m: A hunting ban alone does not save the Arctic fox.

9878.q: What was the main cause of the collapse of Arctic fox populations in Scandinavia at the beginning of the 20th century?
a: Heavy hunting for its valuable fur
9878.e: The Arctic fox's thick winter coat was in great demand, and the animals were hunted in huge numbers. The small remaining populations could hardly recover afterwards.
9878.m: Hunting for fur almost wiped out the Arctic fox in Scandinavia.

9879.q: Which animal is the only land mammal originally native to Iceland?
9879.e: The Arctic fox reached Iceland at the end of the last ice age across the frozen sea. All other land mammals there were introduced by humans.
9879.m: In Iceland, the Arctic fox was there before humans.

9880.q: How did the Arctic fox originally reach Iceland?
a: It migrated across the frozen sea at the end of the ice age
Vikings brought it with them for its fur
It swam across from the European mainland
It was released there in the 19th century
9880.e: At the end of the last ice age, the sea around Iceland was frozen at times. So Arctic foxes were able to migrate across the ice.
9880.m: The Arctic fox reached Iceland across the ice.

9881.q: Which two colour forms (morphs) occur in the Arctic fox?
9881.e: Arctic foxes occur as a white and a blue morph. In winter the blue form is dark greyish blue instead of white.
9881.m: Arctic foxes come in a white and a blue form.

9882.q: Roughly what share of all Arctic foxes worldwide belong to the white colour form?
9882.e: Worldwide, about 90 per cent of Arctic foxes are white. On the Arctic mainland the share is even higher.
9882.m: Most Arctic foxes wear a white coat in winter.

9883.q: Where is the blue colour form of the Arctic fox most common?
9883.e: In Iceland, about two thirds of Arctic foxes belong to the blue morph. The darker form is well camouflaged on ice-free coasts with dark rocks.
9883.m: In Iceland, blue Arctic foxes are more common than white ones.

9884.q: How many times a year does the Arctic fox change its coat?
9884.e: In spring the Arctic fox changes to its shorter, darker summer coat and in autumn to its thick winter coat. This keeps it well camouflaged all year round.
9884.m: The Arctic fox has a summer coat and a winter coat.

9885.q: What colour is the summer coat of a white Arctic fox typically?
a: Brown to greyish brown with a paler belly
9885.e: In summer the white Arctic fox is brownish with a paler underside. This colour camouflages it in the snow-free tundra.
9885.m: In summer the white Arctic fox is camouflaged in brown.

9886.q: What share of an Arctic fox's winter coat consists of fine underfur?
9886.e: About 70 per cent of the winter coat is fine underfur. It traps a lot of air and therefore insulates extremely well.
9886.m: The thick underfur makes the Arctic fox's coat so warm.

9887.q: What is the Arctic fox's fur especially noted for among mammals?
a: It is regarded as the best insulating fur of all mammals
It is the longest fur of all mammals
It is completely waterproof like feathers
It grows all year without moulting
9887.e: The Arctic fox's winter coat is regarded as the best heat insulation of all mammals. This allows it to survive extreme Arctic cold.
9887.m: No mammal is better insulated against cold than the Arctic fox.

9888.q: Roughly how much longer is the Arctic fox's winter coat than its summer coat?
9888.e: The winter coat is about twice as long as the summer coat. The extra length and thickness greatly improve insulation.
9888.m: In winter the Arctic fox's coat is about twice as long.

9889.q: Why does the Arctic fox have small, round ears and a short snout compared with the red fox?
a: So that it loses less body heat
So that it can dig better
So that it can breathe more quietly
So that it can swim better
9889.e: Small body parts sticking out offer little surface through which heat can escape. This pattern in animals of cold regions is called Allen's rule.
9889.m: Small ears help the Arctic fox save heat.

9890.q: Down to what surrounding temperature can a resting Arctic fox manage without shivering from cold?
9890.e: Thanks to its superbly insulating fur, the Arctic fox only starts to shiver at about minus 70 °C. Experiments showed that it can even survive temperatures of around minus 80 °C.
9890.m: The Arctic fox only starts shivering at about minus 70 °C.

9891.q: What is special about the soles of the Arctic fox's feet?
a: They are completely bare and horny
They have long claws like crampons
9891.e: The Arctic fox's paws are thickly furred, even on the soles. This protects against cold and gives grip on ice and snow.
9891.m: Furry paws protect the Arctic fox from icy ground.

9892.q: How does a countercurrent system in its legs protect the Arctic fox from heat loss?
a: Warm blood flowing to the paws warms the cold blood flowing back
The paws are constantly heated by shivering muscles
In winter blood no longer flows into the paws at all
Fat pads in the paws produce heat
9892.e: Arteries and veins lie close together, so the warm blood gives its heat to the cold blood flowing back. This keeps the paws cool without the body losing much heat.
9892.m: The countercurrent principle keeps the Arctic fox's body warm.

9893.q: What does the Arctic fox use its bushy tail for when resting in the cold?
a: It wraps it round its body and face like a warm blanket
It stores fat in it as a food reserve
It uses it to clear away snow
It uses it to signal its position to other foxes
9893.e: When sleeping, the Arctic fox curls up and lays its bushy tail over its nose and paws. This greatly reduces heat loss.
9893.m: The bushy tail serves the Arctic fox as a blanket.

9894.q: Where does the Arctic fox naturally live?
a: Around the North Pole in the Arctic
9894.e: The Arctic fox is found all around the pole, in the tundra and on the coasts of North America, Greenland, Europe and Asia, and on many Arctic islands. There are no foxes in the Antarctic.
9894.m: The Arctic fox lives around the North Pole, but not in the Antarctic.

9895.q: Roughly how much does an adult male Arctic fox weigh on average?
9895.e: Male Arctic foxes weigh on average about 3.5 kg, females a little less. This makes the Arctic fox smaller than a red fox.
9895.m: An Arctic fox weighs about as much as a pet cat.

9896.q: Roughly how long is an adult Arctic fox on average, from nose to the base of the tail?
9896.e: Males measure on average about 55 cm, females about 52 cm in head and body length. The tail comes on top of that.
9896.m: An Arctic fox's body is about half a metre long.

9897.q: By how much can an Arctic fox increase its body weight in autumn through fat reserves?
a: By no more than 5 per cent
Not at all, it stays the same weight
9897.e: In autumn the Arctic fox builds up large fat stores and can become more than half as heavy again. The fat serves as an energy reserve and extra insulation in winter.
9897.m: Before winter the Arctic fox eats its way to a thick layer of fat.

9898.q: Which prey animals are the most important food for many Arctic foxes on the mainland?
9898.e: Lemmings are the main prey of Arctic foxes in the tundra. The rise and fall in their numbers largely decides how many young the foxes raise.
9898.m: Without lemmings, the Arctic fox on the mainland would often not have enough food.

9899.q: How does a year with many lemmings affect the breeding of the Arctic fox?
a: The foxes do not breed at all
The young are only born in winter
9899.e: In good lemming years, white Arctic foxes often have 6 to 18 young. In bad years many females have no young at all.
9899.m: Many lemmings mean many young Arctic foxes.

9900.q: What is the largest number of young an Arctic fox litter can have?
9900.e: Arctic fox litters of up to 25 young have been observed. That is the largest litter in the whole order of carnivores.
9900.m: The Arctic fox has the largest litters of all carnivores.

9901.q: Roughly how long is the Arctic fox's gestation period?
9901.e: The Arctic fox's gestation period is about 52 days. The young are usually born in spring, when food becomes more plentiful.
9901.m: After a gestation of about 52 days, the young Arctic foxes are born.

9902.q: Roughly how much does a newborn Arctic fox weigh?
9902.e: Young Arctic foxes weigh only about 60 to 90 g at birth. They are still blind and deaf then.
9902.m: A newborn Arctic fox weighs less than a bar of chocolate.

9903.q: At what age do young Arctic foxes open their eyes and ears?
9903.e: The young are born blind and deaf. Only after about two weeks do they begin to see and hear.
9903.m: Young Arctic foxes are blind and deaf for the first two weeks.

9904.q: At what age are young Arctic foxes usually weaned?
9904.e: At 3 to 4 weeks the young leave the den for the first time, and at about 7 weeks they are weaned. After that they eat solid food brought by their parents.
9904.m: At about seven weeks, young Arctic foxes stop drinking milk.

9905.q: Which breeding system is typical of the Arctic fox?
a: Pairs are usually monogamous and raise the young together
One male keeps a harem of many females
The females always raise the young alone
The young are raised in a shared nest of many pairs
9905.e: During the breeding season, Arctic foxes usually form fixed pairs. Both parents care for the young, and sometimes older siblings help.
9905.m: In Arctic foxes, mother and father both look after the young.

9906.q: What is special about the Arctic fox's dens?
a: They are branching tunnel systems used for many decades
They are dug anew every year and then abandoned
They are snow caves that melt in summer
They are always in hollow trees
9906.e: Arctic fox dens can cover up to 1000 square metres and have many entrances. They are often used for decades by many generations.
9906.m: A good Arctic fox den is handed down from generation to generation.

9907.q: Why did humans release Arctic foxes on many of the Aleutian Islands?
9907.e: Fur traders released Arctic foxes on many Aleutian islands so that they could later catch them for their fur. The foxes greatly reduced the seabird colonies there.
9907.m: On the Aleutians, Arctic foxes were released for the fur trade.

9908.q: How does the Arctic fox find lemmings under the snow in winter?
a: It hears them and pounces through the snow
It detects them with a heat sense in its nose
It systematically digs up the whole area
It waits until they appear in spring
9908.e: The Arctic fox locates lemmings under the snow with its fine hearing. Then it leaps up and pushes through the snow cover with its front paws.
9908.m: The Arctic fox hunts lemmings with a pounce into the snow.

9909.q: Which large predator does the Arctic fox often follow onto the sea ice in winter to eat leftovers?
9909.e: Arctic foxes accompany polar bears on the sea ice and eat the remains of the seals they have caught. This helps them through times when food is scarce.
9909.m: In winter the Arctic fox often lives on polar bears' leftovers.

9910.q: How does the Arctic fox make sure it has food for lean times?
a: In winter it eats only snow and moss
It migrates to the tropics every year
9910.e: In summer the Arctic fox hides extra prey, such as eggs and lemmings, in the ground. In the cold permafrost the food keeps for a long time.
9910.m: In summer the Arctic fox stores food for the winter.

9911.q: How far did a young female Arctic fox travel that was tracked by GPS from Svalbard to Canada in 2018?
9911.e: The vixen travelled from Svalbard via Greenland to Ellesmere Island in Canada. In total she covered about 3500 km in 76 days.
9911.m: A young female Arctic fox walked over 3000 kilometres in 76 days.

9912.q: In what rhythm do lemming numbers, on which many Arctic foxes depend, typically rise and fall?
9912.e: Lemming numbers rise and crash in cycles of usually 3 to 5 years. The number of young Arctic foxes follows these ups and downs.
9912.m: Lemming years come round about every three to five years.

9913.q: Which competitor is increasingly pushing the Arctic fox further north as the climate warms?
9913.e: The larger red fox spreads north in warmer times. It competes with the Arctic fox for dens and prey and sometimes kills it.
9913.m: With climate change, the red fox is becoming a problem for the Arctic fox.

9914.q: Which bird of prey is one of the natural enemies of the Arctic fox?
9914.e: Golden eagles mainly take young Arctic foxes. Other enemies are wolves, wolverines, polar bears and red foxes.
9914.m: The golden eagle can be dangerous to a young Arctic fox.

9915.q: What caused the Arctic fox population on Medny Island (Commander Islands) to crash by about 85 to 90 per cent in the 1970s?
a: Mange caused by a mite brought in by dogs
9915.e: Dogs brought an ear mite to the island that caused severe mange in the foxes. The population shrank to about 90 animals.
9915.m: Introduced diseases can almost wipe out isolated Arctic fox populations.

9916.q: What is the dark colour form of the Arctic fox called, which does not turn white even in winter?
9916.e: Besides the white form there is the blue fox, which stays bluish grey to brown all year. It is common mainly on coasts where little snow lies in winter. The silver fox and cross fox are colour forms of the red fox.
9916.m: The blue fox is a dark colour form of the Arctic fox.

9917.q: Which physical adaptation protects the Arctic fox from the cold?
a: Short ears, a short snout and furry soles
Long ears that give off excess heat
A thick layer of blubber like whales
A bare tail that loses little heat
9917.e: Small body parts sticking out lose little heat; this is described by Allen's rule. Added to this are a thick winter coat and furry paws that protect against the cold ground.
9917.m: Short ears and snout help the Arctic fox save heat.

9918.q: In exceptional cases, how old can an Arctic fox get in the wild?
9918.e: Most Arctic foxes die in their first year, but some reach up to about 11 years in the wild. In captivity an Arctic fox lived to 16.
9918.m: A wild Arctic fox lives to about eleven years at most.

9919.q: Which international conservation project helped increase the Arctic fox population in Norway and Sweden again?
9919.e: In the Norwegian-Swedish project “Felles Fjellrev”, red foxes were controlled and Arctic foxes were fed and released, among other measures. As a result, the Nordic population rose to about 400 to 500 animals.
9919.m: The Felles Fjellrev project helps the Arctic fox in Scandinavia.

9920.q: What is the scientific name of the musk ox?
9920.e: The musk ox has the name Ovibos moschatus. It is the only living species of the genus Ovibos.
9920.m: The musk ox's scientific name is Ovibos moschatus.

9921.q: What does the musk ox's genus name “Ovibos” literally mean?
9921.e: “Ovibos” is made up of the Latin “ovis” (sheep) and “bos” (ox). The name shows that the animal seems to have features of both.
9921.m: Ovibos means sheep-ox, because the name combines sheep and ox.

9922.q: Which subfamily of the bovids is the musk ox placed in?
9922.e: Despite its name, the musk ox is not a true ox. It belongs to the goat-antelopes and is therefore related to sheep and goats.
9922.m: The musk ox is more closely related to goats and sheep than to cattle.

10123.q: Depending on the classification, how many living species of sloth are recognised?
10123.e: There are two species of two-toed sloth in the genus Choloepus and four species of three-toed sloth in the genus Bradypus. Since 2022 the maned sloth has often been split into two species, which makes seven.
10123.m: Today there are only six or seven sloth species in two genera.

10124.q: What does Bradypus, the Greek genus name of the three-toed sloths, mean?
10124.e: Bradypus is made from the Greek words “bradys” meaning slow and “pous” meaning foot. The name describes the animal’s leisurely way of moving.
10124.m: Bradypus means slow foot in Greek.

10125.q: What does Choloepus, the genus name of the two-toed sloths, mean?
10125.e: Choloepus comes from Greek and means roughly “lame foot”. Like Bradypus, it refers to the slow movement.

10126.q: What exactly do the names “two-toed” and “three-toed” refer to in sloths?
a: The claws on the front legs
The claws on the back legs
The toes on all four legs
The number of teeth in each half of the jaw
10126.e: The names refer only to the front limbs. On the back legs both groups have three claws.
10126.m: In sloths, the two or three “fingers” are counted only on the front legs.

10127.q: About how long can a sloth’s claws grow?
10127.e: The strongly curved claws grow to about 8 to 10 cm long. They work as hooks for hanging from branches and for defence.
10127.m: Sloth claws are long curved hooks of about 8 to 10 cm.

10128.q: What is special about the neck vertebrae of three-toed sloths?
a: They usually have 8 to 9 instead of 7
Their neck vertebrae are fused together
They have no neck vertebrae at all
10128.e: Almost all mammals have seven neck vertebrae, but three-toed sloths usually have eight or nine. This makes their neck especially flexible.
10128.m: Three-toed sloths have more neck vertebrae than almost any other mammal.

10129.q: Thanks to its extra neck vertebrae, about how far can a three-toed sloth turn its head?
10129.e: Thanks to the extra neck vertebrae, the three-toed sloth can turn its head about 270 degrees. This lets it reach leaves without moving its body.
10129.m: A three-toed sloth can turn its head about three quarters of a circle.

10130.q: What is unusual about the neck vertebrae of two-toed sloths?
a: Depending on the animal, they have only 5 to 7
They have up to 12 neck vertebrae
They have neck cartilage instead of vertebrae
They have exactly 7 like all mammals
10130.e: Two-toed sloths have five to seven neck vertebrae, so often fewer than the usual seven of mammals. Along with manatees and dugongs, sloths are among the few exceptions to the rule of seven.
10130.m: Two-toed sloths often have fewer than seven neck vertebrae.

10131.q: What position does a sloth spend most of its time in up in the tree?
a: Hanging from branches with its back facing down
Sitting upright in forks of branches like a monkey
Lying flat on its belly on wide branches
10131.e: Sloths usually hang upside down or with their back facing down from branches. They eat, sleep, mate and even give birth in this position.
10131.m: A sloth spends almost its whole life hanging.

10132.q: Compared with most mammals, in which direction does a sloth’s hair grow?
a: From the belly towards the back
From the back towards the belly
From the tail towards the head
In a spiral around the body
10132.e: In sloths the parting is on the belly and the hair grows towards the back. Since the animal usually hangs, rainwater can run off easily.
10132.m: A sloth’s fur is parted on its belly so that rain runs off.

10133.q: Why does a sloth’s fur often look greenish?
a: Because it rubs leaf sap into it
Because mould breaks down the fur
10133.e: Green algae, for example of the genus Trichophilus, live in grooves and cracks in sloth hair. They tint the fur green and improve camouflage in the leafy canopy.
10133.m: Algae in the fur make the sloth green and well camouflaged.

10134.q: Which insects live on three-toed sloths and lay their eggs in their dung?
10134.e: Sloth moths such as Cryptoses choloepi live in the fur. When the sloth climbs down to the ground to defecate, the females lay their eggs in the fresh dung, where the caterpillars develop.
10134.m: Sloth moths live in the fur and breed in sloth dung.

10135.q: According to a 2014 study, what possible benefit does the three-toed sloth get from the moths in its fur?
a: They supply nutrients that help the algae grow
They eat ticks and lice in the fur
They warn the sloth about birds of prey
They pollinate the sloth’s food trees
10135.e: The moths bring nitrogen into the fur, which helps the algae grow. The sloths might lick off the algae and so take in extra nutrients.
10135.m: Moths fertilise the algae, and the algae may feed the sloth.

10136.q: Roughly how often does a three-toed sloth climb down from its tree to defecate?
10136.e: Three-toed sloths leave the tree about once a week and pass dung and urine on the ground. This descent is dangerous because they can easily meet enemies there.
10136.m: A three-toed sloth goes to the “toilet” on the ground about once a week.

10137.q: How is a sloth’s stomach built?
a: It is a simple small sac
It is missing, digestion happens in the gut
It is a crop like in birds
10137.e: Sloths have a stomach with several chambers in which bacteria ferment the tough leaves. This is similar to the digestion of ruminants.
10137.m: In a sloth’s multi-chambered stomach, bacteria help digest leaves.

10138.q: How long can it take for a meal of leaves to pass all the way through a sloth?
10138.e: Digesting fibre-rich leaves is extremely slow in sloths and takes several weeks. This fits their very low energy use.
10138.m: A sloth needs several weeks to digest one meal.

10139.q: Roughly what is the body temperature of an active sloth?
10139.e: For mammals, sloths have a low and changing body temperature of about 30 to 34 °C, and at rest it can drop even lower. This saves energy, and they sometimes warm up in the sun.
10139.m: For mammals, sloths are unusually cool.

10140.q: How does a sloth’s basal metabolic rate compare with that of other mammals of the same size?
a: It is about twice as high
It is ten times as high
10140.e: Sloths have one of the lowest metabolic rates of all mammals of their size. Their low-energy diet of leaves forces them to save energy.
10140.m: Sloths are energy savers with a very slow metabolism.

10141.q: How does a sloth’s muscle mass compare with that of other mammals of its size?
10141.e: Sloths have relatively little muscle mass. This saves energy, and thanks to their claws they need hardly any muscle power to hang.
10141.m: A sloth manages with few muscles.

10142.q: How well can a sloth swim?
a: Quite well, it even crosses rivers
Not at all, it drowns in water
Only by floating backwards on its back
10142.e: In water, sloths are surprisingly skilful and much faster than on the ground. They swim across rivers and flooded areas.
10142.m: A sloth is faster in water than on land.

10143.q: About how long can a sloth hold its breath when diving?
10143.e: Sloths can slow their heartbeat a great deal and so stay underwater for up to about 40 minutes. That is exceptional for a land mammal.
10143.m: A sloth can hold its breath for a very long time.

10144.q: How does a sloth move along on the ground?
a: It drags itself forward with its front legs
It hops on its back legs
It walks upright on two legs
It runs fast on all fours
10144.e: On the ground, sloths can hardly carry their own weight. They dig in their claws and pull their body along with their front legs.
10144.m: On the ground, a sloth is especially clumsy.

10145.q: According to measurements in Panama, about how many hours a day do wild brown-throated sloths sleep?
10145.e: Measurements of wild brown-throated sloths in Panama showed just under 10 hours of sleep a day. The often quoted 15 to 20 hours come from animals in captivity.
10145.m: Wild sloths sleep less than people often think.

10146.q: When are two-toed sloths mainly active?
10146.e: Two-toed sloths are mainly nocturnal. Three-toed sloths, on the other hand, are often active during the day too.
10146.m: Two-toed sloths are mainly night animals.

10147.q: How does the diet of two-toed sloths differ from that of three-toed sloths?
a: They eat a wider range, including fruit and flowers
10147.e: Three-toed sloths eat almost only the leaves of a few tree species. Two-toed sloths have a more varied diet of leaves, fruit, flowers and occasionally animal food.
10147.m: Two-toed sloths are less fussy eaters.

10148.q: Which tree genus is a well-known food plant of three-toed sloths?
10148.e: Leaves of Cecropia trees are among the well-known food plants of three-toed sloths. These trees often grow at forest edges and in clearings in Central and South America.
10148.m: Cecropia leaves are often on the three-toed sloth’s menu.

10149.q: What is special about a sloth’s teeth?
a: They have no enamel and keep growing
They have sharp incisors like rodents
They have no teeth at all
Their teeth are completely replaced every year
10149.e: Sloth teeth are peg-like teeth without enamel that keep growing throughout life. There are no incisors; leaves are plucked off with the hard lips.
10149.m: Sloth teeth have no enamel and keep on growing.

10150.q: What did genetic studies find out about colour vision in sloths?
a: They probably see no colours because they lack working cones
They see colours very well with four types of cone
They see colours like humans with three types of cone
They see only in the ultraviolet range
10150.e: Genetic studies from 2015 showed that in sloths the genes for the cone visual pigments no longer work. They probably see only with their rods and are colour-blind.
10150.m: Sloths see the world without colours.

10151.q: Which bird of prey is one of the sloth’s most important enemies?
10151.e: The harpy eagle is a very powerful bird of prey of the rainforests of Central and South America. Sloths and monkeys are among its main prey.
10151.m: The harpy eagle is the sloth’s most dangerous enemy from the air.

10152.q: Which big cat is one of the sloth’s natural enemies?
10152.e: The jaguar lives in the same forests as the sloth and catches it mainly when it is on the ground. Leopards, cheetahs and snow leopards do not live in the Americas.
10152.m: The jaguar hunts sloths mainly on the ground.

10153.q: According to the IUCN, which sloth species is critically endangered?
10153.e: The pygmy three-toed sloth lives only on a tiny island off Panama and is critically endangered. According to the IUCN, the other species named are not threatened.
10153.m: The pygmy three-toed sloth is the most threatened sloth species.

10154.q: Where does the pygmy three-toed sloth live, and nowhere else?
a: On Isla Escudo de Veraguas off Panama
10154.e: The pygmy three-toed sloth lives only on Isla Escudo de Veraguas, about 4 km² in size, off Panama’s Caribbean coast. It lives there in mangroves but also in the forest inland.
10154.m: The pygmy three-toed sloth lives on just one island off Panama.

10155.q: Which process explains the small size of the pygmy three-toed sloth?
10155.e: On small islands some animal species become smaller over many generations because food and space are scarce. This island dwarfism explains the pygmy sloth’s small size.
10155.m: The pygmy three-toed sloth became small through island dwarfism.

10156.q: Which sloth species lives in Brazil’s Atlantic coastal rainforest and has a dark mane?
10156.e: The maned sloth lives only in Brazil’s greatly shrunken Atlantic Forest. Its dark mane on the neck and shoulders is striking.
10156.m: You can recognise the maned sloth by its dark mane.

10157.q: What marking do males of many three-toed sloth species have on their back?
a: An orange-yellow patch with a dark stripe
A spiny crest of horny plates
A bare red patch of skin
A white mane down to the tail
10157.e: Males of many three-toed sloths have an orange-yellow patch on the back with a dark central stripe, called the speculum. It probably helps the sexes recognise each other.
10157.m: You can recognise male three-toed sloths by the patch on their back.

10158.q: How do the tails of the two sloth groups differ?
a: Three-toed sloths have a stubby tail, two-toed sloths have no visible one
Both have a long gripping tail
Two-toed sloths have a bushy tail, three-toed sloths have none
Both have a flat paddle-shaped tail
10158.e: Three-toed sloths have a short stubby tail. In two-toed sloths no tail can be seen from the outside.
10158.m: Only the three-toed sloth has a little tail.

10159.q: What are three-toed sloths called, after a word from the South American Tupi language?
10159.e: Three-toed sloths are called “ai”, which recalls their high-pitched call. Two-toed sloths have the name “unau”, which also comes from Tupi.
10159.m: The ai has three toes, the unau has two.

10160.q: In which region does Hoffmann’s two-toed sloth live?
a: In Central America and north-western South America
Only on the islands of the Caribbean
10160.e: Hoffmann’s two-toed sloth lives in the rainforests of Central America, for example in Costa Rica and Panama, and in north-western South America.
10160.m: Hoffmann’s two-toed sloth is at home in Central America and north-western South America.

10161.q: Roughly how long is the pregnancy of a two-toed sloth?
10161.e: Two-toed sloths are pregnant for about 10 to 12 months. In three-toed sloths the pregnancy is shorter, at about six months.
10161.m: Two-toed sloths are pregnant for almost a year.

10162.q: How many young does a female sloth usually have at one birth?
10162.e: Sloths usually have just one baby per birth. After birth it clings to its mother’s belly.
10162.m: A sloth usually has only one baby at a time.

10163.q: Where does a young sloth spend its first months of life?
a: In a tree hollow as a nest
In a burrow on the ground
In a group with other young
10163.e: The baby holds on to the fur on its mother’s belly for several months. There it drinks milk and learns which leaves it can eat.
10163.m: A baby sloth travels along on its mother’s belly.

10164.q: How do adult sloths live socially?
10164.e: Adult sloths usually live alone in their territory. Contact happens mainly for mating and between mother and young.

10165.q: What is the name of the extinct giant sloth that grew up to about 6 m long and weighed several tonnes?
10165.e: Megatherium lived in South America and was one of the largest land mammals of its time. It died out towards the end of the last ice age.
10165.m: Megatherium was a ground sloth as big as an elephant.

10166.q: Which famous naturalist described and named the giant sloth Megatherium in 1796?
10166.e: The Frenchman Georges Cuvier described a skeleton found in Argentina in 1796 and named it Megatherium. It was important evidence that species can die out.
10166.m: Georges Cuvier gave the giant sloth Megatherium its name.

10167.q: Which future US president presented a paper in 1797 about the bones of an extinct ground sloth?
10167.e: In 1797 Thomas Jefferson presented fossils that he called Megalonyx, meaning “great claw”. Later the species was named Megalonyx jeffersonii in his honour.
10167.m: An extinct ground sloth is named after Thomas Jefferson.

10168.q: What do genetic studies show about tree living in two-toed and three-toed sloths?
a: The two groups developed it independently
They descend from a shared tree-living ancestor
Only two-toed sloths really live in trees
10168.e: The two living genera are not closely related but come from different lines of ground sloths. Their hanging life in trees is an example of convergent evolution.
10168.m: Two-toed and three-toed sloths became tree dwellers independently.

10169.q: What is the biggest threat to sloths in many regions?
a: Clearing and breaking up of the rainforests
10169.e: Sloths depend on connected treetops. Clearing forces them onto the ground, where they fall victim to traffic, dogs and power lines.
10169.m: Without connected forest, sloths are in danger.

10170.q: Which animals are the closest living relatives of armadillos?
10170.e: Armadillos, sloths and anteaters together form the Xenarthra, which arose in South America. Pangolins look similar but are not closely related.
10170.m: Armadillos are related to sloths and anteaters.

10171.q: What does Cingulata, the scientific name of the armadillo order, mean?
10171.e: Cingulata comes from the Latin “cingulum”, belt. The name refers to the movable bands across the armour.

10172.q: What does the group name “Xenarthra”, to which armadillos belong, literally mean?
10172.e: “Xenos” means strange and “arthron” means joint (as in arthritis). It refers to extra joint surfaces on the lower back vertebrae that support the spine when digging.

10173.q: Roughly how many living species of armadillo are recognised?
10173.e: Depending on the classification, about 20 to 21 living armadillo species are recognised. Today they are divided into two families.

10174.q: At what time of day are most armadillos active?
a: Mainly at dusk and at night
Only in the hottest part of midday
10174.e: Most armadillos look for insects at dusk and at night. During the day they rest in their burrows, though some species are also out in daytime when it is cool.
10174.m: Most armadillos are active at dusk and at night.

10175.q: Ancient DNA showed that which extinct group of animals belongs to today’s armadillo family Chlamyphoridae?
10175.e: Studies of ancient DNA in 2016 showed that the huge glyptodonts were a subgroup within the armadillos. So they were not a separate, distant line.
10175.m: Glyptodonts were giant armadillos, not a separate line of animals.

10176.q: What size did some glyptodonts, the extinct relatives of armadillos, reach?
a: About the size of a small car
About the size of a dog
About the size of a hare
About the size of a sheep
10176.e: The largest glyptodonts such as Doedicurus grew to about 3 to 4 metres long and probably weighed well over a tonne. Their domed shell looked like a small car.
10176.m: Some glyptodonts were as big as a small car.

10177.q: What special weapon did Doedicurus, an extinct armadillo relative, have?
a: An armoured club on its tail
Venomous spurs on its back legs
10177.e: Doedicurus had a heavy armoured club at the end of its tail. It could probably use it to fight off enemies or rivals.
10177.m: Doedicurus defended itself with an armoured tail club.

10178.q: Where does the word “armadillo” come from?
10178.e: “Armadillo” is a diminutive of the Spanish “armado”, armed or armoured. The Spanish named the animals after their armour.
10178.m: Armadillo means “little armoured one” in Spanish.

10179.q: What does the German name for the armadillo, “Gürteltier” (belt animal), refer to?
a: The movable bands across its armour
A pale stripe of fur on its belly
A belt of fat around its hips
The way it wraps its tail around its body
10179.e: In the middle of the body, armadillos have movable bands of armour that run around the body like belts. They make the stiff armour flexible.
10179.m: The German name refers to the belt-like bands of the armour.

10180.q: What is an armadillo’s armour made of?
a: Bony plates covered with horny scales
Cartilage with a crust of lime
10180.e: The armour is made of bones in the skin (osteoderms), covered by horny scales of keratin. This makes armadillos the only living mammals with bony armour.
10180.m: Armadillo armour is made of skin bones with horny scales.

10181.q: How is the armour of a typical armadillo built?
a: Stiff shoulder and hip shields with movable bands between them
A single stiff shield with no joints
Many loose single scales with no fixed shields
Only a back shield, head and tail are unprotected
10181.e: At the front is a shoulder shield, at the back a hip shield, with movable bands in between. Usually the head and tail are armoured as well.
10181.m: Between an armadillo’s shoulder and hip shields there are movable bands.

10182.q: How many movable bands does the nine-banded armadillo actually have?
a: Usually 8 to 11, so not always 9 despite the name
10182.e: The number of bands in the nine-banded armadillo varies between about 8 and 11. Nine is just the most common number.
10182.m: The nine-banded armadillo does not always have exactly nine bands.

10183.q: Which armadillos are the only ones that can roll up completely into a closed ball?
10183.e: Only the three-banded armadillos of the genus Tolypeutes roll up completely, with the head and tail shields closing the gap. Most other species tend to dig themselves in when in danger.
10183.m: Only three-banded armadillos can roll up into a closed ball.

10184.q: What is the advantage of the three-banded armadillo’s armour not fitting tightly to the body at the sides?
a: It creates an insulating air space and room to roll up
The armour can be shed like a crab’s
The animal can store water under it
The young are carried underneath it
10184.e: In the three-banded armadillo, air stays between armour and body, which insulates. There is also room under the shell for the head and legs when it rolls up.
10184.m: There is an air space under the three-banded armadillo’s armour.

10185.q: How does the southern three-banded armadillo often move when walking?
a: It walks on the tips of its front claws
It hops on its back legs like a kangaroo
It rolls downhill as a ball
It pushes itself along on its belly
10185.e: The southern three-banded armadillo often walks on the tips of the claws of its front feet, almost as if on tiptoe. It can run surprisingly fast like this.
10185.m: The southern three-banded armadillo likes to walk on the tips of its front claws.

10186.q: Which armadillo was the model for “Fuleco”, the mascot of the 2014 Football World Cup in Brazil?
10186.e: Fuleco was based on the Brazilian three-banded armadillo (Tolypeutes tricinctus). The aim was to draw attention to this threatened species.
10186.m: The World Cup mascot Fuleco was a Brazilian three-banded armadillo.

10187.q: What is the IUCN status of the Brazilian three-banded armadillo?
10187.e: The IUCN classes the Brazilian three-banded armadillo as vulnerable. Loss of habitat in the Caatinga and hunting are harming it.
10187.m: The Brazilian three-banded armadillo is classed as vulnerable.

10188.q: Which is the largest living species of armadillo?
10188.e: The giant armadillo (Priodontes maximus) reaches about 1.5 metres in length including its tail. No other living armadillo grows so big.
10188.m: The giant armadillo is the largest living armadillo.

10189.q: About how heavy can an adult giant armadillo get?
10189.e: Giant armadillos usually weigh about 19 to 33 kg, and one wild animal even weighed about 54 kg. That makes them much heavier than all other living armadillos.
10189.m: A giant armadillo can weigh about 50 kg.

10190.q: What record does the giant armadillo hold when it comes to teeth?
a: With up to about 100, it has the most teeth of any land mammal
It has the longest canines of all mammals
It is the only mammal with teeth on its tongue
It has the hardest incisors of all mammals
10190.e: The giant armadillo has up to about 80 to 100 small peg-like teeth. That is a record among land mammals.
10190.m: The giant armadillo has more teeth than any other land mammal.

10191.q: What is especially striking about the giant armadillo’s front foot?
a: A sickle-shaped claw up to about 20 cm long
A thumb that can be spread out for gripping
A sucker on the sole of the foot
10191.e: The giant armadillo’s third front claw grows to about 20 cm long. It uses it to rip open termite mounds and dig large burrows.
10191.m: The giant armadillo has a huge digging claw on its front foot.

10192.q: What is the IUCN status of the giant armadillo?
10192.e: The IUCN classes the giant armadillo as vulnerable. The reasons are habitat destruction, hunting and its very slow breeding.
10192.m: The giant armadillo is classed as vulnerable.

10193.q: Why is the giant armadillo called an “ecosystem engineer”?
a: Many other animal species use its large burrows
As the main pollinator it spreads many flowering plants
It dams streams with branches to make ponds
It is the only animal that eats poisonous fungi
10193.e: Field studies in South America showed that many other species of mammals, birds and reptiles use the giant armadillo’s burrows as shelter. Its digging thus shapes the habitat.
10193.m: Many animal species benefit from the giant armadillo’s burrows.

10194.q: How many young does a female giant armadillo usually have per litter?
10194.e: Giant armadillos usually have only a single young, and the gaps between births are long. This makes the species especially vulnerable to population crashes.
10194.m: A giant armadillo usually has only one young.

10195.q: Which armadillo species is the smallest in the world?
10195.e: The pink fairy armadillo (Chlamyphorus truncatus) grows to only about 9 to 11.5 cm long. That makes it the smallest known armadillo.
10195.m: The pink fairy armadillo is the smallest armadillo.

10196.q: Roughly how much does an adult pink fairy armadillo weigh?
10196.e: The pink fairy armadillo weighs about as much as a bar of chocolate. That makes it one of the lightest xenarthrans.
10196.m: A pink fairy armadillo weighs only about 100 to 120 g.

10197.q: What is special about the pink fairy armadillo’s armour?
a: It is attached to the body almost only along the spine
It consists of just one single bony plate
It is covered with long spines
It is missing on the back and covers only the belly
10197.e: The pink armour of the pink fairy armadillo lies on top like a cloak and is attached only along a narrow line over the back. Underneath, the animal has soft white fur.
10197.m: The pink fairy armadillo’s armour is attached only along its back.

10198.q: What is the upright plate at the rear end of the pink fairy armadillo probably used for?
a: For blocking its tunnel and pressing down soil
For storing fat for the winter
As a sound box for mating calls
For holding on to its young
10198.e: The blunt, armoured rear can seal off the tunnel behind it. It probably also helps to pack down loosened soil.
10198.m: With the plate at its rear, the pink fairy armadillo can block its tunnel.

10199.q: In which country does the pink fairy armadillo live, and nowhere else?
10199.e: The pink fairy armadillo is endemic to central Argentina. It lives there in sandy dry areas and grasslands.
10199.m: The pink fairy armadillo lives only in Argentina.

10200.q: What is the IUCN status of the pink fairy armadillo?
10200.e: The pink fairy armadillo lives almost entirely underground and is very rarely seen. So the IUCN lacks enough data for a reliable assessment.
10200.m: Too little is known about the pink fairy armadillo for a reliable threat assessment.

10201.q: What extraordinary way of reproducing does the nine-banded armadillo have?
a: It usually has identical quadruplets from a single egg cell
It lays eggs and incubates them in its burrow
The males carry the young in a pouch
It reproduces without males by virgin birth
10201.e: In the nine-banded armadillo, one fertilised egg cell usually splits into four embryos. So all the young in a litter are genetically identical and the same sex.
10201.m: The nine-banded armadillo usually gives birth to identical quadruplets.

10202.q: What is the hairy armadillo Chaetophractus vellerosus, known as the “screaming hairy armadillo”, famous for?
a: It squeals loudly when touched or threatened
It sings in a choir during the mating season
10202.e: This hairy armadillo makes loud, shrill squeals when threatened. That is where its English name comes from.
10202.m: The screaming hairy armadillo squeals loudly when it feels threatened.

10203.q: In the nine-banded armadillo, what happens after fertilisation in summer before the embryo develops?
a: Implantation of the embryo is delayed by a few months
The egg is laid at once with a chalky shell
The sperm is stored in the stomach
10203.e: The nine-banded armadillo has delayed implantation (embryonic diapause) of about three to four months. This way the young are born at a good time of year in spring.
10203.m: In the nine-banded armadillo, the embryo implants only after a delay.

10204.q: What does the armour of a newborn nine-banded armadillo feel like?
a: Soft and leathery, it only hardens later
Completely missing, it grows only after years
10204.e: Young armadillos are born with soft, leathery skin. The armour turns to bone only in the following weeks and months.

10205.q: Which human disease can the nine-banded armadillo naturally carry?
10205.e: Besides humans, the nine-banded armadillo is one of the few natural hosts of the leprosy bacterium Mycobacterium leprae. In the southern United States, infections from armadillo to human have been proven.
10205.m: The nine-banded armadillo can carry the leprosy bacterium.

10206.q: Why is the nine-banded armadillo well suited to leprosy research?
a: Its low body temperature helps the bacterium grow
It is immune to all bacteria
It has especially many white blood cells
It lives over 100 years in the laboratory
10206.e: The leprosy bacterium grows best at temperatures below normal human body heat. The armadillo’s low body temperature of about 30 to 35 °C suits it.
10206.m: Their low body temperature makes armadillos valuable for leprosy research.

10207.q: Which armadillo species has spread far into the USA since the 19th century?
10207.e: In the 19th century the nine-banded armadillo crossed the Rio Grande and spread north and east. Today it lives in many southern US states.
10207.m: The nine-banded armadillo has spread far into the USA.

10208.q: What mainly limits the nine-banded armadillo’s spread northwards?
a: Cold winters, as it stores little fat and has a slow metabolism
A lack of rivers to drink from
10208.e: Armadillos have a low basal metabolic rate and hardly any fat reserves. They cope badly with long frosty periods when they cannot find insects.
10208.m: Cold slows the nine-banded armadillo’s spread northwards.

10209.q: Which US state has made the nine-banded armadillo its official “small mammal”?
10209.e: In 1995 Texas named the nine-banded armadillo its official state small mammal. The animal is a well-known symbol there.
10209.m: In Texas the nine-banded armadillo is an official state symbol.

10210.q: How does a startled nine-banded armadillo often react, which proves fatal in road traffic?
a: It jumps straight up into the air
It lies stiff and plays dead
It rolls up into a tight ball
10210.e: When startled, the nine-banded armadillo jumps up by reflex. This can surprise predators but means it hits the underside of cars.
10210.m: A startled nine-banded armadillo jumps into the air.

10211.q: How can a nine-banded armadillo cross a river?
a: It swallows air to swim or walks along the bottom
It builds a raft out of twigs
It waits until the river freezes in winter
10211.e: The nine-banded armadillo can pump air into its stomach and gut to float better. For narrow streams it holds its breath and simply walks along the bottom.
10211.m: An armadillo can swallow air in order to swim.

10212.q: Roughly how long can a nine-banded armadillo hold its breath?
10212.e: The nine-banded armadillo can go without breathing for about six minutes. This helps when crossing water and when digging in loose soil.
10212.m: A nine-banded armadillo can hold its breath for about six minutes.

a: Simple peg teeth without enamel and without incisors
Sharp carnassial teeth like in predators
Broad grinding teeth with thick enamel like in horses
Only two large gnawing teeth like in mice
10213.e: Armadillos have uniform, peg-like cheek teeth without a coat of enamel that keep growing throughout life. Incisors and canines are missing.
10213.m: Armadillos have simple peg teeth without enamel.

10214.q: What do most armadillos mainly eat?
a: Insects such as ants, termites and beetle larvae
10214.e: Most armadillos are insect eaters and dig for ants, termites and larvae. Some species also eat fruit, small vertebrates or carrion.

10215.q: Which body feature helps armadillos pick up ants and termites?
a: A trunk with a gripping finger
A throat pouch for collecting prey
10215.e: Armadillos have a long tongue covered with sticky saliva. With it they can lick up lots of small insects from tunnels and nests.
10215.m: Armadillos collect insects with their sticky tongue.

10216.q: Which sense do armadillos mainly use to find their food?
10216.e: Armadillos see poorly but have an excellent sense of smell. They can even smell insects below the surface of the ground.
10216.m: Armadillos find their food mainly with their nose.

10217.q: Which armadillo is known for going into hibernation or torpor in the cold season?
10217.e: The pichi (Zaedyus pichiy) lives far into the cool south of Argentina and Chile. It survives cold spells in torpor with a greatly lowered body temperature.
10217.m: The pichi survives cold periods in a winter torpor.

10218.q: On which continent or in which part of the world do armadillos live naturally?
a: Only in the Americas, from the southern USA to Patagonia
In Africa south of the Sahara
10218.e: All armadillos come from the Americas, and most species live in South America. Only the nine-banded armadillo reaches the USA.
10218.m: Armadillos live naturally only in the Americas.

10219.q: Which Andean instrument was traditionally made with an armadillo shell as its sound box?
10219.e: The charango is a small stringed instrument from the Andes whose sound box was often made from an armadillo shell in the past. Today it is usually made of wood, partly to protect the animals.
10219.m: Charangos used to be made from armadillo shells.

10220.q: Which animal family does the fennec fox belong to?
10220.e: The fennec is a true fox and so belongs to the dog family, together with the wolf, the jackal and the red fox.
10220.m: The fennec is a small relative of dogs and wolves.

10221.q: Which genus is the fennec fox placed in today?
10221.e: Today the fennec is placed in the genus of true foxes as Vulpes zerda. In the past it was sometimes put in its own genus, Fennecus.
10221.m: The fennec is a true fox of the genus Vulpes.

10222.q: How does the fennec fox protect itself from the cold desert nights?
a: With a thick layer of blubber like a seal
10222.e: In the desert it is hot during the day but often very cold at night. The fennec’s thick, soft fur insulates well and keeps it warm at night.
10222.m: Thick fur keeps the fennec warm on cold desert nights.

10223.q: When the fennec fox was first described in 1780, which genus was it placed in at first?
10223.e: The fennec was first described as Canis zerda, so it was put in the same genus as dogs and wolves. Only later was it placed with the true foxes (Vulpes).
10223.m: The fennec was first placed in the genus of dogs and wolves.

10224.q: What record does the fennec fox hold among the dog family?
a: It is the smallest member of the dog family
It is the fastest member of the dog family
It is the longest-living member of the dog family
It is the most widespread species
10224.e: Usually weighing less than 2 kg, the fennec is the smallest wild member of the dog family.
10224.m: No wild member of the dog family is smaller than the fennec.

10225.q: According to DNA studies, which species is the fennec fox’s closest living relative?
10225.e: Genetic studies show that Blanford’s fox (Vulpes cana) is closest to the fennec.
10225.m: Blanford’s fox is the fennec’s closest relative.

10226.q: Which language does the name “fennec” come from?
10226.e: The word “fennec” goes back to the Arabic word “fanak” for fox, which is probably of Persian origin.
10226.m: The name fennec comes from Arabic.

10227.q: Roughly how much does an adult fennec fox weigh?
10227.e: Depending on the source, adult fennecs weigh about 0.8 to just under 2 kg, usually around 1 to 1.5 kg, so they are lighter than many house cats.
10227.m: A fennec weighs less than an average house cat.

10228.q: About how long is a fennec fox’s body (head and body, without the tail)?
10228.e: The head and body length of adult fennecs is about 30 to 40 cm.
10228.m: A fennec’s body is hardly longer than a school ruler.

10229.q: Roughly how long is a fennec fox’s tail?
10229.e: The bushy tail usually measures about 20 to 30 cm; figures in the literature vary a little.
10229.m: A fennec’s tail is a good 20 cm long.

10230.q: How long can a male fennec fox’s ears grow?
10230.e: The ears of adult males measure about 10 cm, those of females a little less.
10230.m: A fennec’s ears are about 10 cm long.

10231.q: What record do the fennec fox’s ears hold among the dog family?
a: They are the largest relative to body size
They are the only ones that turn independently
They are the only ones without fur on the inside
They are the only ones that pick up ultrasound
10231.e: Measured against its body size, the fennec has the largest ears of all members of the dog family.
10231.m: Relative to its body, no member of the dog family has bigger ears than the fennec.

10232.q: How do its large ears help the fennec fox in the desert heat?
a: They give off body heat through many blood vessels
They store water for dry days
They shade the head like an umbrella
10232.e: The thin ears have a rich blood supply and act like radiators that give off excess heat.
10232.m: The fennec gives off heat through its large ears full of blood vessels.
