10233.q: What does the fennec fox especially use its sharp hearing for when hunting?
a: To hear prey under the sand
To follow prey over long distances
To find water by the sound it makes
10233.e: With its large ears the fennec can pick up quiet sounds of insects and rodents below the surface of the sand and then dig them out.
10233.m: The fennec can hear its prey even under the sand.

10234.q: What is special about the soles of the fennec fox’s feet?
a: They are completely bare and horny
10234.e: Thick fur on the soles protects against hot sand and gives a better grip on loose ground.
10234.m: Furry paws protect the fennec from hot sand.

10235.q: Which fur colour is typical of the fennec fox?
a: Reddish brown with a white chest
10235.e: The pale, sand-coloured fur camouflages the fennec in the desert and reflects sunlight during the day.
10235.m: Sand-coloured fur camouflages the fennec in the desert.

10236.q: What colour is the tip of a fennec fox’s tail typically?
10236.e: The fennec’s bushy, sand-coloured tail usually ends in a dark to black tip.
10236.m: The fennec has a dark tail tip.

10237.q: How many teeth does an adult fennec fox have?
10237.e: Like most members of the dog family, the fennec has 42 teeth. They are rather small compared with the skull.
10237.m: The fennec has 42 teeth, like a dog.

10238.q: How does the fennec fox meet much of its need for water in the desert?
a: Through the moisture in its food
By walking to oases every day
With water it stores in its den
10238.e: The fennec can go a long time without open drinking water because it takes in fluid from prey, fruit and plants.
10238.m: The fennec gets its water mainly from its food.

10239.q: Which adaptation of the kidneys helps the fennec fox save water?
a: They produce only a little highly concentrated urine
They store water for several weeks
They stop working completely during the day
They turn fat directly into drinking water
10239.e: The fennec’s kidneys are built to lose as little water as possible through urine.
10239.m: The fennec’s kidneys waste hardly any water.

10240.q: At what time of day is the fennec fox mainly active?
10240.e: The fennec is mainly nocturnal and spends the hot hours of the day in its cool den.
10240.m: The fennec hunts at night and sleeps in its den by day.

10241.q: How large can a fennec fox’s den become in firm ground?
10241.e: In firmer ground a fennec den can cover an area of up to about 120 square metres.
10241.m: A fennec den can be as big as a large flat.

10242.q: How many entrances can a fennec fox den have?
10242.e: Large dens have many entrances, up to about 15 in firm ground.
10242.m: A fennec den can have many entrances.

10243.q: What is partnership typically like in fennec foxes?
a: Pairs usually stay together for life
Males live with many females in a harem
Males and females meet only once
10243.e: Fennecs are considered monogamous. A pair shares a territory and raises the young together.
10243.m: Fennec pairs usually stay together for life.

10244.q: What do fennec foxes mark their territory with?
10244.e: Fennecs mark the edges of their territory with urine and droppings. In the mating season, males also become more aggressive towards rivals.
10244.m: The fennec marks its territory with urine and droppings.

10245.q: In which months is the fennec fox’s mating season?
10245.e: Depending on the area, fennecs mate between January and April, often as early as January and February. The young are then born between about March and June.
10245.m: Fennecs mate in winter and spring.

10246.q: About how long does a female fennec fox’s fertile phase (oestrus) last?
a: Only about one to two days
10246.e: In the fennec, oestrus lasts only about one to two days, so mating has to happen exactly then.
10246.m: A female fennec is fertile for only a very short time.

10247.q: How often a year does a female fennec fox normally have young?
10247.e: As a rule there is only one litter a year. If a litter is lost early, a second one can follow.
10247.m: A female fennec usually has only one litter a year.

10248.q: Where does a female fennec fox give birth to her young?
a: In a lined chamber in the den
In the open in the shade of a bush
In a nest high in a palm tree
In a rock crevice by the sea
10248.e: The female lines a chamber in the underground den with plant material, hair and feathers. There the blind young are protected from heat, cold and enemies.
10248.m: Fennec cubs are born safely in the den.

10249.q: How long does pregnancy usually last in the fennec fox?
10249.e: Pregnancy usually lasts 50 to 52 days; in captivity up to 63 days has occasionally been seen.
10249.m: A fennec is pregnant for about 50 days.

10250.q: How many young does a fennec fox usually have per litter?
10250.e: A fennec litter usually has 2 to 4 young, rarely up to 6.
10250.m: A fennec litter is small, usually two to four young.

10251.q: When do young fennec foxes open their eyes?
a: After about one to two weeks
10251.e: Fennec cubs are born blind and open their eyes after about 8 to 14 days.
10251.m: Fennec cubs can see only after a good week.

10252.q: At what age are young fennec foxes weaned, so no longer fed with milk?
a: At about two to three months
10252.e: Depending on the source, the young are weaned after about 61 to 70 days or only at almost three months.
10252.m: Young fennecs drink milk for about two to three months.

10253.q: Up to roughly what age do fennec fox parents look after their young?
10253.e: Both parents feed and protect the young until they are about 16 to 17 weeks old.
10253.m: Fennec parents look after their young for about four months.

10254.q: At about what age do fennec foxes in captivity become sexually mature?
10254.e: In captivity, fennecs usually reach sexual maturity at about 9 months.
10254.m: A fennec is sexually mature at about nine months.

10255.q: How old did the oldest known male fennec fox in captivity live to be?
10255.e: The oldest recorded male fennec in captivity lived to about 14 years.
10255.m: In captivity a fennec can live to about 14 years.

10256.q: What kind of diet does the fennec fox have?
10256.e: The fennec eats rodents, insects, lizards, birds and eggs, but also fruit, leaves and roots.
10256.m: The fennec eats both animals and plants.

10257.q: Which reptiles are among the fennec fox’s prey?
10257.e: As well as rodents and insects, the fennec hunts small lizards such as geckos and skinks.
10257.m: Small lizards such as geckos are on the fennec’s menu.

10258.q: Which plant parts does the fennec fox eat, among other things?
10258.e: The fennec also digs up roots and tubers, which give it extra water.
10258.m: The fennec also digs up roots and tubers.

10259.q: Which bird is a known predator of young fennec foxes?
10259.e: The pharaoh eagle-owl, a desert eagle-owl, has been shown to catch young fennecs. Other enemies are probably jackals and striped hyenas.
10259.m: The pharaoh eagle-owl is a dangerous enemy of young fennecs.

10260.q: In which region does the fennec fox mainly live?
a: In the Sahara in North Africa
In the Kalahari in southern Africa
In the Atacama in South America
10260.e: The fennec’s range covers the Sahara from Morocco and Mauritania to Egypt and into northern Sudan.
10260.m: The fennec is a fox of the Sahara.

10261.q: In the east, as far as which peninsula does the fennec fox’s range reach?
10261.e: In north-eastern Egypt the fennec is found as far as the north-western Sinai Peninsula.
10261.m: In the east, the fennec’s range reaches the Sinai.

10262.q: Roughly how much rain falls each year in the northern part of the fennec fox’s habitat?
10262.e: At the northern edge of its range only about 100 mm of rain or less falls a year, in the south about 300 mm.
10262.m: The fennec lives where it hardly ever rains.

10263.q: Which habitat does the fennec fox prefer?
10263.e: The fennec prefers sandy desert areas where it can dig well and dunes give shelter for its dens.
10263.m: The fennec is at home in desert sand.

10264.q: What is the fennec fox’s status on the IUCN Red List?
10264.e: The IUCN classes the fennec as Least Concern because it is widespread.
10264.m: According to the IUCN, the fennec is not threatened.

10265.q: In which appendix of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) is the fennec fox listed?
10265.e: The fennec is listed in CITES Appendix II. So international trade is allowed but controlled.
10265.m: Trade in fennecs is controlled under CITES Appendix II.

10266.q: Which human activity threatens the fennec fox in some areas?
a: Capture for the pet trade and for display
10266.e: In many places fennecs are caught to be sold as pets or shown to tourists, and some are also hunted for their fur.
10266.m: Capture for the pet trade harms the fennec.

10267.q: Of which country is the fennec fox the national animal?
10267.e: The fennec is the national animal of Algeria and an important symbol of the country.
10267.m: The fennec is Algeria’s national animal.

10268.q: Which national team has the nickname “Les Fennecs”?
10268.e: The Algerian national football team is called “Les Fennecs” after the national animal.
10268.m: Algeria’s footballers are named after the fennec.

10269.q: How does the fennec fox react when it gets too hot even in its den?
a: It pants to lose heat through evaporation
It sweats all over like a human
It falls into a summer sleep lasting months
It changes its coat within an hour
10269.e: Like dogs, the fennec hardly sweats through its skin. From about 35 °C it pants, with up to about 690 breaths a minute, and cools down by evaporation.
10269.m: In great heat, the fennec cools down by panting.

10270.q: Which family does the serval belong to?
10270.e: The serval is a true cat of the family Felidae and belongs to the subfamily of small cats.
10270.m: The serval is a small cat of the cat family.

10271.q: What is the scientific genus name of the serval?
10271.e: The scientific name of the serval is Leptailurus serval, and it is the only species in its genus.
10271.m: The serval has the genus name Leptailurus.

10272.q: Roughly what does the serval’s genus name Leptailurus mean?
10272.e: Leptailurus is made from the Greek “leptos” meaning slender or delicate and “ailouros” meaning cat.
10272.m: Leptailurus means something like slender cat.

10273.q: How many living species does the serval’s genus contain?
10273.e: The genus Leptailurus is monotypic, which means it contains only the serval.
10273.m: The serval is the only species in its genus.

10274.q: Which cats is the serval most closely related to?
10274.e: Genetic studies place the serval in the caracal lineage, together with the caracal and the African golden cat.
10274.m: The serval forms one lineage together with the caracal and the golden cat.

10275.q: Which language does the word “serval” originally come from?
10275.e: The name goes back to the Portuguese “lobo-cerval”, an old name for lynx-like cats.
10275.m: The name serval comes from Portuguese.

10276.q: When the serval was first described scientifically in 1776, which genus was it placed in?
a: Felis, the genus of the wildcat and house cat
Panthera, the genus of the lion and tiger
Canis, the genus of the wolf and dog
Lynx, the genus of the lynxes
10276.e: Johann Christian Daniel von Schreber described the serval in 1776 as Felis serval. Later it was given its own genus, Leptailurus.
10276.m: The serval was first called Felis serval.

10277.q: On which continent does the serval live in the wild?
10277.e: The serval is widespread across large parts of Africa south of the Sahara, with small remaining populations in the north of the continent.
10277.m: The serval is a purely African wild cat.

10278.q: In which region north of the Sahara does a small, highly threatened remnant population of servals still live today?
a: On the Mediterranean coast of the Maghreb
10278.e: North of the Sahara there is only a small population on the Mediterranean coast of Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, where the serval was reintroduced. Regionally it is considered critically endangered.
10278.m: In North Africa the serval survives only in small remnant groups in the Maghreb.

10279.q: Which habitat is especially typical of the serval?
a: Bare rocky mountains with no plants
10279.e: Servals prefer tall grass near water, such as wet savannahs, marshes and floodplains, where many rodents live.
10279.m: The serval loves tall grass near water.

10280.q: Which habitats does the serval largely avoid?
10280.e: Servals need cover in grass and water nearby, so they are missing from extreme deserts and closed rainforest.
10280.m: Desert and dense rainforest are no home for the serval.

10281.q: Up to what altitude can the serval be found in African mountains?
10281.e: In East Africa, servals have been recorded in highland grasslands and moors up to about 3,800 metres, for example in Kenya and on Kilimanjaro.
10281.m: The serval is found even in high mountains up to about 3,800 metres.

10282.q: Which part of the serval’s body is longer, relative to its size, than in any other cat?
10282.e: Relative to its body size, the serval has the longest legs of all cats, which gives it a good view over tall grass.
10282.m: No other cat has legs as long, relative to its body, as the serval.

10283.q: What are the serval’s very large ears mainly an adaptation for?
a: Communicating over long distances by ear wiggling
10283.e: With its large, movable ears the serval hears even quiet sounds of rodents in the grass or even underground.
10283.m: The serval hunts almost more with its ears than with its eyes.

10284.q: What striking marking does the serval have on the back of its ears?
a: Black with a white band or spot
10284.e: The backs of the ears are black with a striking white band, which probably helps with communication, for example between mother and young.
10284.m: The serval’s ears are black at the back with a white marking.

10285.q: Roughly how heavy does an adult serval get?
10285.e: Servals are slender, medium-sized cats, and males are usually a little heavier than females.
10285.m: A serval weighs about as much as a medium-sized dog.

10286.q: Roughly how tall is a serval at the shoulder?
10286.e: Thanks to its long legs, the serval reaches a shoulder height of about 55 to 65 cm, even though it is relatively light.
10286.m: The serval is long-legged and about 60 cm tall at the shoulder.

10287.q: How is the serval’s tail built compared with that of many other cats?
a: Rather short, ringed with black and with a black tip
Longer than its head and body together
10287.e: At about 30 cm, the serval’s tail is relatively short and has black rings and a black tip.
10287.m: The serval has a short, ringed tail.

10288.q: What does the serval’s coat typically look like?
a: Golden yellow with black spots and stripes
10288.e: The yellowish coat is covered with black spots, which often merge into lengthwise stripes on the neck and back.
10288.m: The serval has a golden yellow coat with black spots.

10289.q: Where have black (melanistic) servals mainly been seen?
a: In the highlands of East Africa
10289.e: Melanistic servals are known mainly from highland areas of East Africa, such as the Aberdare Mountains in Kenya and the Ethiopian Highlands.
10289.m: Black servals live mainly in the East African highlands.

10290.q: What is meant by the “servaline” form of the serval?
a: Servals with very small, fine spots
Crosses between servals and house cats
Especially large servals from the south
10290.e: Instead of large spots, the servaline form has many small fine dots, and in 1839 it was mistakenly described as a separate species, Felis servalina.
10290.m: The finely spotted servaline form is not a separate species but a colour variant of the serval.

10291.q: What does the serval mainly feed on?
10291.e: Rodents such as rats and mice make up most of its prey, along with birds, frogs, reptiles and insects.
10291.m: The serval is above all a mouse hunter.

10292.q: Which typical hunting technique does the serval use to catch mice in the grass?
a: A high arching leap, pinning the prey with its front paws
A long chase over several kilometres
Digging out whole burrows with its back legs
10292.e: The serval listens, then leaps onto the prey in a high arc and presses it to the ground with its front paws.
10292.m: The serval catches mice with an elegant arching leap.

10293.q: Roughly how high can a serval jump to catch birds out of the air?
10293.e: From a standing start, servals spring up to about 3 metres high and can so catch birds as they take off.
10293.m: A serval can jump up to three metres high.

10294.q: How successful is the serval at hunting compared with many other cats?
a: Very successful, about every second attempt works
Very unsuccessful, about one in 50 attempts
10294.e: In studies in the Ngorongoro Crater, about half of the serval’s hunting attempts were successful, far more than for lions or leopards.
10294.m: The serval is one of the most successful hunters among cats.

10295.q: Roughly how much does a newborn serval weigh?
10295.e: Young servals are born blind with soft, woolly fur and weigh just under 250 grams.
10295.m: A newborn serval weighs about 250 grams.

10296.q: How does the serval often deal with water in its habitat?
a: It goes into shallow water to catch frogs or fish
It never drinks and gets all it needs from prey
It dives for minutes for crabs in deep lakes
10296.e: In marshy areas, servals also hunt in shallow water, fishing with their paws for frogs and fish.
10296.m: The serval is not afraid of water and also hunts in marshes.

10297.q: At which times of day is the serval usually active?
a: Mainly at dusk and at night
10297.e: Servals are mostly active at dusk and at night, but in undisturbed or cool areas they also hunt during the day.
10297.m: The serval is mainly a twilight hunter.

10298.q: How do adult servals usually live?
a: In colonies of a hundred animals
10298.e: Apart from mothers with young and pairs during the mating season, servals live alone and avoid each other.

10299.q: How does the serval mark its territory especially often?
10299.e: Servals mark their home ranges with urine, droppings and scratch marks, and males spray urine especially often.
10299.m: The serval marks its territory with urine scent marks.

10300.q: What can a serval not do, unlike lions and tigers?
10300.e: Like other small cats, the serval can purr but cannot roar, because its larynx is built differently.
10300.m: The serval purrs, but it does not roar.

10301.q: Roughly how long is a serval’s pregnancy?
10301.e: Pregnancy lasts about 65 to 75 days, so about ten weeks.
10301.m: A female serval is pregnant for about ten weeks.

10302.q: How many young does a female serval usually have per litter?
10302.e: A litter usually has one to four young, often two or three.
10302.m: A serval usually has two to three young.

10303.q: Where does a female serval usually give birth to her young?
a: In a hiding place in thick grass or an abandoned burrow
In a shared den with other females
10303.e: The female uses thick vegetation or the abandoned burrows of other animals, such as aardvarks, as a place to give birth.
10303.m: Young servals are born well hidden.

10304.q: Who raises the young in servals?
10304.e: The male takes no part in raising the young; the female feeds and defends them on her own.
10304.m: In servals, the mother looks after the young alone.

10305.q: At roughly what age do young servals leave their mother?
10305.e: Young servals hunt for themselves from about six months but stay with their mother for about a year before looking for their own area.
10305.m: Young servals stay with their mother for about a year.

10306.q: Roughly how old can a serval live to be in captivity?
10306.e: In zoos, servals reach an age of about 20 years; in the wild the life expectancy is usually much lower.
10306.m: In a zoo, a serval can live to about 20 years.

10307.q: How does the IUCN classify the serval on the Red List?
10307.e: Because it is so widespread, the serval as a whole is not considered threatened, but in some regions it has become rare.
10307.m: Worldwide, the serval is not considered threatened.

10308.q: The serval is listed in Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES). What does that mean?
a: International trade is allowed but needs a permit
All trade in servals is banned worldwide
Servals may be traded without any control
The serval is considered extinct in the wild
10308.e: Species in CITES Appendix II are not directly threatened with extinction. International trade is allowed but needs permits and is controlled so that populations are not overused.
10308.m: CITES Appendix II means trade only with a permit and under control.

10309.q: What is one of the biggest threats to the serval?
a: The loss of wetlands and grassland
10309.e: Draining of wetlands, spreading farmland and overgrazing destroy the serval’s habitats.
10309.m: Without wetlands and grassland, the serval loses its home.

10310.q: What have servals traditionally been hunted for in parts of Africa?
10310.e: In some regions the serval’s spotted fur is used for clothing and ceremonies, and it is sometimes sold as leopard skin.
10310.m: The serval is hunted for its beautiful fur.

10311.q: Which predators are among the serval’s natural enemies?
10311.e: Servals are killed mainly by larger predators such as leopards, lions, hyenas and African wild dogs.
10311.m: The serval must watch out for leopards and hyenas.

10312.q: How does a serval typically escape from enemies?
a: With fast zigzag leaps into tall grass
By burying itself in the sand
By swimming out into the open sea
10312.e: When in danger, the serval races away in high, changing leaps and disappears into cover; sometimes it also climbs trees.
10312.m: The serval escapes into the grass with great leaps.

10313.q: What is the name of the domestic cat breed that came from crosses between servals and house cats?
10313.e: The Savannah cat came from a cross between a serval and a house cat in the 1980s, whereas the Bengal comes from the leopard cat.
10313.m: The Savannah cat has a serval as an ancestor.

10314.q: Roughly how large is a serval’s home range?
10314.e: Males and females use home ranges of about 10 to 32 km², which can overlap a lot.
10314.m: A serval roams an area of a few dozen square kilometres.

10315.q: Which habitat does the serval prefer in Africa?
a: Wet savannahs and grassland with tall grass
10315.e: The serval lives mainly in savannahs, grassland and marshes with tall grass and water nearby. There it finds many rodents and good cover.
10315.m: The serval loves tall grass near water.

10316.q: What importance does the serval often have for farmers in Africa?
a: It keeps rodents in the fields under control
It eats large amounts of grain
10316.e: Because servals eat a great many rodents, they can reduce crop damage from rats and mice, even though they sometimes kill chickens.
10316.m: The serval helps farmers by eating mice.

10317.q: How well can a serval climb?
a: It can climb but does so rather rarely
It lives almost only in treetops
10317.e: Servals are mainly ground hunters in the grass, but they climb trees when needed, for example when escaping.
10317.m: The serval hunts on the ground but can escape up trees.

10318.q: Why does a serval have to catch a great many prey animals in one day?
a: Because its prey is usually very small
Because it eats only every tenth day
Because it stores food for the winter
Because it shares its prey with the young of other cats
10318.e: The serval mainly hunts mice, rats, frogs and insects. Because each prey animal gives only a little food, in studies it catches about 15 animals a day.
10318.m: The serval catches many small prey animals in a day.

10319.q: Like most cats, how many teeth does an adult serval have?
10319.e: Like almost all cats, the serval has 30 teeth, including strong canines and sharp carnassials for cutting meat.
10319.m: Like most cats, the serval has 30 teeth.

10320.q: What is the scientific name of the ocelot?
10320.e: The ocelot’s scientific name is Leopardus pardalis. Leopardus wiedii is the margay, Leptailurus serval the serval and Lynx pardinus the Iberian lynx.
10320.m: The ocelot’s scientific name is Leopardus pardalis.

10321.q: Which genus does the ocelot belong to?
10321.e: The ocelot belongs to the genus Leopardus, the small spotted cats of the Americas. This genus also includes the margay, the oncilla and the kodkod.
10321.m: The ocelot is one of the small spotted cats of the Americas.

10322.q: Which naturalist first described the ocelot scientifically in 1758?
10322.e: Carl Linnaeus described the ocelot in 1758 as Felis pardalis. Later the species was placed in the genus Leopardus.
10322.m: Linnaeus gave the ocelot its first scientific name in 1758.

10323.q: Which species is considered the ocelot’s closest relative?
10323.e: Genetic studies show that the margay (Leopardus wiedii) is the ocelot’s sister species. The two lines split about 1 to 2.4 million years ago.
10323.m: The margay is the ocelot’s closest relative.

10324.q: How are the two subspecies of ocelot recognised today distributed?
a: One in Central America, one in South America
One in North America, one in Africa
One in the rainforest, one in the desert
One on the Caribbean islands, one in Patagonia
10324.e: Since 2017 only two subspecies have been recognised: L. p. pardalis in Central America and L. p. mitis in South America. In the past many more subspecies were distinguished.
10324.m: The ocelot has one Central American and one South American subspecies.

10325.q: What is special about the genetic make-up of the ocelot and the other Leopardus cats?
a: They have 36 chromosomes instead of 38 like most cats
They have twice as many chromosomes as house cats
They have the same genes as the jaguar
10325.e: The species of the genus Leopardus have 36 chromosomes. Most other cats, including the house cat, have 38.
10325.m: The ocelot has two chromosomes fewer than most cats.

10326.q: Roughly how much does an adult ocelot weigh?
10326.e: Adult ocelots usually weigh about 7 to 15.5 kg. Females are lighter, and strong males can reach up to about 18 kg.
10326.m: An adult ocelot weighs about as much as a medium-sized dog.

10327.q: Roughly what head and body length does an ocelot reach?
10327.e: The ocelot’s head and body length is about 55 to 100 cm. The tail comes on top of that.
10327.m: Without its tail, an ocelot usually measures between just over half a metre and a metre.

10328.q: Roughly how long is an ocelot’s tail?
10328.e: The ocelot’s tail measures about 30 to 45 cm. Relative to its body it is shorter than that of the tree-living margay.
10328.m: For a cat of its size, the ocelot has a rather short tail.

10329.q: Roughly how tall is an ocelot at the shoulder?
10329.e: The ocelot’s shoulder height is about 40 to 50 cm. That makes it about twice as tall as a house cat.
10329.m: An ocelot reaches about to an adult’s knee or a little higher.

10330.q: Where does the ocelot rank in body size within the genus Leopardus?
a: It is the largest species of the genus
It is the smallest species of the genus
It is the second smallest species of the genus
It is smaller than the oncilla
10330.e: At up to about 15 kg and more, the ocelot is the largest of the Leopardus cats. Relatives such as the margay, the oncilla or the kodkod are much smaller and lighter.
10330.m: The ocelot is the largest Leopardus cat.

10331.q: Which pattern is typical of the ocelot’s coat?
a: Elongated rosettes, often joined into chains
A plain coat with no pattern at all
Large round rosettes with a dot in the middle
10331.e: The ocelot has dark-edged, elongated rosettes that often merge into chains or bands on the flanks. Round rosettes with a central dot are typical of the jaguar instead.
10331.m: Chain-like rosettes make the ocelot’s coat unmistakable.

10332.q: What can be said about the spot pattern of individual ocelots?
a: It is unique to each animal
It is the same in all animals
10332.e: Every ocelot has its own spot pattern, like a fingerprint. Researchers use this to tell animals apart in camera trap pictures.
10332.m: Individual ocelots can be reliably recognised by their coat pattern.

10333.q: What marking does the ocelot have on the back of its ears?
a: A white spot on a black background
A long black tuft of hair
10333.e: The ocelot’s round ears are dark at the back and have a striking white spot. Such spots probably help with communication, for example between mother and young.
10333.m: Behind its ears the ocelot has a white spot on a black background.

10334.q: What colour is an ocelot’s underside?
10334.e: The ocelot’s underside is pale, usually whitish, and dotted with dark spots. The upper side, on the other hand, is yellowish to grey-brown.
10334.m: The ocelot has a pale, spotted belly.

10335.q: Roughly how many teeth does an ocelot have?
10335.e: Like other cats, the ocelot has a shortened set of 28 to 30 teeth. The sharp carnassials cut meat like scissors.
10335.m: An ocelot manages with about 30 teeth.

10336.q: What does the popular Spanish name “manigordo” for the ocelot mean?
10336.e: “Manigordo” literally means “fat hand”. The name refers to the ocelot’s strikingly broad front paws and is used, for example, in Costa Rica, Panama and Venezuela.
10336.m: Because of its broad front paws, the ocelot is also called “manigordo”.

10337.q: Which language does the word “ocelot” probably come from?
a: Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs
Quechua, the language of the Incas
10337.e: The word probably goes back to the Nahuatl word “ōcēlōtl”. Surprisingly, this word usually meant the jaguar.
10337.m: The ocelot’s name probably comes from the Aztec language.

10338.q: What does the species name “pardalis” in the ocelot’s scientific name mean?
10338.e: “Pardalis” is the Greek and Latin word for the leopard or panther. Linnaeus used it to refer to the spotted, leopard-like coat.
10338.m: The species name “pardalis” refers to the ocelot’s leopard-like coat.

10339.q: How far does the ocelot’s range stretch from north to south?
a: From the south-western USA to northern Argentina
From Colombia to Tierra del Fuego
10339.e: The ocelot is found from southern Texas and Arizona through Mexico, Central America and large parts of South America to northern Argentina. It is missing from Tierra del Fuego and Canada.
10339.m: The ocelot lives from the southern USA to northern Argentina.

10340.q: In which US state does the best-known and highly threatened remnant population of ocelots live?
10340.e: Only a few dozen ocelots survive in southern Texas; estimates from 2014 give about 50 to 80 animals. There are also occasional records in Arizona.
10340.m: In the USA the ocelot survives mainly in small numbers in southern Texas.

10341.q: From which US states has the ocelot disappeared today?
10341.e: The ocelot used to live in Louisiana and Arkansas too, but there it is now considered wiped out. It is still found in Texas and Arizona.
10341.m: The ocelot has disappeared from Louisiana and Arkansas.

10342.q: Up to roughly what altitude has the ocelot been recorded in mountains?
10342.e: The ocelot usually lives in the lowlands but has been recorded in the mountains up to about 3,000 m. Higher up, the vegetation is usually too sparse for it.
10342.m: In the mountains the ocelot climbs up to about 3,000 m.

10343.q: Which habitats does the ocelot prefer?
a: Dense vegetation such as rainforest, mangroves and thorn scrub
10343.e: The ocelot needs dense cover, for example in tropical forests, mangroves, thorn forests or overgrown savannahs. It avoids open landscapes.
10343.m: The ocelot feels at home wherever dense plants give cover.

10344.q: At what time of day is the ocelot mainly active?
10344.e: Ocelots hunt mainly at dusk and at night. During the day they usually rest hidden in hollow trees, in thickets or on branches.
10344.m: The ocelot hunts mainly under cover of darkness.

10345.q: Which structure in the eye helps the ocelot see well at night?
10345.e: The tapetum lucidum is a reflecting layer behind the retina. It sends light through the sensory cells a second time and makes cats’ eyes shine in a beam of light.
10345.m: Thanks to the tapetum lucidum, the ocelot makes the best use even of little light.

10346.q: How does the adult ocelot live socially?
a: In fixed pairs all year round
10346.e: Adult ocelots live alone and defend a territory. Partners meet only to mate, and the young are raised by the mother alone.
10346.m: The ocelot is a loner with its own territory.

10347.q: How do the territories of male ocelots relate to those of females?
a: They are larger and overlap several female territories
They are smaller and lie inside a female’s territory
They are the same size and never overlap
Males have no territory at all
10347.e: Male ocelots use areas of up to about 46 km², females usually much smaller ones. A male’s territory typically overlaps with those of several females.
10347.m: A male ocelot claims a large territory in which several females live.

10348.e: Ocelots often leave their droppings in fixed spots used by several animals. These latrines probably serve to communicate through scents.
10348.m: At shared dropping sites, ocelots exchange scent messages.

10349.q: Which prey animals make up most of the ocelot’s diet?
a: Small mammals such as rodents and opossums
Large hoofed animals such as deer
10349.e: The ocelot mainly eats small mammals such as rats, agoutis, opossums and armadillos. Birds, reptiles, fish and crustaceans add to the menu.
10349.m: Small mammals are the ocelot’s most important food.

10350.q: How heavy are most of the ocelot’s prey animals?
10350.e: The ocelot’s typical prey weighs less than about 1 kg. It only rarely catches larger animals such as monkeys, anteaters or young deer.
10350.m: The ocelot mostly hunts animals lighter than a kilogram.

10351.q: Roughly how much food does an ocelot need per day?
10351.e: An ocelot needs about 600 to 800 g of meat a day. That is roughly a few small rodents or one larger prey animal.
10351.m: An ocelot eats a little less than a kilogram of meat a day.

10352.q: What did studies in Venezuela show about the ocelot’s diet?
a: It eats different prey depending on the season
It eats only rodents all year round
It eats almost nothing in the rainy season
It lives on fruit in the dry season
10352.e: In Venezuela, iguanas and rodents were the main prey in the dry season, and land crabs in the rainy season. So the ocelot flexibly uses whatever is plentiful at the time.
10352.m: The ocelot adapts its menu to what each season offers.

10353.q: How does an ocelot deal with water?
a: It swims well and does not avoid water
It drowns quickly and avoids all water
It never drinks and gets everything from its prey
It lives almost entirely in water
10353.e: The ocelot is a good swimmer and also crosses rivers. Sometimes it catches fish or amphibians while doing so.
10353.m: Unlike many house cats, the ocelot is a good swimmer.

10354.q: Where does the ocelot mostly hunt, even though it is a good climber?
10354.e: The ocelot climbs and jumps well but hunts mainly on the ground. Its close relative the margay, on the other hand, is much more adapted to life in trees.
10354.m: The ocelot is a good climber but usually hunts on the ground.

10355.q: Roughly how long is an ocelot’s pregnancy?
10355.e: The ocelot’s pregnancy lasts about 2 to 3 months, usually about 80 days. That is a little longer than in the house cat.
10355.m: A female ocelot is pregnant for about two and a half months.

10356.q: How many young does a female ocelot usually have per litter?
10356.e: A litter usually has only 1 to 3 young, often just one. For a cat of this size that is a low birth rate.
10356.m: Ocelots have small litters of usually only one to three young.

10357.q: Roughly how much does a newborn ocelot weigh?
10357.e: Young ocelots weigh about 200 to 340 g at birth. They are born blind and already spotted.
10357.m: A newborn ocelot weighs about as much as a packet of butter.

10358.q: Roughly when do young ocelots open their eyes?
10358.e: Young ocelots are blind at birth and open their eyes after about two weeks. In house cats this happens much earlier.
10358.m: Young ocelots stay blind for a good two weeks.

10359.q: Where does a female ocelot usually give birth to her young?
a: In a sheltered hiding place such as a tree hollow or thicket
Unprotected in the middle of open ground
In a nest she builds from mud
In the shallow water of a river
10359.e: The female chooses a hidden spot, for example a hollow tree, a rock crevice or thick bushes. There the helpless young are protected from enemies.
10359.m: Ocelot young are born in a well-hidden shelter.

10360.q: How long can young ocelots stay with their mother?
10360.e: Young ocelots leave the hiding place from about 3 months, but they often stay in their mother’s area for up to 2 years. Only then do they look for their own territory.
10360.m: Young ocelots stay near their mother for a remarkably long time.

10361.q: At about what age does an ocelot become sexually mature?
10361.e: Ocelots become sexually mature at about 2 years. Together with the small litters, this means the population grows slowly.
10361.m: An ocelot can breed from the age of about two years.

10362.q: What maximum age can ocelots reach in captivity?
10362.e: In zoos, ocelots can live to about 20 years. In the wild their life expectancy is usually much shorter because of enemies, diseases and traffic.
10362.m: In a zoo an ocelot can live to twenty years.

10363.q: Which animals are among the natural enemies of adult ocelots?
10363.e: Adult ocelots are killed mainly by the larger cats, the jaguar and the puma. Young ocelots are also threatened by birds of prey, snakes and other predators.
10363.m: Only larger cats such as the jaguar and puma are dangerous to adult ocelots.

10364.q: How does the ocelot adapt its behaviour when many pumas or people are about in its area?
a: It shifts its times of activity
It switches to a purely plant diet
It forms large groups for protection
10364.e: Camera trap studies suggest that ocelots shift their active hours to avoid pumas and people as far as possible. This reduces dangerous encounters.
10364.m: The ocelot avoids pumas and people by being active at other times.

10365.q: What is the ocelot’s worldwide status on the IUCN Red List?
10365.e: The IUCN classes the ocelot worldwide as “Least Concern” because it has a huge range. However, the population trend is considered to be falling, and local populations such as in Texas are highly threatened.
10365.m: Worldwide the ocelot is not threatened, but in some regions it is highly threatened.

10366.q: Why were ocelots hunted in very large numbers around 1970?
a: For their spotted fur for fur coats
Because they threatened cattle herds as pests
Because their meat was a delicacy
10366.e: Around 1970, well over a hundred thousand ocelot skins were traded internationally every year. Fur coats made of ocelot skin were a luxury and put the populations under great pressure.
10366.m: The fashion for ocelot fur put the species in great danger around 1970.

10367.q: What does it mean for the ocelot that it has been listed in Appendix I of CITES since 1989?
a: International trade in ocelots and their skins is banned
It may only be kept in zoos
Hunting it as a sport is allowed worldwide
10367.e: Species in CITES Appendix I may not be traded internationally for commercial purposes. Since 1989 this has also applied to the ocelot and its skins.
10367.m: Since 1989, international trade in ocelot skins has been banned.

10368.q: What are among the biggest dangers to ocelots in southern Texas today?
10368.e: In southern Texas, most of the dense thorn scrub that ocelots need has been cleared. Many of the few remaining animals also die on roads, which is why wildlife underpasses are being built there.
10368.m: Land clearing and roads are the biggest threats to the last ocelots in Texas.

10369.q: Which famous artist kept an ocelot called Babou as a pet?
10369.e: The Spanish painter Salvador Dalí even took his ocelot Babou to restaurants. He is said to have told a frightened guest that it was just a painted house cat.
10369.m: Salvador Dalí with his ocelot Babou was a striking sight.

10370.q: Which family does the mandrill belong to?
10370.e: The mandrill is an Old World monkey and belongs to the family Cercopithecidae, which also includes baboons and macaques.
10370.m: The mandrill belongs to the Old World monkey family.

10371.q: What is the scientific genus name of the mandrill?
10371.e: The mandrill’s scientific name is Mandrillus sphinx. The genus Mandrillus contains only the mandrill and the drill.
10371.m: The mandrill has the genus name Mandrillus.

10372.q: Which species is the mandrill’s closest living relative?
10372.e: The drill (Mandrillus leucophaeus) is the only other species in the genus Mandrillus and so the mandrill’s sister species.
10372.m: The drill is the mandrill’s closest relative.

10373.q: Which genus were the mandrill and the drill placed in together in the past?
10373.e: Because of their long snouts and life on the ground, the mandrill and drill used to be considered baboons of the genus Papio.
10373.m: The mandrill used to be classed with the baboons.

10374.q: What did genetic studies show about the mandrill’s relationships?
a: It is less closely related to baboons than long thought
It is actually a great ape
It descends from New World monkeys from the Americas
It is a cross between a baboon and a drill
10374.e: For a long time the mandrill was counted among the baboons. But genetic studies show that it is more closely related to the mangabeys than to the baboons.
10374.m: The mandrill is not a close relative of the baboons.

10375.q: Roughly how many years ago did the lines of the mandrill and the drill split?
10375.e: Genetic estimates date the split between mandrill and drill to about 3.2 million years ago.
10375.m: The mandrill and drill went their separate ways about three million years ago.

10376.q: What is known about fossils of the mandrill’s genus?
a: None have been found so far
Many are known from South America
10376.e: No fossils of the genus Mandrillus are known so far, so its history is studied mainly through genetics.
10376.m: No fossils of the mandrill or its genus are known so far.

10377.q: Why is the mandrill important for the rainforest?
a: It spreads the seeds of many fruits in its droppings
It fells old trees and creates clearings
It pollinates flowers like a bee
It keeps the forest free of insects
10377.e: The mandrill eats a great deal of fruit. It passes out the seeds in other places, and so helps plants spread through the forest.
10377.m: As a seed spreader, the mandrill helps the rainforest.

10378.q: Who described the mandrill scientifically in 1758, and under what name?
10378.e: In 1758 Carl Linnaeus included the mandrill in his Systema Naturae as Simia sphinx.
10378.m: Linnaeus described the mandrill in 1758 as Simia sphinx.

10379.q: Which well-known film character is inspired by a mandrill?
10379.e: The wise monkey Rafiki has the colourful face of a mandrill. King Louie is an orangutan, Abu a capuchin monkey and Caesar a chimpanzee.
10379.m: Rafiki from “The Lion King” is reminiscent of a mandrill.

10380.q: Which Swiss naturalist drew the mandrill as early as the 16th century?
10380.e: In his “Historia animalium” (1551 to 1558), Conrad Gessner from Zurich published the first clear picture of a mandrill. However, he thought the bristly, dog-like animal was a kind of hyena.
10380.m: Conrad Gessner drew the mandrill as early as the 16th century.

10381.q: What parts is the name “mandrill” made up of?
a: “Man” and a West African word for monkey
10381.e: The name combines the English “man” with “drill”, a West African word for baboon or monkey.
10381.m: The name mandrill contains the word “drill” for monkey.

10382.q: What does the mandrill’s species name “sphinx” refer to?
10382.e: Linnaeus chose the name “sphinx” after the sphinx, a hybrid creature from ancient legend.
10382.m: The species name sphinx recalls the sphinx of ancient times.

10383.q: What record does the male mandrill hold among monkeys?
a: It is the largest monkey species, not counting great apes
It is the fastest runner of all monkeys
It has the longest tail of all monkeys
It lives longest of all monkeys
10383.e: Adult male mandrills are the largest and heaviest monkeys; only great apes grow bigger.
10383.m: The mandrill is the largest primate after the great apes.

10384.q: How much does an adult male mandrill typically weigh?
10384.e: Male mandrills usually weigh between 19 and 30 kg, and some animals in captivity weigh more.
10384.m: A male mandrill usually weighs 19 to 30 kg.

10385.q: Roughly how much does an adult female mandrill weigh?
10385.e: Females weigh about 10 to 15 kg, so they are only about half as heavy as the males.
10385.m: A female mandrill weighs about 10 to 15 kg.

10386.q: Among all primates, what is the mandrill an especially striking example of?
a: The strongest difference between males and females
The largest brain relative to the body
10386.e: In the mandrill, males and females differ in size, weight, teeth and colouring more than in any other primate.
10386.m: In the mandrill, males and females are extremely different.

10387.q: Roughly how long is a mandrill’s tail?
10387.e: The mandrill has only a short stubby tail a few centimetres long.
10387.m: The mandrill has a very short stubby tail.

10388.q: How long can a male mandrill’s canine teeth grow?
10388.e: The males’ canines reach up to about 4.5 cm, the females’ only about 1 cm.
10388.m: Male mandrills have canines up to 4.5 cm long.

10389.q: What did researchers find out about male mandrills with short canines under about 3 cm?
10389.e: Males with canines under about 30 mm have less breeding success than males with long canines.
10389.m: Long canines increase a mandrill’s chances of having young.

10390.q: What causes the red colour on the male mandrill’s face?
a: Blood vessels just under the skin
Pigments from food in the fur
Bacteria on the surface of the skin
10390.e: The red of the nose ridge and lips comes from vessels with a rich blood supply close to the surface of the skin.
10390.m: The red on a mandrill’s face comes from blood in the skin.

10391.q: What causes the blue colour on the mandrill’s ridged cheeks?
a: Light scattered by neatly arranged collagen fibres
A blue pigment in the skin
Deposits from berries it has eaten
10391.e: The blue is a structural colour: collagen fibres arranged in parallel in the skin scatter light so that it looks blue.
10391.m: The mandrill’s blue is a structural colour made by collagen fibres.

10392.q: Which male mandrills have the brightest colours on the face and rear?
10392.e: High-ranking males have stronger colours, larger testes and more fat padding, and they father most of the young.
10392.m: In mandrills, the boss wears the strongest colours.

10393.q: What does the mandrill use the gland on its chest for?
10393.e: Both sexes have a sternal gland on the chest that they use to leave scent marks on trees. Dominant males mark especially often.
10393.m: The mandrill leaves scent marks with its chest gland.

10394.q: How are adult male mandrills part of the large hordes?
a: They join mainly when females are ready to mate
They lead the horde all year as fixed leaders
They form their own bachelor groups within the horde
They look after the young as permanent members
10394.e: The core of the hordes is made up of related females with their young. Adult males are not permanent members; they join mainly in the mating season and otherwise usually live alone.
10394.m: Adult male mandrills come to the horde mainly in the mating season.

10395.q: On average, how many animals did the mandrill hordes in Lopé National Park have?
10395.e: Hordes counted in Lopé had about 620 animals on average, the largest about 845. That makes them some of the largest groups of wild primates.
10395.m: A mandrill horde in Lopé often has over 600 members.

10396.q: How large was the home range of a mandrill horde of about 700 animals in Gabon?
10396.e: A horde of about 700 mandrills used an area of about 182 km², about half of which was suitable habitat.
10396.m: A large mandrill horde needs a huge area of forest.

10397.q: From what age do young male mandrills usually leave their horde?
10397.e: Young males move away after their sixth year and often live alone for a while, whereas females stay in the horde.
10397.m: Young male mandrills leave their group from about six years old.

10398.q: At what time of day is the mandrill mainly active?
10398.e: The mandrill is active by day and awake about 10 hours a day. It looks for food mainly on the ground.
10398.m: The mandrill is a day-active, ground-living monkey.

10399.q: Where does the mandrill sleep at night?
a: In trees, often a different one every night
On the ground in thick grass
10399.e: To sleep, the mandrill climbs into trees and often chooses a new sleeping tree every night.
10399.m: The mandrill sleeps in trees at night.

10400.q: What makes up most of the mandrill’s food in Lopé National Park?
10400.e: Studies in Lopé showed that fruit makes up about half the diet, followed by seeds at about a quarter.

10401.q: Roughly how many plant species does the mandrill use as food?
10401.e: The mandrill is a flexible omnivore and uses more than a hundred different plant species.
10401.m: The mandrill eats over a hundred different plant species.

10402.q: What is special about male mandrills when they eat hard seeds?
a: They crack very hard seed shells with their teeth
They throw seeds onto stones until they break
They let ants open the seeds
They soak seeds in water for days
10402.e: Thanks to their strong jaws, adult males are among the few primates that can bite open the very hard seed shells of Detarium trees.
10402.m: Male mandrills can crack hard seeds with their teeth.

10403.q: Which mammal does the mandrill occasionally hunt?
10403.e: Besides insects, frogs, birds’ eggs and rodents, the mandrill sometimes also catches young duikers.
10403.m: The mandrill sometimes even catches young duikers.

10404.q: Among predators, which enemy is the greatest danger to mandrills of all ages?
10404.e: Leopards hunt mandrills of all ages. For young animals, crowned eagles and rock pythons are also dangerous.
10404.m: The leopard is the mandrill’s most important natural enemy.

10405.q: Which bird of prey can be dangerous to young mandrills?
10405.e: The crowned eagle is a powerful African forest bird of prey that also catches monkeys and can kill young mandrills.
10405.m: The crowned eagle can catch young mandrills.

10406.q: In which region of Africa does the mandrill live?
10406.e: The mandrill is found in southern Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon and the south-west of the Republic of the Congo.
10406.m: The mandrill lives in the rainforest of western Central Africa.

10407.q: In Cameroon, what separates the mandrill’s range from that of its closest relative, the drill?
10407.e: The Sanaga River in Cameroon forms the border: south of it lives the mandrill, north of it the drill.
10407.m: A river in Cameroon separates the mandrill and the drill.

10408.q: Which country is considered the mandrill’s most important stronghold?
10408.e: Gabon is home to most of the population, while the habitat in Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea has shrunk more.
10408.m: Most mandrills today live in Gabon.

10409.q: Why can large rivers separate mandrill populations genetically?
a: Mandrills hardly ever cross large rivers
The river water changes their genes
Only males live by the river
10409.e: Mandrills live on the forest floor and hardly ever cross wide rivers. So groups on the two banks do not mix for a long time, as on the Ogooué in Gabon, for example.
10409.m: Large rivers keep mandrill groups apart for a long time.

10410.q: In which habitat does the mandrill mainly live?
a: High mountains above the tree line
10410.e: The mandrill lives mainly in dense tropical rainforests but also uses forest edges and gallery forests.
10410.m: The mandrill is a rainforest dweller.

10411.q: Roughly how long is a mandrill’s pregnancy?
10411.e: A female mandrill is pregnant for about 175 days on average, so just under six months.
10411.m: A mandrill’s pregnancy lasts just under six months.

10412.q: Roughly how much does a newborn mandrill weigh?
10412.e: A mandrill usually gives birth to a single baby with a birth weight of about 600 to 640 g.
10412.m: A newborn mandrill weighs about 600 grams.

10413.q: In which months are most mandrill babies born in Gabon?
10413.e: Mating peaks in the dry season, so most young are born between January and March.
10413.m: Mandrill babies are usually born from January to March.

10414.q: On average, how much time passes between two births of a female mandrill?
10414.e: The gap between two births is about 405 days on average, so a good year.
10414.m: A female mandrill has a baby about every year.

10415.q: At what age do male mandrills reach their full body size?
10415.e: Males grow more slowly and are fully grown only at about 10 years, females at about 7 years.
10415.m: Male mandrills are fully grown only at about ten years.

10416.q: How old can a mandrill live to be in captivity?
10416.e: In zoos, mandrills reach 30 to 40 years, in the wild usually much less.
10416.m: In a zoo a mandrill can live up to 40 years.

10417.q: What is the mandrill’s status on the IUCN Red List?
10417.e: The IUCN classes the mandrill as vulnerable because its numbers are falling clearly due to hunting and habitat loss.
10417.m: The IUCN classes the mandrill as vulnerable.

10418.q: What does it mean that the mandrill is listed in the strictest appendix of CITES?
a: Commercial international trade in wild-caught animals is banned
It may only be kept in African zoos
Hunting is allowed worldwide but must be reported
It is counted worldwide every year
10418.e: The mandrill is listed in CITES Appendix I. This bans commercial trade across borders in animals caught in the wild.
10418.m: International trade in wild mandrills is banned.

10419.q: What is the main threat to the mandrill in the wild?
a: Hunting for bushmeat and forest clearing
Poisoning by pesticides in rice fields
10419.e: Mandrills are heavily hunted for bushmeat, and logging and road building make it easier for hunters to get into the forest.
10419.m: Hunting and forest clearing are the biggest threats to the mandrill.

10420.q: Which family do macaques belong to?
10420.e: Macaques are Old World monkeys of the family Cercopithecidae. The capuchin family, on the other hand, lives in the Americas.
10420.m: The macaque belongs to the Old World monkeys.

10421.q: What is the scientific genus name of the macaques?
10421.e: All macaques form the genus Macaca. Papio are the baboons, Cercopithecus the guenons and Colobus the colobus monkeys.

10422.q: From which language did the word “macaque” come into European languages?
10422.e: The word goes back to the Portuguese “macaco” for monkey, which in turn comes from a Bantu language from the Congo region of Africa.
10422.m: The name macaque reached us through Portuguese.

10423.q: Roughly how many species does the macaque genus include today?
10423.e: Depending on the classification, about 23 to 25 species of macaque are recognised today. That makes the macaques one of the most species-rich primate genera.
10423.m: There are over 20 species of macaque.

10424.q: Which macaque species is the only one that does not live in Asia?
10424.e: The Barbary macaque lives in North Africa and on Gibraltar. All other macaque species live in Asia.
10424.m: The Barbary macaque is the only macaque outside Asia.

10425.q: In which countries does the Barbary macaque mainly live in the wild today?
10425.e: Wild Barbary macaques live mainly in the mountain forests of the Atlas and Rif in Morocco and in Algeria.
10425.m: The Barbary macaque lives in the mountain forests of Morocco and Algeria.

10426.q: Where does Europe’s only free-living population of monkeys, made up of Barbary macaques, live?
10426.e: About 300 Barbary macaques live on the Rock of Gibraltar. They were probably brought there by people.
10426.m: Europe’s only free monkeys live on Gibraltar.

10427.q: What does a well-known legend say about the Barbary macaques on Gibraltar?
a: If the monkeys disappear, the British will leave Gibraltar
If the monkeys disappear, the Rock will fall into the sea
If the monkeys disappear, a great drought will come
If the monkeys disappear, a war will break out
10427.e: According to legend, Gibraltar will stay British as long as Barbary macaques live there. That is why the animals are still looked after with special care today.
10427.m: According to legend, the Rock stays British as long as Barbary macaques live on Gibraltar.

10428.q: Which politician had the number of Barbary macaques on Gibraltar topped up during the Second World War?
10428.e: When the population had shrunk greatly during the Second World War, Winston Churchill ordered more Barbary macaques to be brought to Gibraltar.
10428.m: During the war, Churchill had new Barbary macaques brought to Gibraltar.

10429.q: What is special about the tail of the Barbary macaque?
a: It is longer than the body
10429.e: The Barbary macaque has at most a tiny boneless tail stump a few millimetres long. That is why it is often wrongly taken for an ape.
10429.m: The Barbary macaque has almost no tail.

10430.q: Which behaviour is especially striking in male Barbary macaques?
a: They carry and look after young
They build nests for the young
10430.e: Male Barbary macaques care intensively for young in the group, even if they are not sure they are the father, and sometimes carry them around for hours.
10430.m: Male Barbary macaques look after young remarkably often.

10431.q: What is the Barbary macaque’s status on the IUCN Red List?
10431.e: The Barbary macaque has been classed as endangered since 2008. Habitat loss and illegal capture of young for the pet trade threaten it.

10432.q: What was the effect of listing the Barbary macaque in the strictest appendix of CITES in 2016?
a: Commercial trade in wild-caught animals is banned
The animals may only live in zoos
Hunting it is now allowed if reported
It may only be kept in Europe
10432.e: Since 2016 the Barbary macaque has been listed in CITES Appendix I, the strictest appendix. This bans commercial international trade in animals caught in the wild.
10432.m: Since 2016, trade in wild Barbary macaques has been banned.

10433.q: Which record among primates belongs to the Japanese macaque?
a: It lives highest in the mountains
It is the heaviest Old World monkey
10433.e: Apart from humans, the Japanese macaque is the primate that lives furthest north. The northernmost group lives on the Shimokita Peninsula.
10433.m: The Japanese macaque is the northernmost monkey in the world.

10434.q: What is the Japanese macaque in Jigokudani park famous for?
a: It bathes in hot springs in winter
It catches salmon from the river
It builds caves in the snow
10434.e: In the Jigokudani Monkey Park, Japanese macaques warm themselves in hot springs in winter. That is why they are often called “snow monkeys”.
10434.m: Japanese macaques warm up in hot springs in winter.

10435.q: What did the female Japanese macaque Imo invent on the island of Koshima in the 1950s?
10435.e: Imo began washing sandy sweet potatoes in water. The behaviour spread through her group and is seen as an early example of animal culture.
10435.m: The macaque Imo invented washing sweet potatoes.

10436.q: Thanks to its thick fur, down to what temperatures can the Japanese macaque cope?
10436.e: The Japanese macaque’s fur grows thicker in the cold. This lets it survive temperatures down to about minus 20 degrees.
10436.m: The Japanese macaque can bear cold down to about minus 20 degrees.

10437.q: What does an adult Japanese macaque’s face typically look like?
10437.e: Japanese macaques have a hairless, pink to red face. In the mating season the males’ face and genital area turn a stronger red.
10437.m: The Japanese macaque has a bare, red face.

10438.q: On which of Japan’s four large main islands do no Japanese macaques live?
10438.e: Japanese macaques live on Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu as well as on smaller islands such as Yakushima. They are not found on Hokkaido, the northernmost main island.
10438.m: No Japanese macaques live on Hokkaido.

10439.q: Which medical term is named after the rhesus macaque?
a: A bone in the inner ear
A muscle in the upper arm
10439.e: Karl Landsteiner and Alexander Wiener named the rhesus factor after experiments with the blood of rhesus macaques. It is important in blood transfusions and pregnancy.
10439.m: The rhesus factor in blood is named after the rhesus macaque.

10440.q: Who is the name of the rhesus macaque based on?
a: Rhesus, a king from Greek legend
10440.e: The name comes from the Thracian king Rhesus from Greek legend. Jean-Baptiste Audebert, who gave the name, said himself that it had no meaning.
10440.m: The rhesus macaque is named after the legendary King Rhesus.

10441.q: What pioneering role did the rhesus macaque Albert II play in 1949?
a: He was the first primate in space
He was the first cloned monkey
He was the first monkey to have a heart transplant
He was the first to learn sign language
10441.e: In 1949 Albert II flew on an American V-2 rocket across the boundary into space. He died on landing because the parachute failed.
10441.m: In 1949 the rhesus macaque Albert II was the first primate in space.

10442.q: What record does the rhesus macaque hold for its distribution?
a: The largest range of any primate except humans
The highest-altitude range of all monkeys
The smallest range of all macaques
The only monkey on every continent
10442.e: The rhesus macaque is found from Afghanistan through India to China. No other non-human primate has such a large range.
10442.m: The rhesus macaque has the largest range of all monkeys.

10443.q: In which US state has an introduced population of rhesus macaques lived since the 1930s?
10443.e: Around 1938 a boat tour operator on the Silver River in Florida released rhesus macaques. Their descendants still live wild there today.
10443.m: Feral rhesus macaques live in Florida.

10444.q: Where is the island of Cayo Santiago with its well-known research colony of free-living rhesus macaques?
10444.e: Cayo Santiago is a small island off Puerto Rico. The rhesus macaques settled there have been studied by researchers for decades.
10444.m: The monkey island of Cayo Santiago lies off Puerto Rico.

10445.q: What did rhesus macaques become known for in the 1950s through the psychologist Harry Harlow?
a: Experiments on the ability to speak
10445.e: Harlow separated young rhesus macaques from their mothers and gave them substitute mothers made of wire or cloth. The experiments showed the importance of closeness but are ethically controversial.
10445.m: Harlow’s experiments with rhesus macaques showed how important the bond with the mother is.

10446.q: Which virus, carried by many macaques without symptoms, can be life-threatening for humans?
10446.e: The herpes B virus is usually harmless in macaques. In humans, after bites or scratches, it can cause a serious inflammation of the brain.
10446.m: Macaques can carry the herpes B virus, which is dangerous to humans.

10447.q: What are macaques’ cheek pouches for?
a: Storing food for a short time
10447.e: Macaques quickly stuff food into their cheek pouches and eat it later in peace. This lets them grab food fast before higher-ranking animals arrive.
10447.m: Macaques keep food in their cheek pouches.

10448.q: Like all Old World monkeys, which body structure do macaques have on their rear?
10448.e: Macaques have tough, hairless sitting pads on their rear. On these they can sit comfortably on branches or rocks and even sleep.
10448.m: Macaques sit on tough sitting pads.

10449.q: In macaques, which sex usually stays in its birth group for life?
10449.e: In macaques the females stay in their birth group and form family lines. Young males move away when they become sexually mature.
10449.m: In macaques the females stay in the group and the males move away.

10450.q: How do females of many macaque species show their fertile phase?
a: The skin of the genital area swells and turns red
By changing the colour of their fur
10450.e: In many macaque species the skin of the genital area swells and turns red. This signals to the males that the female is ready to mate.
10450.m: Female macaques show they are fertile by a swollen red genital area.

10451.q: Roughly how long is a macaque’s pregnancy?
10451.e: A macaque’s pregnancy lasts about 160 to 170 days on average, so about five and a half months.
10451.m: A female macaque is pregnant for about five and a half months.

10452.q: How many young does a female macaque normally have at one birth?
10452.e: Macaques usually have a single baby, which is fed with milk for about a year. Twins are rare.
10452.m: A female macaque usually has only one baby.

10453.q: How old can macaques live to be in captivity?
10453.e: In the wild, macaques usually live 15 to 20 years. In zoos and research stations they can reach over 30 years.
10453.m: In captivity, macaques can live over 30 years.

10454.q: Which macaque species is considered the smallest in its genus?
a: The toque macaque from Sri Lanka
10454.e: The toque macaque (Macaca sinica) from Sri Lanka is the smallest macaque species. It has a swirling cap of hair on its head.
10454.m: The toque macaque from Sri Lanka is the smallest macaque.

10455.q: How long is the tail of the crab-eating macaque, also called the long-tailed macaque, compared with its body?
a: About as long as its head and body together
About a tenth of its body length
About twice as long as its body
10455.e: The crab-eating macaque’s tail is about as long as its head and body together. That is where the name long-tailed macaque comes from.
10455.m: The crab-eating macaque has a tail as long as its body.

10456.q: Why is the long-tailed macaque called the “crab-eating macaque”?
a: It was seen eating crabs on the beach
Its hands look like crab claws
It walks sideways like a crab
10456.e: The name goes back to sightings of the animals looking for crabs on the beach. But mainly they eat fruit.
10456.m: The crab-eating macaque is named after crabs, although it mainly eats fruit.

10457.q: What special thing does the crab-eating macaque do on the coasts of Thailand and Myanmar?
a: It cracks shellfish with stone tools
It catches fish with nets made of plants
It digs wells for fresh water
It builds dams out of branches
10457.e: There, crab-eating macaques use stones to smash open oysters, snails and crabs. They are thought to be the only Old World monkeys that use stone tools in daily life to find food.
10457.m: Crab-eating macaques crack shellfish with stones.

10458.q: What status did the crab-eating macaque receive on the IUCN Red List in 2022?
10458.e: In 2008 the crab-eating macaque was still classed as not threatened. After a first upgrade in 2020, in 2022 it was classed as endangered because of hunting, conflicts with people and strong demand for research.
10458.m: The crab-eating macaque has been classed as endangered since 2022.

10459.q: On which island in the Indian Ocean is the introduced crab-eating macaque considered a harmful invasive species?
10459.e: People brought the crab-eating macaque to Mauritius. There it harms native plants and animals, and the species is on the list of the 100 worst invasive species.
10459.m: On Mauritius the crab-eating macaque is an invasive species.

10460.q: Which scientific breakthrough was achieved with crab-eating macaques in China in 2018?
a: The first primates were cloned from body cells
A monkey heart was transplanted for the first time
A monkey spoke whole sentences for the first time
The first monkeys were born in space
10460.e: Chinese researchers cloned the crab-eating macaques Zhong Zhong and Hua Hua using the same method as for Dolly the sheep. They were the first primates cloned this way.
10460.m: Zhong Zhong and Hua Hua were the first primates cloned from body cells.

10461.q: Which well-known boundary in animal distribution does the crab-eating macaque’s range cross, a rare example among land mammals?
a: The equator, only in the west
10461.e: The Wallace Line separates Asian wildlife from Australian wildlife. The crab-eating macaque lives on both sides and, east of the line, as far as the Lesser Sunda Islands.
10461.m: The crab-eating macaque lives on both sides of the Wallace Line.

10462.q: Where does the lion-tailed macaque, also called the wanderoo, live?
a: In the Western Ghats in southern India
10462.e: The lion-tailed macaque is endemic to the Western Ghats, a mountain range in south-western India. It lives there in evergreen rainforests.
10462.m: The lion-tailed macaque lives only in the Western Ghats in southern India.

10463.q: Where does the lion-tailed macaque get its name from?
a: From the tuft at the end of its tail
10463.e: The lion-tailed macaque’s thin tail ends in a black tuft, like a lion’s. It also has a silvery grey mane around its face.
10463.m: The lion-tailed macaque has a tail tuft like a lion.

10464.q: According to estimates, roughly how many lion-tailed macaques still live in the wild?
10464.e: An IUCN estimate gives only about 3,000 to 3,500 wild lion-tailed macaques, scattered across small patches of forest. The species is classed as endangered, mainly because its rainforest has been broken up.
10464.m: There are only a few thousand wild lion-tailed macaques left.

10465.q: What is the status of the crested macaque from northern Sulawesi on the IUCN Red List?
10465.e: The jet-black crested macaque is hunted and eaten as a delicacy. Its numbers on Sulawesi have shrunk greatly, so it is classed as critically endangered.
10465.m: The crested macaque is critically endangered.

10466.q: How did one crested macaque become famous around the world?
a: Through a selfie with a camera
Through an appearance in a circus film
10466.e: A crested macaque pressed the shutter of a photographer’s camera and took a selfie. This was followed by a dispute lasting years over the copyright of the picture.
10466.m: The famous monkey selfie was taken by a crested macaque.

10467.q: Which island, with several macaque species found only there, is a centre of macaque diversity?
10467.e: Several endemic macaque species live on Sulawesi, such as the crested macaque, the moor macaque and the Tonkean macaque.
10467.m: Especially many of their own macaque species live on Sulawesi.

a: As omnivores eating lots of fruit
10468.e: Macaques eat mainly fruit, plus leaves, flowers, seeds, insects and small animals. This flexible diet helps them settle in many habitats.
10468.m: Macaques are omnivores that especially like fruit.

10469.q: Which important discovery in brain research did scientists in Parma make in macaques in the 1990s?
10469.e: Giacomo Rizzolatti’s team found nerve cells in macaques that are active both when the animal grasps something and when it watches grasping. They were named mirror neurons.
10469.m: Mirror neurons were discovered in macaques.

10470.q: Which of these monkeys is a close relative of the capuchin monkey?
10470.e: Like capuchins, squirrel monkeys live in Central and South America and belong to the same family. Baboons, gibbons and orangutans are Old World primates from Africa and Asia.
10470.m: The squirrel monkey is a close relative of the capuchin monkey.

10471.q: Which of these groups of monkeys lives in South and Central America, like the capuchin?
10471.e: Like capuchins, howler monkeys belong to the New World monkeys of the Americas. Baboons live in Africa, gibbons and macaques mainly in Asia.
10471.m: Howler monkeys and capuchins are both New World monkeys.

10472.q: Which large group of primates do capuchin monkeys belong to?
10472.e: Capuchin monkeys live in Central and South America and belong to the New World monkeys. These are also called platyrrhines, “flat-nosed”, because their nostrils are separated by a wide septum and point sideways.
10472.m: Capuchins are New World monkeys with a wide nasal septum.

10473.q: Why are capuchin monkeys divided into two genera today?
a: Robust and slender forms differ clearly in genes and build
Some live in Africa, the others in the Americas
Some are nocturnal, the others active by day
Some eat only meat, the others only leaves
10473.e: Genetic studies showed that robust capuchins (Sapajus) and slender capuchins (Cebus) have gone separate ways for millions of years. Their skulls, jaws and build also differ clearly.
10473.m: Capuchin monkeys are divided into robust and slender forms.

10474.q: How can you recognise the robust, so-called tufted capuchins especially easily?
a: By tufts or a crest of hair on the head
10474.e: Robust capuchins have tufts of hair or a crest on the head, hence the name “tufted”. Slender capuchins usually have a smooth cap.
10474.m: Tufted capuchins have a crest of hair on their head.

10475.q: Around 2012, which method did researchers use to show that robust and slender capuchins belong in separate genera?
10475.e: Comparisons of genetic material showed how long the two lines have been separate. After that, the robust forms were put in their own genus, Sapajus.
10475.m: DNA comparisons split the capuchin monkeys into two genera.

10476.q: According to genetic estimates, how long ago did the lines of robust and slender capuchins split?
10476.e: Studies estimate the split at about 6.2 million years. That is roughly as long ago as the split between the lines of humans and chimpanzees.
10476.m: Robust and slender capuchins have gone separate ways for about six million years.

10477.q: Which forest, home to several threatened capuchin monkeys, survives today at only about an eighth of its size?
a: The rainforest of the Congo Basin
10477.e: Only about an eighth of the Atlantic Forest (Mata Atlântica) on Brazil’s coast is left. The Congo and Borneo lie outside the capuchins’ range, and most of the Amazon rainforest still survives.
10477.m: Most of Brazil’s Atlantic Forest has been destroyed.

10478.q: Where does the capuchin monkey get its name from?
a: From the habits of the Capuchin friars
From a hood-shaped fold of skin
10478.e: The colouring, with a dark head and pale face or shoulders, reminded people of the brown hooded habits of the Capuchin order. So European sailors gave the friars’ name to the monkeys.
10478.m: Capuchin monkeys are named after the habits of the Capuchin friars.

10479.q: Which well-known drink is named, like the capuchin monkey, after the habit of the Capuchin friars?
10479.e: The brown colour of cappuccino reminded people of the habits of the Capuchin friars. The capuchin monkeys also owe their name to this habit.
10479.m: Cappuccino and the capuchin monkey are both named after the Capuchin friars.

10480.q: Roughly how many species of capuchin monkey are recognised today?
10480.e: Depending on the classification, just over 20 species are recognised, about 15 in the genus Cebus and 7 in the genus Sapajus. The exact number of species is disputed among experts.
10480.m: About 20 species of capuchin monkey are recognised today.

10481.q: How heavy do adult capuchin monkeys usually get?
10481.e: Capuchin monkeys usually weigh between about 1.5 and 4.5 kg. The males are usually much heavier than the females.
10481.m: A capuchin monkey usually weighs only a few kilograms.

10482.q: Roughly how long is a capuchin monkey’s body without its tail?
10482.e: The head and body length is about 30 to 56 cm. The tail is about as long as the body.
10482.m: Without its tail, a capuchin is about as long as an adult’s forearm and hand.

10483.q: What is special about the capuchin monkey’s tail compared with that of spider monkeys?
a: It can grip but has no bare touch pad at the tip
It is completely stiff and used only for balance
It is shorter than ten centimetres
It has a bare touch pad at the tip like a finger
10483.e: Capuchin monkeys can hold on with their tail, for example while eating. Unlike spider monkeys, though, they lack the hairless patch of skin under the tail that makes a fully gripping tail.
10483.m: The capuchin has a tail that can grip but has no bare touch pad.

10484.q: Which feature of their hands makes capuchin monkeys especially skilful?
a: A movable thumb that allows a precision grip
Fused fingers that cannot move separately
Sharp claws instead of flat nails
No thumb, as in spider monkeys
10484.e: The capuchin’s thumb is considered pseudo-opposable, but it is so movable that they can hold small things between thumb and index finger. This lets them grip and work on stones or nuts very precisely.
10484.m: Thanks to their movable thumb, capuchins can grip very precisely.

10485.q: What is the capuchin monkey’s brain known for among experts?
a: It is exceptionally large relative to body size
It is the largest of all primates in absolute terms
It is especially small relative to the body
10485.e: Relative to their body, capuchin monkeys have one of the largest brains among non-human primates. They are considered the most intelligent New World monkeys.
10485.m: For its body size, the capuchin has a remarkably large brain.

10486.q: How do most capuchin monkeys see colours?
a: All males see two colour channels, some females three
All animals see three colour channels like humans
All animals see only shades of grey
All males see three colour channels, all females two
10486.e: In capuchin monkeys, a gene for colour vision pigments sits on the X chromosome. Males, with only one X chromosome, therefore have two-colour vision, while females with two different versions can have three-colour vision.
10486.m: In capuchins, only some females can tell red from green.

10487.q: Which features do robust capuchins of the genus Sapajus have as an adaptation to hard food?
a: Strong jaws and, in males, a skull crest
Long, thin canines and a narrow jaw
Cheek pouches and a ruminant stomach
A horny beak instead of incisors
10487.e: Sapajus species have stronger lower jaws and shorter, sturdier canines, and the males have a crest on the skull for large chewing muscles. This lets them crack hard nuts and palm fruits.
10487.m: Robust capuchins have strong jaws for hard nuts.

10488.q: How far does the range of capuchin monkeys reach overall?
a: From Mexico to Tierra del Fuego
10488.e: Capuchin monkeys live from Central America, from about Honduras, through the Amazon Basin to south-eastern Brazil and northern Argentina. Brazil has the most capuchins.
10488.m: Capuchin monkeys live from Honduras to northern Argentina.

10489.q: Which capuchin monkey has the northernmost range of its group?
10489.e: White-faced capuchins live in the far north-west of South America and in Central America as far as Honduras. The Central American animals are now often split off as a separate species, the Panamanian white-faced capuchin (Cebus imitator); no other capuchin lives so far north.
10489.m: The white-faced capuchin lives furthest north of all capuchins.

10490.q: In which countries can you see white-faced capuchins in the wild?
10490.e: White-faced capuchins live in Central America, for example in Costa Rica and Panama, and in north-western South America. They are often seen in Costa Rica’s national parks.
10490.m: White-faced capuchins live mainly in Central America.
