10491.q: How does the tufted capuchin differ in build from the slender white-faced capuchin?
a: It is sturdier and has stronger jaws
It is bigger than a chimpanzee
It has no tail at all
It has gliding membranes between its legs
10491.e: The tufted capuchin is one of the robust capuchins. With its strong jaws it can crack hard nuts and palm fruits.
10491.m: The tufted capuchin is a robust capuchin with strong jaws.

10492.q: In which habitats are capuchin monkeys found?
a: In rainforests, dry forests and even mangroves
Only in mountain forests above 3,000 metres
Only in open grassy steppes with no trees
10492.e: Capuchin monkeys are very adaptable and live in rainforests, dry deciduous forests, mangroves and mountain forests. This flexibility is one reason why many species are less threatened than other New World monkeys.
10492.m: Capuchin monkeys live in many different types of forest.

10493.q: What is a capuchin monkey’s daily routine typically like?
a: They are active by day and sleep high in trees at night
They are active at night and sleep in burrows by day
They are active at dusk and sleep in rock crevices
They hibernate for several months in winter
10493.e: Capuchin monkeys are day-active tree dwellers. They spend the night in tall trees and often change their sleeping places.
10493.m: Capuchin monkeys are active by day and sleep in the treetops at night.

10494.q: How is the capuchin monkey’s diet best described?
10494.e: Capuchin monkeys mainly eat fruit, plus seeds, flowers, insects, spiders, eggs and small vertebrates. In the dry season, seeds and hard nuts become more important.
10494.m: Capuchin monkeys are omnivores that especially like fruit.

10495.q: How do wild capuchin monkeys crack hard palm nuts?
a: With a hammer stone on a surface used as an anvil
By letting birds open the nuts
By stamping on the nuts with their back legs
By soaking the nuts in water for weeks
10495.e: Capuchin monkeys put the nut on a flat stone or tree trunk and hit it with a heavy stone. They are thought to be the only New World monkeys that regularly use such tools in the wild.
10495.m: Capuchin monkeys crack nuts with a stone hammer and anvil.

10496.q: What do capuchin monkeys choose their hammer stones by?
10496.e: Experiments showed that capuchin monkeys choose stones by weight and size and prefer heavier stones for hard nuts. Some animals carry suitable stones over long distances.
10496.m: Capuchin monkeys check a stone’s weight before using it as a hammer.

10497.q: According to archaeological digs in Brazil (2019), how old at least is the stone-tool tradition of wild capuchin monkeys?
10497.e: In Serra da Capivara National Park, researchers found capuchins’ hammer stones that are about 3,000 years old. The size of the stones changed over time, which points to changing food.
10497.m: Capuchin monkeys have used stone tools for at least 3,000 years.

10498.q: What did researchers discover in 2016 in capuchin monkeys of the species Sapajus libidinosus that bashed stones together?
a: They accidentally made sharp stone flakes like early human tools
They deliberately sharpened knives for cutting meat
They lit small fires with the sparks
They built small walls out of the stones
10498.e: The monkeys struck quartzite stones against rocks and then licked them. This produced sharp-edged flakes that look like early human tools, but the monkeys never used them for cutting.
10498.m: Capuchin monkeys make sharp stone flakes without using them as knives.

10499.q: What do capuchin monkeys on islands off the coast of Panama crack with stones?
a: Sea urchins they collect by diving
Sea turtle eggs in the sand
Shellfish from coral reefs at great depth
10499.e: In Coiba National Park, white-faced capuchins use stones as hammers for crabs, snails and hard fruit. They do not dive for them.
10499.m: Capuchin monkeys in Panama crack crabs and snails with stones.

10500.q: Why do wedge-capped capuchins in Venezuela rub crushed millipedes into their fur?
a: To protect themselves from mosquitoes and other insects
To attract females with the scent
10500.e: The millipedes give off defensive chemicals that keep insects such as mosquitoes away. Capuchins do this rubbing mainly in the rainy season, when there are many mosquitoes about.
10500.m: Capuchin monkeys use millipedes as a natural mosquito repellent.

10501.q: How large are groups of capuchin monkeys usually?
10501.e: Capuchin monkeys usually live in groups of about 10 to 35 animals with several adult males and females. Depending on the species, the average group has about 15 to 20 animals.
10501.m: Capuchin monkeys live in groups of usually 10 to 35 animals.

10502.q: In capuchin monkeys, which sex normally leaves the birth group?
10502.e: In capuchin monkeys the females stay in their birth group, while the males move away around sexual maturity. So the groups are built around related females.
10502.m: In capuchins the females stay and the males move away.

10503.q: How is the ranking in a group of white-faced capuchins usually organised?
a: An alpha male leads, the females have their own ranking
All animals are completely equal in rank
The youngest animal always leads the group
The ranking changes randomly every day
10503.e: In the group there is a top-ranking male, who often keeps his position for many years. Alongside this, the females form their own clear ranking.
10503.m: In white-faced capuchins, an alpha male leads the group.

10504.q: What do capuchin monkeys mark the core area of their territory with?
a: Piles of droppings on the ground
10504.e: Capuchin monkeys mark the core of their home range with urine and defend it against other groups. In the outer zones, the areas of neighbouring groups often overlap.
10504.m: Capuchin monkeys mark their territory with urine.

10505.q: Roughly how long is a capuchin monkey’s pregnancy?
10505.e: Pregnancy lasts about 150 to 180 days, so a good five to six months. Usually a single baby is born.
10505.m: A female capuchin is pregnant for about half a year.

10506.q: How often does a female capuchin monkey usually have a baby?
10506.e: Females usually have a single baby about every two years. The long care of the young explains these long gaps.
10506.m: A female capuchin has a baby about every two years.

10507.q: In capuchin monkeys, which sex becomes sexually mature later?
a: Both at the same time, at one year
Both at the same time, at ten years
10507.e: Females become sexually mature at about four years, males often much later, at up to about eight years. Males also first have to establish themselves in a new group.
10507.m: Male capuchin monkeys grow up later than females.

10508.q: How old can capuchin monkeys live to be in captivity?
10508.e: In zoos and research facilities, some capuchin monkeys have reached an age of over 50 years. In the wild they usually live much shorter lives.
10508.m: In captivity, capuchin monkeys can live over 50 years.

10509.q: Which bird of prey is considered the main enemy of the tufted capuchin?
10509.e: The harpy eagle is a mighty bird of prey of the South American rainforests and specifically hunts monkeys in the treetops. Big cats and snakes also catch capuchin monkeys.
10509.m: The harpy eagle is the tufted capuchin’s most dangerous enemy.

10510.q: What did the famous experiment by Sarah Brosnan and Frans de Waal (2003) with capuchin monkeys show?
a: They refused cucumber when a partner got grapes for the same task
They did not recognise themselves in a mirror
They learnt sign language in a few days
10510.e: The monkeys swapped tokens for food. If the partner got a much-wanted grape for the same task, many animals refused their slice of cucumber, which is interpreted as a sense of unfair treatment.
10510.m: Capuchin monkeys react angrily to unequal rewards.

10511.q: Which ability did capuchin monkeys show in experiments at Yale University around 2005?
a: They learnt to swap tokens for food like money
They learnt to forge metal tools
They learnt to say simple words
10511.e: After a few months of training, the capuchins used coins deliberately to trade and even reacted to price changes. This suggests a simple understanding of money.
10511.m: Capuchin monkeys can learn to use coins like money.

10512.q: What did the organisation Helping Hands in the USA train capuchin monkeys for from 1979?
a: As helpers for people with paralysis
As search animals for earthquake victims
10512.e: Helping Hands in Boston trained capuchin monkeys to help people with paralysis in everyday life, for example by fetching things. In 2021 the organisation stopped placing monkeys for good and has used technical aids since then.
10512.m: Capuchin monkeys used to be trained as helpers for paralysed people.

10513.q: According to the IUCN, what is the status of the tufted capuchin (Sapajus apella) as a species?
10513.e: The tufted capuchin has a huge range and is very adaptable. So the IUCN classes the species as a whole as not threatened, even though some subspecies are at risk.
10513.m: The tufted capuchin as a whole is not considered threatened.

10514.q: Why are capuchin monkeys on small islands especially at risk of dying out?
a: Small populations cannot move away and quickly lose genetic diversity
On islands it is always too cold for monkeys
They drink sea water and get ill from it
10514.e: Only a few animals live on an island, and they cannot move away if the forest is lost. Small populations also lose genetic diversity and become more prone to disease.
10514.m: Small island populations die out more easily.

10515.q: How do zoos help highly threatened capuchin monkeys such as the yellow-breasted capuchin?
a: By crossing them with other monkey species
10515.e: Zoos breed threatened species such as the yellow-breasted capuchin in joint programmes, so that a healthy reserve population survives. They also support conservation projects in Brazil.
10515.m: Conservation breeding in zoos helps threatened capuchin monkeys.

10516.q: The blond capuchin was “rediscovered” in Brazil in 2006. What does that mean?
a: For a long time it was known only from old descriptions and was found again in the wild
It was bred anew from fossils
It had died out in all zoos
It was genetically modified for the first time
10516.e: The blond capuchin had been described since the 18th century but was considered lost. In 2006 it was found again in remnants of forest in north-eastern Brazil.
10516.m: A rediscovered species is found again in the wild after a long time.

10517.q: What does the IUCN status “Critically Endangered”, which some capuchin monkeys have, mean?
a: The species has an extremely high risk of soon dying out in the wild
The species now lives only in zoos
The species is common but protected
10517.e: “Critically Endangered” is the highest threat level before “Extinct in the Wild”. Species such as the Ka’apor capuchin urgently need protection.
10517.m: Critically Endangered is the highest threat level on the Red List.

10518.q: Which threats endanger many capuchin species the most?
a: Logging, hunting and the illegal pet trade
10518.e: Many species are losing their forest to farming and logging. Capuchin monkeys are also hunted for bushmeat and are among the wild animals most often traded illegally in Brazil.
10518.m: Forest loss, hunting and the pet trade threaten capuchin monkeys.

10519.q: Which famous TV character was played by a white-faced capuchin?
a: The monkey Marcel in the series “Friends”
The monkey King Louie in “The Jungle Book”
The monkey Rafiki in “The Lion King”
10519.e: Marcel, Ross’s pet in the series “Friends”, was played by a white-faced capuchin. Abu, King Louie and Rafiki, on the other hand, are drawn cartoon characters.
10519.m: Marcel from “Friends” was a capuchin monkey.

10520.q: Which family do squirrel monkeys (genus Saimiri) belong to?
10520.e: Squirrel monkeys are placed with the capuchin monkeys in the family Cebidae. Depending on the classification, the marmosets and tamarins are also counted in this family.
10520.m: Squirrel monkeys are close relatives of capuchin monkeys.

10521.q: How do squirrel monkeys mainly differ from the closely related capuchin monkeys?
a: They are much smaller and lighter
They live on a different continent
10521.e: Squirrel monkeys usually weigh under 1.1 kg, capuchins often two to four times as much. Both are day-active group animals in Central and South America. The squirrel monkeys form their own subfamily.
10521.m: Squirrel monkeys are the small relatives of capuchin monkeys.

10522.q: Squirrel monkeys are New World monkeys. Which feature of their nose is typical of this group?
a: The nose is stretched out like a trunk
10522.e: New World monkeys are also called platyrrhines, “flat-nosed”, because their nostrils are separated by a wide septum and point sideways outwards. Squirrel monkeys also have a hairless muzzle.
10522.m: New World monkeys like the squirrel monkey have wide noses with nostrils facing sideways.

10523.q: Where does the squirrel monkey get its German name “Totenkopfaffe” (death’s-head monkey) from?
a: From the black muzzle in its pale, mask-like face
From its night-time call in graveyards
From the dark rings around the eyes of old animals
10523.e: The black muzzle in the white-rimmed face looks like a skull. The animal has a similar name in other Germanic languages too.
10523.m: The squirrel monkey’s face looks like a little skull.

10724.q: How many living species of flamingo are usually recognised?
10724.e: Usually the greater, American, Chilean, lesser, Andean and James's flamingo are recognised. They are often divided into three genera.
10724.m: Usually six species of flamingo are counted.

10725.q: Which species of flamingo is the largest?
10725.e: The greater flamingo (Phoenicopterus roseus) reaches a height of about 110 to 150 cm and weighs 2 to 4 kg. This makes it the largest living flamingo species.
10725.m: The greater flamingo is the largest of all flamingos.

10726.q: Which species of flamingo is the smallest?
10726.e: The lesser flamingo (Phoeniconaias minor) is about 80 to 90 cm tall and weighs around 1.2 to 2.7 kg. This makes it the smallest species.
10726.m: The lesser flamingo is the smallest flamingo species.

10727.q: Which species of flamingo is considered the rarest?
10727.e: A count in the year 2000 found fewer than 34,000 Andean flamingos. No other flamingo species has such a small population.
10727.m: The Andean flamingo is the rarest flamingo.

10728.q: At its peak, roughly how many birds make up the population of the lesser flamingo, the most common flamingo species?
10728.e: The lesser flamingo is considered the most common flamingo species, with up to about two million birds. In East Africa, single gatherings can reach a million birds.
10728.m: With up to two million birds, the lesser flamingo is the most common flamingo.

10729.q: Where does the word “flamingo” come from?
10729.e: The word goes back to Portuguese or Spanish “flamengo”, which means flame-coloured. It ultimately comes from the word for flame.
10729.m: The flamingo carries a flame in its name.

10730.q: What does Phoenicopterus, the genus name of flamingos, mean?
10730.e: Phoenicopterus comes from the Ancient Greek “phoinikopteros” and means roughly purple-red or crimson feathered. The part “Phoenic” is related to the phoenix.

10731.q: Where does the pink colour of flamingos come from?
a: From a red feather pigment of their own
From blood vessels under the skin
From light refraction in the feathers
10731.e: Flamingos take in carotenoids with algae and small crustaceans. These are turned into pigments in the liver and stored in the feathers. If they are missing from the food, the plumage fades.
10731.m: A flamingo is pink because it stores pigments from its food.

10732.q: How do flamingos hold their bill when feeding?
a: Upside down, with the head facing down
10732.e: Flamingos lower their head and hold their curved bill upside down in the water. So the upper bill is at the bottom and the lower bill is on top.
10732.m: The flamingo eats with its head down and its bill upside down.

10733.q: What are the fine lamellae in a flamingo's bill for?
a: For filtering food out of the water
10733.e: Flamingos are filter feeders. The hair-like lamellae hold back algae and tiny animals while the water is pushed back out.
10733.m: The lamellae in a flamingo's bill work like a sieve.

10734.q: What role does the flamingo's tongue play in feeding?
a: It pumps water through the bill like a piston
It catches insects like a sticky trap
It grinds hard seeds against the palate
It is only used for swallowing
10734.e: The large, rough tongue moves quickly back and forth, sucking water into the bill and pressing it back out through the lamellae.
10734.m: The flamingo's tongue works like a pump.

10735.q: What does the lesser flamingo mainly feed on?
10735.e: The lesser flamingo mainly eats spirulina, blue-green cyanobacteria that grow in huge amounts in strongly alkaline soda lakes. It also eats diatoms and tiny invertebrates.
10735.m: The lesser flamingo lives mainly on spirulina from soda lakes.

10736.q: What food does the Andean flamingo mainly filter out of the water?
10736.e: The Andean flamingo mainly filters diatoms from the bottom layer of shallow salt lakes in the Andean highlands.
10736.m: The Andean flamingo feeds mainly on diatoms.

10737.q: Which lake in Tanzania is the most important breeding site of the lesser flamingo?
10737.e: Most of East Africa's lesser flamingos breed at the strongly alkaline Lake Natron in northern Tanzania. The caustic water keeps many predators away from the nests.
10737.m: Lake Natron is the nursery of the lesser flamingos.

10738.q: Which industrial project was seen as a threat to the lesser flamingos' breeding site at Lake Natron?
10738.e: A planned plant for producing soda ash would have endangered the most important breeding site at Lake Natron. Conservationists warned that the colony could be lost.
10738.m: A soda factory at Lake Natron would threaten the lesser flamingos.

10739.q: How many eggs does a female flamingo normally lay per brood?
10739.e: Flamingos almost always lay just a single egg. Clutches of two eggs occur in fewer than 2 per cent of nests.
10739.m: A flamingo pair usually hatches only a single egg.

10740.q: Roughly how long is the incubation period of a flamingo?
10740.e: The egg is incubated for around 27 to 31 days. Both parents take turns.
10740.m: A flamingo chick hatches after about a month.

10741.q: What does a typical flamingo nest look like?
a: A round nest in the reeds
A nesting hole in the bank
A platform high up in a tree
10741.e: Flamingos build cone-shaped mounds of mud, usually 30 to 45 cm high, with a hollow at the top. This keeps the egg safe from floods and hot ground.
10741.m: The flamingo nests on a mound of mud.

10742.q: Who feeds a flamingo chick with crop milk?
10742.e: In flamingos, both males and females produce a nutritious crop milk in glands of the upper digestive tract.
10742.m: In flamingos, mother and father both feed crop milk.

10743.q: Which hormone triggers the production of crop milk in flamingos?
10743.e: As in pigeons, the hormone prolactin controls the production of crop milk. The same hormone triggers milk production in mammals.
10743.m: Prolactin makes the flamingos' crop milk flow.

10744.q: What colour is flamingo crop milk?
10744.e: In the first weeks, the crop milk is bright red because it contains the carotenoid pigment canthaxanthin. Despite its blood-like colour, it contains no red blood cells, but fat and protein instead.
10744.m: Flamingos feed their chicks with red milk.

10745.q: What does the bill of a newly hatched flamingo chick look like?
10745.e: Chicks hatch with a straight bill. Only after a few weeks does it start to bend, before they can filter food themselves.
10745.m: Young flamingos have a straight bill at first.

10746.q: What are the large groups of chicks that young flamingos form in the colony called?
10746.e: At about one to two weeks old, chicks join small groups, which later merge into crèches with thousands of young birds. The parents find their chick there by its voice.
10746.m: Flamingo chicks grow up in huge nurseries.

10747.q: After how long do young greater flamingos usually have their full pink adult plumage?
a: After about three to four years
10747.e: The grey juvenile plumage is replaced only slowly. Most greater flamingos have their full adult plumage only at about four years old, a few at around two and a half years.
10747.m: A flamingo only becomes properly pink after a few years.

10748.q: What did a 2017 study show about flamingos standing on one leg?
a: The posture is held largely passively without muscle power
Flamingos never sleep in this position
The standing leg gets a lot of blood flow
The stance is used to attract fish
10748.e: Young-Hui Chang and Lena Ting showed that even the body of a dead flamingo stays stable in the one-legged posture. Body structure and gravity keep the bird upright with almost no muscle work.
10748.m: Standing on one leg costs a flamingo hardly any muscle power.

10749.q: Which joint is the seemingly “backwards” bending knee in the middle of a flamingo's leg really?
a: The base joint of the toes
10749.e: The striking joint in the middle of the leg corresponds to our heel or ankle. The real knee is hidden under the feathers close to the body.
10749.m: What looks like a knee on a flamingo is actually the heel.

10750.q: Which two flamingo species have no hind toe?
10750.e: The Andean flamingo and James's flamingo have only three forward-pointing toes. The other four species have a small hind toe.
10750.m: Andean and James's flamingos have only three toes.

10751.q: Which flamingo species is the only one with yellow legs?
10751.e: The Andean flamingo is the only species with yellow legs and also has three-toed feet. Its black flight feathers are also striking.
10751.m: Yellow legs give away the Andean flamingo.

10752.q: How can you recognise the legs of the Chilean flamingo?
10752.e: The Chilean flamingo has grey legs on which only the joints are pink. This distinguishes it from the greater and American flamingo.
10752.m: The Chilean flamingo has grey legs with pink joints.

10753.q: What did people long believe about James's flamingo before it was found again in the Andes?
a: That it was a cross between a stork and a flamingo
That it only lived in Africa
That it only survived in zoos
10753.e: James's flamingo was thought to be extinct for decades. In the 1950s, a population was found again in a remote area of the Andes.
10753.m: James's flamingo was long thought to be extinct.

a: At salt lakes in the Andean highlands
On tropical mangrove coasts of the Caribbean
In the river deltas of West Africa
At freshwater lakes in southern Europe
10754.e: James's flamingo lives at shallow salt lakes in the Andean highlands, in Peru, Bolivia, Chile and Argentina, often at over 4000 m.
10754.m: James's flamingo is a flamingo of the high Andes.

10755.q: What is special about the bill of James's flamingo?
a: It has the densest filter lamellae of all flamingos
It has no lamellae at all
It is the longest of all flamingos
10755.e: James's flamingo has around 21 lamellae per centimetre, more than twice as many as other flamingos. This lets it filter particularly small food.
10755.m: James's flamingo has the finest bill sieve.

10756.q: What is the status of the Andean flamingo on the IUCN Red List?
10756.e: The Andean flamingo is classed as vulnerable. Borax and lithium mining, egg collecting and habitat loss are taking their toll.
10756.m: The Andean flamingo is listed as vulnerable on the Red List.

10757.q: What is the status of the greater flamingo on the IUCN Red List?
10757.e: The greater flamingo is widespread and has a large population. This is why it is considered not threatened.
10757.m: The greater flamingo is considered not threatened.

10758.q: What is the status of the lesser flamingo on the IUCN Red List?
10758.e: Despite its large numbers, the lesser flamingo is considered near threatened because it has only a few breeding sites and its population is falling.
10758.m: Despite being common, the lesser flamingo is near threatened.

10759.q: How old at least was the oldest known flamingo, which died at Adelaide Zoo in 2014?
10759.e: A greater flamingo called “Greater” died in January 2014 at Adelaide Zoo in Australia. It was at least 83 years old.
10759.m: The oldest known flamingo lived to over 80.

10760.q: Roughly how old do wild flamingos live to on average?
10760.e: Depending on the source and species, wild flamingos live to about 20 to 40 years on average. In captivity they can live much longer.
10760.m: A wild flamingo can live for several decades.

10761.q: What is a group of flamingos called in English?
10761.e: A group of flamingos is called a “flamboyance”, which refers to splendour and a blaze of colour. “Murder” is used for crows, “pride” for lions and “parliament” for owls.
10761.m: A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance.

10762.q: Which part of the flamingo was considered a delicacy in ancient Rome?
10762.e: At the feasts of rich Romans, flamingo tongues were considered a treat. Pliny the Elder reported that their taste was thought to be particularly exquisite.
10762.m: The Romans ate flamingo tongues as a delicacy.

10763.q: What did a flamingo stand for in ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs?
10763.e: In ancient Egypt, the sign for the colour red was written with a flamingo.
10763.m: For the ancient Egyptians, the flamingo stood for the colour red.

10764.q: Which country has chosen the American flamingo as its national bird?
10764.e: The American flamingo (Phoenicopterus ruber) is the national bird of the Bahamas. It lives there in salt lagoons and coastal waters.
10764.m: The flamingo is the national bird of the Bahamas.

10765.q: What happened to the American flamingos in southern Florida?
a: They were largely wiped out by about 1900
They were declared a separate species
10765.e: Southern Florida used to be part of the American flamingo's range. Because of hunting, it had largely disappeared from there by around 1900.
10765.m: In Florida, the American flamingo was almost wiped out by around 1900.

10766.q: On which group of islands in the Pacific does a genetically distinct population of the American flamingo live?
10766.e: The American flamingo also lives on the Galápagos Islands. This population differs genetically from the one in the Caribbean.
10766.m: Flamingos also live on the Galápagos Islands.

10767.q: Roughly how fast do flamingos fly?
10767.e: Flamingos fly with their neck and legs stretched out at about 50 to 60 km/h. They often cover longer distances at night.
10767.m: A flying flamingo is about as fast as a car in town.

10768.q: What did watching the roughly 110 ringed flamingos at Basel Zoo show?
a: Most pairs breed together again for years
The pairs change partners every year
Only the females raise the chicks
The birds only breed every ten years
10768.e: Because every flamingo at Basel Zoo has its own ring, it was possible to follow their choice of partner. Pairs often get together again; only about 5 per cent stray.
10768.m: Flamingo pairs at Basel Zoo usually stay faithful.

10769.q: Where is the northernmost flamingo breeding colony in the world?
a: In the Zwillbrocker Venn in Germany
10769.e: In the Zwillbrocker Venn on the German-Dutch border lives a small flamingo colony, usually with a few dozen birds. It is considered the northernmost flamingo breeding site in the world.
10769.m: The northernmost flamingos breed in the Zwillbrocker Venn.

10770.q: Which bird family does the great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo) belong to?
10770.e: The great cormorant gives its name to the family of cormorants and shags, scientifically Phalacrocoracidae.
10770.m: The great cormorant belongs to the cormorant and shag family.

10771.q: Which seabirds is the great cormorant closely related to?
10771.e: Cormorants, together with gannets, frigatebirds and darters, form the order Suliformes.
10771.m: Cormorants are close relatives of gannets and frigatebirds.

10772.q: What does the species name “carbo” in the great cormorant's scientific name mean?
10772.e: The Latin carbo means coal and refers to the dark, almost black plumage.
10772.m: The cormorant has coal in its name because of its black plumage.

10773.q: Which Late Latin expression does the word “cormorant” come from?
10773.e: Via the Old French cormareng, the name goes back to corvus marinus, which means sea raven.
10773.m: In terms of language, the cormorant is a raven of the sea.

10774.q: The genus name Phalacrocorax contains the Greek word “korax”. Which bird does it mean?
10774.e: Korax is Greek for raven. Phalacrocorax means bald raven, probably because of the white head feathers in breeding plumage.
10774.m: The genus name calls the cormorant a bald raven.

10775.q: Roughly how long is an adult great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo)?
10775.e: The great cormorant reaches a body length of around 77 to 94 cm, making it one of the largest cormorant species.
10775.m: A great cormorant is about the size of a goose.

10776.q: Roughly what wingspan does the great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo) reach?
10776.e: The wingspan of the great cormorant is about 121 to 149 cm.
10776.m: With its wings spread, the great cormorant is well over a metre wide.

10777.q: How heavy is a male great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo) typically?
10777.e: Males weigh around 1.9 to 3.2 kg; females are a little lighter at about 1.7 to 2.6 kg.
10777.m: Male cormorants are heavier than females.

10778.q: What colour are the eyes of adult cormorants?
10778.e: Adult cormorants have striking emerald green eyes; in young birds they are grey-brown to grey-green.
10778.m: Adult cormorants look out of green eyes.

10779.q: What shape is the tip of a cormorant's bill?
a: Straight and pointed like a dagger
With little teeth along the edge
10779.e: The cormorant's upper bill ends in a hook, which it uses to hold slippery fish securely.
10779.m: The cormorant holds fish with its hooked bill.

10780.q: What is special about the cormorant's feet?
a: All four toes are joined by webbing
The toes have no webbing, only claws
Three toes are joined and the hind toe is missing
10780.e: Cormorants have so-called totipalmate feet, in which all four toes are joined by webbing.
10780.m: In the cormorant, all four toes are joined by webbing.

10781.q: What does the cormorant mainly use to propel itself when diving under water?
10781.e: Unlike penguins or auks, the cormorant paddles under water with its large webbed feet.
10781.m: The cormorant dives using foot power.

10782.q: Why does the cormorant often sit with its wings spread out?
a: Its feathers get wet and need to dry
10782.e: The cormorant's feathers soak up water, so after diving it spreads its wings out to dry.
10782.m: The cormorant hangs its wet wings out to dry.

10783.q: What advantage does its water-permeable plumage give the cormorant?
a: It makes it faster in flight
10783.e: Because the plumage soaks up water, less air stays in it and the cormorant can dive down more easily.
10783.m: Wet plumage helps the cormorant dive down.

10784.q: Which statement about the cormorant's preen gland is true?
a: It has one, contrary to a common myth
It is located on its neck
10784.e: It is often claimed that cormorants have no preen gland, but that is wrong. The wing drying has other reasons.
10784.m: The cormorant has a preen gland too.

10785.q: How long does a typical dive of the great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo) usually last?
10785.e: The great cormorant usually stays under water for about 15 to 60 seconds.
10785.m: A cormorant usually dives for less than a minute.

10786.q: At what depth does the great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo) usually hunt?
10786.e: The great cormorant usually fishes at a depth of 1 to 3 m, but much deeper dives have also been recorded.
10786.m: The cormorant mostly hunts in shallow water.

10787.q: What does the great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo) eat almost exclusively?
10787.e: The great cormorant feeds almost only on live small to medium-sized fish from fresh and salt water.
10787.m: The cormorant is a pure fish hunter.

10788.q: Roughly how much fish does a cormorant eat per day on average?
10788.e: Depending on the study, a cormorant needs about 400 to 500 g of fish a day; estimates range from about 250 to almost 800 g.
10788.m: A cormorant eats about half a kilo of fish every day.

10789.q: Where does a cormorant typically grab a fish with its bill?
10789.e: The cormorant usually grabs the fish with its hooked bill just behind the gills and then swallows it head first.
10789.m: The cormorant grabs fish behind the gills.

10790.q: What hunting behaviour do cormorants often show on Swiss lakes in autumn and winter?
a: They fish together in large groups
They only hunt alone at night
They stand in shallow water like herons
They plunge into the water from a great height
10790.e: Cormorants often hunt in groups and drive shoals of fish together, which increases their hunting success.

10791.q: How does the great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo) normally breed?
a: Alone in burrows in the ground
In other birds' nests as a brood parasite
10791.e: Cormorants breed in colonies and often build their nests close together in trees, on rocks or on the ground.

10792.q: What material does the cormorant mainly build its nest from?
10792.e: The nest consists mainly of branches and twigs, often in trees near water.
10792.m: The cormorant builds its nest from branches.

10793.q: How many eggs does a female great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo) usually lay per clutch?
10793.e: A clutch usually has 3 to 4 eggs, rarely 5 or even 6.
10793.m: A cormorant usually lays three or four eggs.

10794.q: What colour are the eggs of the great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo)?
a: Pale blue with a chalky coating
10794.e: The eggs are pale blue and covered with a chalky, whitish layer.
10794.m: Cormorant eggs are pale blue with a chalky coating.

10795.q: Roughly how long is the incubation period of the great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo)?
10795.e: The eggs are incubated for about 23 to 30 days.
10795.m: Cormorant eggs take about a month to hatch.

10796.q: At about what age can young great cormorants (Phalacrocorax carbo) fly?
10796.e: The nestling period lasts about 50 days; the young can fly at roughly 60 days.
10796.m: Young cormorants fly after about two months.

10797.q: At what age does a great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo) usually breed for the first time?
10797.e: Most cormorants breed for the first time at the age of 3 or 4, rarely as early as 2.
10797.m: Cormorants only become parents after a few years.

10798.q: What colour is the cormorant's juvenile plumage mostly?
10798.e: Young cormorants are mostly brown to blackish brown and only get their full adult colours after about four years.

10799.q: Which feature does the cormorant (subspecies sinensis) show on its thighs in breeding plumage?
10799.e: In breeding plumage, the cormorant has a striking white thigh patch, which is missing in non-breeding plumage.
10799.m: The white thigh patch gives away the cormorant in breeding plumage.

10800.q: What maximum age has been recorded in wild great cormorants (Phalacrocorax carbo)?
10800.e: Ringing has shown that cormorants can reach an age of over 27 years.
10800.m: A cormorant can live for over a quarter of a century.

10801.q: What is the IUCN status of the great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo) worldwide?
10801.e: Because of its huge range and large populations, the IUCN considers the great cormorant not threatened.
10801.m: The great cormorant is not threatened worldwide.

10802.q: How many subspecies of the great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo) are usually recognised?
10802.e: Usually six subspecies are recognised, including carbo, sinensis and lucidus.
10802.m: The great cormorant comes in six subspecies.

10803.q: Where does the cormorant subspecies sinensis, which breeds in Switzerland, get its name from?
10803.e: Sinensis is Latin for Chinese. This subspecies lives from central Europe to East Asia and also breeds in Switzerland.
10803.m: Inland in Europe lives the cormorant of the subspecies sinensis.

10804.q: On which continent does the white-breasted cormorant, a subspecies of the great cormorant, live?
10804.e: The subspecies lucidus lives in Africa and has a white breast, which is why it is called the white-breasted cormorant.
10804.m: The African cormorant lucidus has a white breast.

10805.q: On which continents does the great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo) live, among others?
10805.e: The great cormorant has a huge range from Europe through Asia and Africa to Australia and New Zealand, plus Greenland and the east coast of North America.
10805.m: The great cormorant is found almost all over the world.

10806.q: How large was the world population of the great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo) estimated to be around 2009?
10806.e: For 2009, the world population was estimated at about 1.4 to 2.9 million individuals.
10806.m: There are millions of great cormorants worldwide.

10807.q: What happened to the cormorant in inland central Europe by about 1920?
a: It was practically wiped out by persecution
It was bred as a pet
It was introduced from Asia for the first time
It was more common than ever before
10807.e: Because of heavy hunting, the cormorant had almost completely disappeared from inland central Europe by around 1920.
10807.m: The cormorant was once nearly wiped out in central Europe.

10808.q: Since when has the cormorant been proven to breed in Switzerland?
10808.e: The first breeding in Switzerland was recorded in 2001, after the cormorant had long been only a passage migrant and winter visitor.
10808.m: The cormorant has bred in Switzerland since 2001.

10809.q: Where did the first recorded cormorant breeding in Switzerland take place?
a: In the Fanel on Lake Neuchâtel
10809.e: According to the canton of Bern, the cormorant first bred in 2001 in the Fanel area on Lake Neuchâtel.
10809.m: The Fanel on Lake Neuchâtel was the first nursery of Swiss cormorants.

10810.q: Roughly how many cormorant breeding pairs were counted in the whole of Switzerland in the early 2020s?
10810.e: In 2021, around 3250 breeding pairs were counted in Switzerland, and about 3400 in 2022. The largest colony is in the Fanel on Lake Neuchâtel.
10810.m: Today a few thousand cormorant pairs breed in Switzerland.

10811.q: Which fish species do Swiss fishing circles especially often name as threatened by the cormorant?
10811.e: Above all the endangered grayling is considered at risk, which is why cantons can have cormorants shot even in the closed season to protect its spawning grounds.
10811.m: To protect the grayling, the cormorant is partly controlled in Switzerland.

10812.q: What is the cormorant's legal status under Swiss hunting law?
a: It is a huntable species with a closed season
It is strictly protected all year round
It may be hunted all year without rules
10812.e: Under the federal hunting law, the cormorant may be hunted from 1 September to the end of February. In waterbird and migratory bird reserves, hunting is generally banned.
10812.m: In Switzerland, the cormorant may be hunted, but with a closed season.

10813.q: What do fishermen in China and Japan use to stop trained cormorants from swallowing their catch?
a: A bill that is stuck shut
10813.e: A neck ring stops the cormorant from swallowing larger fish, so the fisherman can take them from it.
10813.m: A neck ring holds on to the fishing cormorant's catch.

10814.q: Since roughly when has fishing with cormorants been recorded in China and Japan?
a: Since the Stone Age 50,000 years ago
10814.e: Fishing with trained cormorants can be traced in East Asia back to about the 3rd century.
10814.m: People in Asia have fished with cormorants for many centuries.

10815.q: What was the cormorant chosen as in Germany and Austria in 2010?
a: The animal on a series of hunting stamps
10815.e: Conservation organisations named the cormorant Bird of the Year in 2010 to draw attention to the conflict with fishing.
10815.m: The cormorant was Bird of the Year in 2010.

10816.q: What migration behaviour does the great cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo) show in Europe?
a: Depending on the population, resident, partial migrant or migrant
Always a long-distance migrant to South Africa
Only a night migrant to South America
10816.e: Depending on where it comes from, the cormorant stays in its breeding area or moves partly or completely south, for example to the Mediterranean.
10816.m: Not all cormorants fly away in winter.

10817.q: Which cormorant species from the Galápagos Islands cannot fly?
10817.e: The flightless cormorant has greatly shortened wings and is the only living cormorant species that cannot fly.
10817.m: On Galápagos lives a cormorant that cannot fly.

10818.q: Roughly how many species does the cormorant family (Phalacrocoracidae) include?
10818.e: Depending on the classification, around 40 cormorant species are recognised, found on every continent except Antarctica.
10818.m: There are around forty species of cormorant.

10819.q: How do the droppings of a large cormorant colony often affect the nesting trees?
a: They can damage the trees and kill them
They make the trees grow faster
They turn the leaves permanently blue
They have no effect at all on the trees
10819.e: The droppings, rich in nitrogen and phosphorus, are caustic in large amounts and can damage nesting trees until they die.
10819.m: Cormorant droppings can kill whole nesting trees.

10820.q: How does a toucan get a fruit it has picked with the tip of its bill into its throat?
a: It tosses it up and catches it with its bill open
It holds it with its foot and bites pieces off
It dips it in water first
It pushes it back bit by bit with its tongue
10820.e: With its long bill, the toucan cannot simply move food to the back. So it tosses it up with a jerk of its head and catches it in its throat.
10820.m: A toucan throws its food into the air and catches it with its bill open.

10821.q: Which order do toucans belong to?
10821.e: Toucans belong to the order Piciformes and are therefore related to woodpeckers and barbets.
10821.m: The toucan is a close relative of woodpeckers.

10822.q: Roughly how many species does the toucan family include?
10822.e: Depending on the classification, the family Ramphastidae includes around 35 to just over 40 species. Newer lists include about 43 species.
10822.m: There are around 40 species of toucan.

10823.q: What makes the toucans of the genus Ramphastos different from most other toucans?
a: They are the largest and have the most massive bills
They are the only ones living in Africa
They are the only ones that are completely black
They are the only ones that cannot fly
10823.e: The genus Ramphastos includes the large toucans such as the toco toucan and the keel-billed toucan. Other genera such as the aracaris or mountain toucans are smaller.
10823.m: The large toucans belong to the genus Ramphastos.

10824.q: Which birds are especially closely related to toucans?
10824.e: The closest relatives of toucans are the barbets, especially the toucan barbets from South America. The similarity to hornbills is only due to convergent evolution.
10824.m: Barbets are the closest relatives of toucans.

10825.q: Which toucan species is the largest of the whole family?
10825.e: With a length of just over half a metre and the largest bill, the toco toucan is the largest toucan species.
10825.m: The toco toucan is the largest of all toucans.

10826.q: Roughly how heavy is an adult toco toucan, a member of the toucan family?
10826.e: Depending on sex and origin, an adult toco toucan weighs about 500 to just over 850 grams, on average around 540 to 700 grams.
10826.m: Despite its large bill, a toco toucan weighs less than a kilogram.

10827.q: Roughly how long is the toco toucan, the largest toucan, from bill to tail tip?
10827.e: The toco toucan reaches a total length of around 56 to 63 centimetres, a large part of which is the bill.
10827.m: A toco toucan is just over half a metre long.

10828.q: How long is the bill of a male toco toucan on average?
10828.e: In males of the nominate form, the bill measures about 20 centimetres on average; in females it is a little shorter.
10828.m: The bill of a male toco toucan is about 20 centimetres long.

10829.q: Why is the toucan's huge bill still very light?
a: Inside it is an airy bone foam under a thin keratin shell
It is made entirely of soft cartilage without a horn layer
It is filled with light fatty tissue instead of bone
It is made of solid horn with a very low density
10829.e: Inside the toucan's bill, fine bony struts with membranes support a foam-like core that is mostly filled with air.
10829.m: The toucan's bill is airy like foam inside.

10830.q: Which property makes the toucan's bill interesting for engineers?
a: It is both very light and very strong
It is soft and stretchy like rubber
10830.e: A thin shell of overlapping keratin plates surrounds an airy bone foam. This design serves as a model for light, impact-resistant materials.
10830.m: The toucan's bill is a model for light and strong materials.

10831.q: Which function of the toucan's bill did researchers prove in the journal “Science” in 2009?
a: It acts as a heat exchanger to regulate body temperature
It acts as a sound box for especially deep calls
It stores water for dry seasons
It produces ultraviolet light for courtship
10831.e: Using thermal imaging cameras, Glenn Tattersall and colleagues showed that the toco toucan controls the blood flow in its bill and can thus release or save heat as needed.
10831.m: The toucan uses its bill as air conditioning.

10832.q: Roughly what share of its body surface does the bill of the toco toucan, a member of the toucan family, make up?
10832.e: The toco toucan's bill makes up about 30 to 50 per cent of its body surface. This makes it one of the largest bird bills of all relative to body size.
10832.m: In the toco toucan, the bill makes up to half of the body surface.

10833.q: What can a toucan do thanks to a special tail spine?
a: Fold its tail forwards up to its head
Hang upside down from branches by its tail
Shed its tail when in danger
Raise its tail in a round fan
10833.e: The rear tail vertebrae are fused and can move via a kind of ball joint. This lets the toucan fold its tail forwards over its back.
10833.m: A toucan can fold its tail forwards to its head.

10834.q: What does a sleeping toucan typically look like?
a: Like a ball of feathers, with its bill on its back and its tail folded up
Hanging upside down like a bat
Lying flat on its belly with its wings spread
Standing on one leg with its bill in the water
10834.e: When sleeping, toucans lay their bill on their back under the feathers and fold their tail over it, which reduces heat loss through the bill.
10834.m: A sleeping toucan looks like a ball of feathers.

10835.q: What is the toucan's tongue like?
a: Long, narrow and frayed at the sides
Short, thick and fleshy like a parrot's
With sticky saliva and barbs like a woodpecker's
10835.e: The toucan's tongue can be up to about 15 centimetres long. It is narrow and fringed at the sides, which probably helps with tasting.
10835.m: The toucan has a long, fringed tongue.

10836.q: What does the Greek word “selene” in Selenidera, the genus name of some toucans, mean?
10836.e: Selenidera is made up of “selene” for moon and “dere” for neck. The name describes a yellow band in the shape of a crescent moon on the neck.
10836.m: Selenidera means something like moon neck.

10837.q: How are a toucan's toes arranged?
10837.e: Toucans have climbing feet in which the first and fourth toes point backwards, like in woodpeckers and parrots.
10837.m: The toucan has climbing feet with two toes in front and two behind.

10838.q: Why did early naturalists wrongly think toucans ate meat and fish?
a: Because of the tooth-like notches on the edge of the bill
Because of their sharp, curved claws
Because of the red feathers on their belly
10838.e: The serrated edges of the bill look like teeth, which is why people used to believe toucans caught fish. In fact, toucans feed mainly on fruit.
10838.m: The little teeth on a toucan's bill make it look like a meat eater.

10839.q: What do toucans mainly feed on?
10839.e: Toucans are mainly fruit eaters, but they occasionally also take insects, eggs, nestlings and small lizards.
10839.m: The toucan is first and foremost a fruit eater.

10840.q: What important ecological role do toucans play in the rainforest?
a: They spread the seeds of many fruit trees
They dig nesting holes for other birds
10840.e: Toucans swallow fruit and often pass the seeds out again hundreds of metres away. In this way, they help many trees to spread.
10840.m: Toucans plant new trees with their droppings.

10841.q: The toco toucan is the main egg thief of which endangered parrot species in the Pantanal?
10841.e: Studies in the Pantanal showed that toco toucans are responsible for over half of the stolen eggs of the hyacinth macaw.
10841.m: The toco toucan especially often steals hyacinth macaw eggs.

10842.q: The toco toucan steals hyacinth macaw eggs, but it also spreads the seeds of the tree the macaw nests in. What does this mean?
a: The toucan harms the macaw and helps it at the same time
The toucan does not matter to the macaw
The macaw feeds the toucan's young
The two birds share the same nesting hole
10842.e: The toco toucan steals many macaw eggs. At the same time, it spreads over 80 per cent of the seeds of the manduvi tree, in which the hyacinth macaw nests.
10842.m: The toco toucan harms the hyacinth macaw and helps it at the same time.

a: In tree holes, often left by woodpeckers
In open cup nests on branches
10843.e: Most toucans cannot chisel out holes themselves and use natural tree holes or old woodpecker holes.

10844.q: How many eggs does a female toucan usually lay per clutch?
10844.e: Toucans usually lay two to four eggs.
10844.m: A toucan clutch usually has two to four eggs.

10845.e: As in many hole-nesting birds, toucan eggs are white, because camouflage colours are not needed in the dark hole.

10846.q: How long is the incubation period of the toco toucan, a member of the toucan family?
10846.e: In the toco toucan, both parents usually take turns incubating for about 17 to 18 days.
10846.m: A toco toucan egg is incubated for about two and a half weeks.

10847.q: After roughly how many days do young toco toucans, members of the toucan family, leave the nest?
10847.e: Young toco toucans fledge after around six to seven weeks.
10847.m: Young toco toucans stay in the nest for six to seven weeks.

10848.q: What do newly hatched toucan chicks look like?
a: Naked, without down and with closed eyes
With a thick coat of grey down
Already with a colourful bill and open eyes
10848.e: Toucans are nidicolous, which means the chicks stay in the nest. They hatch naked, and their eyes stay closed for about three weeks.
10848.m: Toucan chicks are born naked and blind.

10849.q: What special adaptation do toucan chicks have to the rough floor of the nesting hole?
a: Horny heel pads on their legs
A thick pad of down on their belly
Extra-long claws for gripping the wall
A sticky disc on their tail
10849.e: Toucan chicks sit on their heels. Pads on the heels protect them from the hard, uneven floor of the hole.
10849.m: Toucan chicks rest on heel pads.

10850.q: How long does the bill of a young toco toucan, a member of the toucan family, keep growing after it leaves the nest?
a: Not at all, it is finished when it hatches
All its life, by several centimetres a year
10850.e: When they leave the nest, young toco toucans still have a much shorter bill, which only reaches its full size at an age of a few months.
10850.m: A young toco toucan's bill needs months after fledging to reach full size.

10851.q: In which area do toucans live naturally?
a: From southern Mexico to northern Argentina
In tropical Africa south of the Sahara
In South-East Asia and New Guinea
From the southern USA to Canada
10851.e: Toucans are limited to the Neotropics, meaning Central and South America from southern Mexico to northern Argentina.
10851.m: Toucans live only in Central and South America.

10852.q: Which area near their range have toucans never settled naturally?
10852.e: Toucans are poor flyers over open water and have never reached the West Indies. On Trinidad, which lies close to the coast, toucans do live.
10852.m: There are no wild toucans in the West Indies.

10853.q: How is the habitat of the toco toucan different from that of most other toucans?
a: It also lives in savannahs and open landscapes
It lives only in dense mountain cloud forest
It lives on sea coasts and in mangroves
It lives in deserts without trees
10853.e: Unlike most toucans, which live in closed forests, the toco toucan also lives in semi-open landscapes such as the Cerrado, in palm groves and in the Pantanal.
10853.m: The toco toucan is the savannah toucan.

10854.q: Up to what altitude do mountain toucans climb in the Andes?
a: Up to about the tree line
Up to the glacier zone above 5000 m
Only to the foot of the mountains
10854.e: The mountain toucans of the genus Andigena live in the mountain forests of the Andes and climb up to the tree line.
10854.m: Mountain toucans live high up in the Andes.

a: Smaller, slender toucans with long tails
10855.e: The aracaris form the toucan genus Pteroglossus. They usually have yellow undersides with dark or red bands.

10856.q: How did toucans become known in Europe in the 19th century?
a: Through beautifully painted picture books by naturalists
Through wildlife films at the cinema
Through live toucans in almost every zoo
10856.e: The British naturalist John Gould published a richly illustrated monograph on toucans in the 1830s. Picture books like this made exotic animals known in Europe.
10856.m: Splendid picture books made toucans known in Europe in the 19th century.

10857.q: In what groups do many toucan species live for a large part of the year?
a: In pairs or small flocks, sometimes of over 20 birds
In colonies of several thousand birds
In harems with one male and many females
10857.e: Toucans are usually sociable and roam around in pairs or flocks. In many species these groups include up to 20 or more birds.
10857.m: Toucans often travel in small groups.

10858.q: What are toucans probably doing when they “fence” with their bills?
a: Probably sorting out their pecking order
10858.e: Toucans playfully knock their bills together. Researchers think this bill fencing helps sort out the pecking order.
10858.m: Toucans probably sort out their pecking order by bill fencing.

10859.q: What do the calls of many toucans sound like?
a: Croaking like frogs, creaking or barking
Like a woodpecker drumming on a trunk
10859.e: Depending on the species, toucans make frog-like croaks, creaks or barks, and mountain toucans even make donkey-like sounds.
10859.m: Many toucans croak like frogs rather than sing.

10860.q: How do males and females differ in most toucan species?
a: Hardly in their plumage, males often have the longer bill
Females are black and white, males are colourful
Only the males have a large bill
Females are twice as big as males
10860.e: In most toucans both sexes look the same, but the males often have a slightly longer bill. An exception is the toucanets of the genus Selenidera.
10860.m: In most toucans, males and females look almost the same.

10861.q: What is the threat status of the toco toucan, a member of the toucan family, on the IUCN Red List?
10861.e: The toco toucan is widespread and common and is therefore considered not threatened.
10861.m: The toco toucan is currently not threatened.

10862.q: Why are toucan species with a very small range particularly at risk?
a: Even a little forest clearing can destroy their whole habitat
Because they breed too quickly there
Because small areas are always too cold
Because they have no enemies there
10862.e: Aulacorhynchus huallagae lives only in a small area of mountain forest in Peru and is considered endangered. If forest is cleared there, there is nowhere else to go.
10862.m: Anyone who lives in only one place is especially vulnerable.

10863.q: Which country has the keel-billed toucan as its national bird?
10863.e: The keel-billed toucan, with its rainbow-coloured bill, is the national bird of Belize in Central America.
10863.m: The keel-billed toucan is the national bird of Belize.

10864.q: Which language family does the word “toucan” originally come from?
a: From the Tupí-Guaraní languages of South America
10864.e: The word goes back to “tukana” from Tupí or “tukã” from Guaraní and reached Europe via Portuguese.
10864.m: The word toucan comes from an indigenous language of South America.

10865.q: How are animal species such as the toco toucan named scientifically?
a: With a Latin genus and species name
With a number from the Red List
Only with the name of their discoverer
With the name of the country they live in
10865.e: Since Carl Linnaeus, species have been given a two-part name made up of genus and species. The toco toucan was described in 1776 as Ramphastos toco.
10865.m: Every animal species has a two-part scientific name.

10866.q: Which beer brand was advertised by a drawn toucan from 1935?
10866.e: From 1935, the artist John Gilroy drew the toucan which, with a glass of Guinness on its bill, became the brewery's advertising symbol for decades.
10866.m: The toucan became famous through Guinness adverts.

10867.q: A constellation in the southern sky is named after the toucan. Which sky object lies mostly within it?
10867.e: The constellation Toucan (Tucana) contains most of the Small Magellanic Cloud, a neighbouring galaxy of the Milky Way.
10867.m: The Small Magellanic Cloud lies in the constellation Toucan.

10868.q: Why are toucans in zoos given food that is especially low in iron?
a: They absorb iron very well, and otherwise it builds up in the liver
Iron makes their feathers too heavy to fly
Iron makes them aggressive towards keepers
10868.e: Toucans absorb iron very efficiently. With iron-rich food, it builds up in the liver and makes them ill. This is called iron storage disease.
10868.m: Toucans in zoos need low-iron food.

10869.q: Which group of Old World birds resembles toucans through convergent evolution, although it is not closely related?
10869.e: The African and Asian hornbills also have huge bills and nest in holes and eat a lot of fruit, but they belong to a different order.
10869.m: Hornbills are the toucans of the Old World.

10870.q: Which group of parrots do macaws belong to?
a: The long-tailed parrots of the Americas
10870.e: Macaws belong to the long-tailed New World parrots of Central and South America. Cockatoos and lorikeets live in Australia and Asia, grey parrots in Africa.
10870.m: Macaws are long-tailed parrots of the Americas.

10871.q: Which statement about the group of macaws is true?
a: It includes several genera, not just the genus Ara
It consists of a single species
It belongs to the birds of prey
10871.e: Several genera count as macaws, such as Ara, Anodorhynchus with the hyacinth macaw, or Cyanopsitta with Spix's macaw. The genus Ara is only one of them.
10871.m: Macaws are spread over several genera.

10872.q: Where does the name “Ara”, used for macaws, originally come from?
a: From an indigenous language of South America, imitating the call
10872.e: The name comes from an indigenous language of South America and imitates the loud, harsh scream of the large species.
10872.m: The name Ara sounds like the birds' scream.

10873.q: Which outward feature distinguishes macaws from most other parrots?
a: Bare or barely feathered facial skin
A small crest of feathers on the head
10873.e: Macaws have a bare or only sparsely feathered, usually pale facial mask. Together with the long, graduated tail, it is typical of the group.
10873.m: You can recognise macaws by their bare facial skin.

10874.q: How are a macaw's toes arranged?
a: Two forwards, one sideways, one backwards
10874.e: Like all parrots, macaws have zygodactyl feet with two toes pointing forwards and two backwards. This lets them grip branches firmly and hold food as if with a hand.
10874.m: Macaws grip with two toes in front and two behind.

10875.q: In the species of the genus Ara, is there a clear difference in colour between males and females?
a: No, both sexes look almost the same
Yes, only the males are colourful
Yes, only the females have a face mask
Yes, the females are twice as big
10875.e: In the macaws of the genus Ara there is no obvious sexual dimorphism. Males and females can hardly be told apart from the outside.
10875.m: In macaws, males and females look almost the same.

10876.q: Which macaw is considered the largest flying parrot in the world?
10876.e: The hyacinth macaw reaches about one metre in length from the crown to the tip of the tail. This makes it the longest parrot and the largest one that can fly.
10876.m: The hyacinth macaw is the largest flying parrot.

10877.q: Roughly how long is an adult hyacinth macaw?
10877.e: A hyacinth macaw measures about one metre from head to tail tip, a large part of which is tail.
10877.m: A hyacinth macaw is about one metre long.

10878.q: Which parrot is heavier than the hyacinth macaw?
10878.e: The hyacinth macaw weighs up to about 1.7 kg, making it the second heaviest parrot. Only the flightless kakapo from New Zealand is heavier.
10878.m: Only the kakapo is heavier than the hyacinth macaw.

10879.q: Roughly how much can a hyacinth macaw weigh?
10879.e: Hyacinth macaws usually weigh between about 1.2 and 1.7 kg. For a flying parrot that is a lot.
10879.m: A hyacinth macaw weighs up to about 1.7 kilograms.

10880.q: Which parts of the otherwise blue hyacinth macaw are bright yellow?
a: A ring around the eyes and a strip of skin below the bill
The tip of the tail and the feet
The back of the neck and the edges of the wings
10880.e: In the hyacinth macaw, only the bare skin around the eyes and a strip at the base of the lower bill are yellow. The rest of the plumage is cobalt blue.
10880.m: The blue hyacinth macaw wears yellow only at its eyes and the base of its bill.

10881.q: Where does the hyacinth macaw get its name from?
a: From its blue plumage, which looks like hyacinths
From its call, which sounds like “hyacinth”
10881.e: The hyacinth macaw is almost completely cobalt blue, like the flowers of some hyacinths. Its scientific species name hyacinthinus also refers to this colour.
10881.m: The hyacinth macaw is named after its blue colour.

10882.q: How old can large macaws live to in captivity?
10882.e: Large macaws are among the longest-living birds. When well kept, they often reach 50 to 60 years, some even more.
10882.m: A large macaw can live as long as a human.

10883.q: In which wetland region of Brazil does the largest population of the hyacinth macaw live?
10883.e: The largest wild population of the hyacinth macaw lives in the Pantanal, a huge wetland in western Brazil. There are smaller populations in the Cerrado and in eastern Amazonia.
10883.m: Most hyacinth macaws live in the Pantanal.

10884.q: What does the hyacinth macaw mainly feed on?
10884.e: The hyacinth macaw eats almost only the seeds of palms such as acuri and bocaiuva. With its huge bill it cracks shells that are too hard for other animals.
10884.m: The hyacinth macaw mainly cracks hard palm nuts.

10885.q: What special role does grazing cattle play in the hyacinth macaw's diet in the Pantanal?
a: Cattle eat acuri fruit, and the macaws use the cleaned nuts they pass out
Cattle drive birds of prey away from the feeding places
Cattle provide nesting material with their hair
Cattle uncover salt licks where the macaws lick
10885.e: Cattle eat the flesh of the acuri palm fruit and pass out the hard stones again. Hyacinth macaws collect these cleaned nuts from the ground.
10885.m: In the Pantanal, cattle help the hyacinth macaw find food.

10886.q: Why does the hyacinth macaw often find too few nesting sites in the Pantanal?
a: It needs large holes in old trees
It only builds nests on the ground in tall grass
It only nests in cliffs by the sea
It only nests in freshly felled trunks
10886.e: Around 90 per cent of nests in the Pantanal are in holes of old manduvi trees. Only old, large trees form wide enough holes, and there are fewer and fewer of them.
10886.m: The hyacinth macaw needs old trees with large holes.

10887.q: Which bird is both an egg thief and important for the nesting trees of the hyacinth macaw?
10887.e: The toco toucan eats a large share of the stolen macaw eggs. At the same time, it spreads most of the seeds of the manduvi tree, in which the macaws nest.
10887.m: The toco toucan steals macaw eggs and also plants their nesting trees.

10888.q: How many eggs does a female hyacinth macaw normally lay per brood?
10888.e: A clutch consists of one or two eggs. Usually, however, only one chick survives.
10888.m: The hyacinth macaw lays only one to two eggs.

10889.q: Roughly how long is the incubation period of the hyacinth macaw?
10889.e: The eggs are incubated for about 28 to 30 days. After that, the young stay in the nesting hole for more than three months.
10889.m: Hyacinth macaw eggs are incubated for around four weeks.

10890.q: What IUCN status has the hyacinth macaw had since 2016?
10890.e: Since 2016, the IUCN has classed the hyacinth macaw as vulnerable. At that time the population was estimated at around 4300 adult birds.
10890.m: The IUCN considers the hyacinth macaw vulnerable.

10891.q: According to the 2016 estimate, roughly how many adult hyacinth macaws lived in the wild?
10891.e: For 2016, the wild population was estimated at just under 4300 adult hyacinth macaws. The population is still considered to be falling.
10891.m: Only a few thousand hyacinth macaws still live in the wild.

10892.q: What reduced the hyacinth macaw population especially sharply in the 20th century?
a: Capture from the wild for the pet trade
Hunting for its meat for markets in Europe
Poisoning by insecticides on rice fields
10892.e: In the 1980s, thousands of hyacinth macaws were caught for the pet trade. On top of that, there is still the loss of habitat today.
10892.m: The pet trade has done great harm to the hyacinth macaw.

10893.q: The hyacinth macaw is listed in Appendix I of the CITES species protection agreement. What does that mean?
a: Commercial trade in wild-caught birds is banned
Trade is free with a simple permit
The species may be hunted in Brazil
10893.e: Appendix I lists the most strictly protected species. This means commercial trade in wild-caught hyacinth macaws is banned.
10893.m: The hyacinth macaw is protected under the strictest CITES Appendix I.

10894.q: Which Swiss zoo keeps hyacinth macaws and coordinates the European conservation breeding programme?
a: Peter and Paul Wildlife Park in St Gallen
10894.e: Zurich Zoo keeps a large breeding group of hyacinth macaws and coordinates the European breeding programme. Since 2020 it has also supported a conservation project in Brazil.
10894.m: Zurich Zoo breeds hyacinth macaws for the whole of Europe.

10895.q: With which measure does the conservation project in the Pantanal, supported by Zurich Zoo, especially help hyacinth macaws?
a: With feeding stations full of sunflower seeds
By moving all the birds to Europe
10895.e: Because old trees with large holes are missing, artificial nest boxes are put up in the Pantanal. There are now over 300 of these boxes there.
10895.m: Artificial nest boxes help the hyacinth macaw breed.

10896.q: How can you recognise the scarlet macaw?
a: Red with a yellow wing patch and blue flight feathers
Red with green wing coverts and red lines on the face
Completely cobalt blue with a yellow eye ring
10896.e: The scarlet macaw is bright red; its wings show a yellow patch and blue flight feathers. The similar red-and-green macaw has green wing coverts instead of yellow.
10896.m: The scarlet macaw wears red, yellow and blue.

10897.q: Who first described the scarlet macaw and the blue-and-yellow macaw in 1758?
10897.e: Both species were described in 1758 by Carl Linnaeus in his work Systema Naturae, at that time still in the genus Psittacus.
10897.m: Linnaeus described the first macaws as early as 1758.

10898.q: Which country has the scarlet macaw as its national bird?
10898.e: The scarlet macaw is the national bird of Honduras. It lives from southern Mexico to the Amazon region.
10898.m: The scarlet macaw is the national bird of Honduras.

10899.q: How large a share of the scarlet macaw's total length is its tail?
a: Almost nothing, the tail is stubby
10899.e: The scarlet macaw measures around 84 cm, and more than half of that is the long tail feathers.
10899.m: More than half of a scarlet macaw is tail.

10900.q: Where does the scarlet macaw live in the wild?
a: From southern Mexico to the Amazon region
Only in the Andes above 4000 m
10900.e: The scarlet macaw has a huge range from southern Mexico through Central America to the Amazon region. In Central America, however, it has become rare in many places.
10900.m: The scarlet macaw lives from southern Mexico to Amazonia.

10901.q: Why do macaws in the western Amazon visit clay walls on riverbanks?
a: To eat clay with important minerals such as sodium
To bury their eggs in the warm clay
To peck insects out of the clay
To protect themselves from sunburn with clay
10901.e: Macaws eat clay there, especially clay with a lot of sodium. Far from the sea, salt is scarce in their food.
10901.m: Macaws eat clay to take in minerals such as sodium.

10902.q: What is the IUCN status of the scarlet macaw as a whole species?
10902.e: Because the scarlet macaw has a huge range, it is considered not threatened overall. In some regions, such as Central America, it has become rare.
10902.m: The scarlet macaw is not yet threatened worldwide.

10903.q: How can you tell the red-and-green macaw from the similarly red scarlet macaw?
a: Green instead of yellow wing coverts and red feather lines on the face
A completely blue head and yellow feet
A green breast and a black tail
A yellow eye ring like the hyacinth macaw
10903.e: The red-and-green macaw has green wing coverts with no yellow patch. Fine lines of tiny red feathers run across its pale facial skin.
10903.m: The red-and-green macaw has green wings and red lines on its face.

10904.q: Which species is the largest member of the genus Ara?
10904.e: The red-and-green macaw grows to around 90 to 95 cm long, making it the largest species of the genus Ara. Only the hyacinth macaw, from another genus, is longer.
10904.m: The red-and-green macaw is the largest macaw of the genus Ara.

10905.q: What colours is the blue-and-yellow macaw?
a: Blue on top, yellow on the breast and belly
Red with a yellow wing patch
Completely cobalt blue with a yellow eye ring
10905.e: The blue-and-yellow macaw is blue on its back, wings and tail and bright yellow to orange on its breast and belly. It is one of the best-known macaws in zoos.
10905.m: The blue-and-yellow macaw is blue on top and yellow underneath.

10906.q: Which is the only country in Central America where the blue-and-yellow macaw lives naturally?
10906.e: The blue-and-yellow macaw lives mainly in South America. In Central America, it is found only in Panama.
10906.m: In Central America, the blue-and-yellow macaw lives only in Panama.

10907.q: On which Caribbean island was the almost vanished blue-and-yellow macaw reintroduced with birds from Guyana around 1999 to 2003?
10907.e: On Trinidad, the blue-and-yellow macaw had been almost wiped out by the 1970s. With birds from Guyana, a population was established again in the Nariva Swamp.
10907.m: Thanks to reintroduction, blue-and-yellow macaws live on Trinidad again.

10908.q: In which country is the blue-throated macaw (Ara glaucogularis) endemic?
10908.e: The blue-throated macaw lives only in the Llanos de Moxos in the Beni department of Bolivia. It is considered critically endangered.
10908.m: The blue-throated macaw lives only in Bolivia.

10909.q: Where does the red-fronted macaw nest, since there are hardly any large trees in its dry habitat?
a: In abandoned woodpecker holes in cacti
10909.e: The red-fronted macaw lives in a semi-arid mountain region of Bolivia with cacti and thorn bushes. It breeds in crevices of vertical rock faces.
10909.m: The red-fronted macaw breeds in rock crevices.

10910.q: Why does deforestation in Costa Rica hit the great green macaw especially hard?
a: It depends heavily on one tree species for feeding and breeding
It can only breed in coffee plantations
It needs freshly cleared land to feed
It lives only in conifer forests
10910.e: In Costa Rica, during the breeding season the great green macaw eats mainly fruit of the almendro tree and usually nests in its holes. If this tree is cut down, it loses food and nesting site at the same time.
10910.m: The great green macaw needs the almendro tree.

10911.q: What is the smallest macaw species called?
10911.e: The red-shouldered macaw (Diopsittaca nobilis), also called the dwarf macaw, is the smallest macaw. It is hardly bigger than some parakeets.
10911.m: The red-shouldered macaw is the smallest of all macaws.

10912.q: Who is Lear's macaw named after?
a: The poet and painter Edward Lear
10912.e: Charles Lucien Bonaparte named the species after Edward Lear in 1856. The English poet and painter had earlier painted a very similar parrot.
10912.m: Lear's macaw honours the poet and painter Edward Lear.

10913.q: Where does Lear's macaw breed and sleep in Bahia (Brazil)?
a: In mangrove forests on the coast
10913.e: Lear's macaw lives in the dry Caatinga in north-eastern Bahia. It uses natural holes in sandstone rocks.
10913.m: Lear's macaw lives in sandstone cliffs.

10914.q: How has the population of Lear's macaw developed since the 1980s?
a: It has grown from around 60 to over 1600 birds
It has fallen from around 5000 to 60 birds
It has stayed completely unchanged since 1980
It has died out completely in the wild
10914.e: In 1983 only about 60 Lear's macaws were counted; by 2018 there were already around 1700. This is why the species was downgraded in 2009 from “critically endangered” to “endangered”.
10914.m: Thanks to protection, Lear's macaw has recovered strongly.
